title: Elementary Arabic 2
description: This course builds on the knowledge and skills that students acquire in Elementary Arabic 1 (ARABL-UH 1110) which is a prerequisite course for this class. This is a full semester (or equivalent session) course during which students continue learning formal Arabic (MSA), expand their knowledge of the grammar, build on previously learnt vocabulary, and be exposed to a variety of cultural and daily life themes and situations. It is an interactive course designed to build the student’s abilities in listening, speaking, reading, and writing. At the end of the semester students should be able to read texts on familiar topics and understand the main ideas; speak about themselves and their environment; carry out basic daily life transactions; and initiate and sustain conversations on a variety of topics. Types of tasks and assignments required for this course include daily homework assignments, periodic quizzes, brief presentations, short essay writing, and a final exam. Students joining the course from outside NYU Abu Dhabi are required to take a placement test.

title: Arabic Language and Heritage 1
description: This course is the first in a series of courses meant for students who come from Arabic-speaking families and who grew up in an Arabic-speaking environment but have not had sufficient training in Arabic. These courses are designed to help those students master formal Arabic language skills and empower them, as citizens, to become more engaged in their society, culture, and heritage. The series achieves this goal by reactivating the students’ acquired but dormant knowledge of their native tongue even as it provides new accessible and relevant instruction in the language.

title: Elementary Qur'anic Arabic 1
description: This Introductory course is designed for students who are interested in the language of Qur’an and other cultural aspects related to it. Students will be learning the language through progressive study of the Arabic alphabet, vocabulary, syntax, and interactive conversation. They will learn to speak, read and write basic words and phrases that are commonly used in the Quran and throughout the Arab world in common everyday interaction. Furthermore, they will also be able to enhance their knowledge of the Arab and Muslim peoples and their rich religious, social and cultural life. Verses of chapters will be presented and analyzed; vocabulary and grammatical structures will be discussed, explained, and practiced systematically; and cultural aspects of the Qur’an (i.e. Texts, basic Tajweed, Recitation Styles, etc.) will be introduced through simple and short Arabic readings, audios and videos. This is a content-driven course that integrates language and culture. It is a proficiency-based course, where the four language skills, speaking, listening, reading and writing, are integrated and practiced to simulate real life situations. No prerequisite for this class is required. By the end of this course, students are expected to reach at least the Novice High level of ACTFL proficiency in Arabic.

title: Intermediate Arabic 1
description: This course builds on the knowledge and skills that students acquire in Elementary Arabic 2 This course builds on the knowledge and skills that students acquire in Elementary Arabic 2 (ARABL-UH 1120) which is a prerequisite course for this class. Students joining the course from outside NYU Abu Dhabi are required to take a placement test. This is a full semester (or equivalent session) course during which students continue learning the modern standard form of the language, with limited exposure to phrases and expressions in colloquial. It is a student-centered course where the four language skills (reading, writing, listening and speaking) are integrated along with culture to simulate real life situations. By the end of this course, students should be able to narrate in all verb tenses, describe their daily life, personal relations, and report information. Types of tasks and assignments required include daily homework assignments, periodic quizzes, presentations, essays, and a final exam.

title: Colloquial Arabic: Levantine Dialect 1
description: This course complements the student’s knowledge of Standard Arabic to include proficiency in Levantine Arabic, one of the major Arabic dialects, with emphasis on daily life tasks, conversational fluency, and cultural sensibility. A prerequisite for this class is Intermediate Arabic 201 (ARABL-UH 2110) or an equivalent proficiency level determined through a placement test. This is a full semester conversation-based course during which students focus on the communicative skills, and develop automated production skills necessary to function in an Arabic speaking environment. It is designed to build student’s abilities in listening and speaking. At the end of the semester students should be able to use the Shami dialect to participate actively in conversations by using linguistic and cultural expressions to make requests, express, and describe preferences. Tasks and assignments required for this course include daily homework, periodic quizzes, weekly oral entries, presentation skits, oral film summary, oral interviews, a homestay, and an oral final exam.

title: Literature & Methodology of Costume Studies
description: An introduction to foundation literature and research methodologies in costume studies. Includes sessions on academic writing, interpretation of material culture, the use of visual and literary sources, theories of fashion, and the role of museum and gallery exhibitions in furthering scholarship in this field. The course requires written work in diverse formats as well as presentations that prepare students for subsequent coursework.

title: Research in Costume Studies
description: This course provides guidance on process and methodology in preparation for the thesis. Students define the subject of their thesis research, share their work in progress, and participate in discussions, working sessions, and critiques. By the end of the semester, students will have completed several crucial steps in the thesis process including bibliography, proposal, and outline.

school: Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development - Graduate
title: Case Studies in Fashion History: Prehistory to 1800
description: Traces the evolution of dress from early body practices to the rise of consumer culture during the 18th century through topics including clothing as signifier of status and morality; the mechanics of the clothing trades and the impact of technology; trends and personalities; the politicization of dress during the French Revolution. The class considers the materiality of clothing and accessories and the relationship between dress and the body. Through lectures, discussions, and projects students are encouraged to seek their individual concentration in the field.

sections.notes: Priority for Costume Studies Students. Open to non-majors with permission code. Please write to artadvising@nyu.edu with questions regarding class information or issues with registration.

school: Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development - Graduate
title: 20th Century Fashion
description: Examines the evolution of fashionable dress and practices from 1900 to the 1980s, investigating high style as well as mainstream fashion, changing materials and silhouette, and the interplay between fashion and the arts. Original research via primary materials including museum objects, periodicals, designer archives, and film is emphasized, as the class explores the dynamics of dress in the international culture of the 20th century through lectures, readings and discussions.

sections.notes: Costume Studies Students only. Please write to artadvising@nyu.edu with questions regarding class information or issues with registration.

school: Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development - Graduate
title: History of Textiles: The Modern Era
description: Investigates textiles in terms of design, creation, marketing, and use from the 19th century to present. With particular attention to the rapid technological advances of the past two centuries, visual and structural analysis of objects is combined with consideration of historical developments to situate textiles in the context of the surrounding culture. Includes object examination sessions at the Ratti Textile Center at the Metropolitan Museum as well as other New York collections.

sections.notes: Costume Studies students only. Please write to artadvising@nyu.edu with questions regarding class information or issues with registration.

description: Internships can take place in a variety of settings including museums, galleries, publishers, foundations, fashion houses, libraries, archives and other institutions. description: This project-based course explores contemporary curatorial practice and its application to the display and interpretation of fashion. Through the development of an original and timely topic, students co-curate an exhibition, participating in all aspects of mounting and staging the exhibition along with producing the related research, text, and supporting programming.

school: Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development - Graduate
title: History of Fashion Photo
description: Traces the development of fashion photography in relation to contemporary fashion, aesthetic influence, photographic styles and techniques, cultural customs and commercial needs. Fashion photography is more than a medium dedicated to commerce: it is a record of artistic movements, ideals of beauty, and social trends. The course begins in the early 20th century with the growth of periodicals devoted to fashion and continues through the work of the present day.

school: Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development - Undergraduate
title: History of Fashion Photography
description: Photography is an indispensable component of fashion. It is both a persuasive tool for selling clothing and accessories and a record of artistic movements, expressions of beauty, gender and social trends. This course traces the development of fashion photography in relation to contemporary fashion, aesthetic influence, photographic styles and techniques, cultural customs and commercial needs. It begins in the 1920s with the growth of periodicals devoted to fashion and continues through the work of the present day.

title: Fashion in Context
description: Why do fashion designers and brands exert such influence in contemporary society? What explains the trajectory from The House of Worth to Chanel to this season’s hottest label? This course investigates the interlocking forces shaping fashion: the designer system, celebrities, technology, politics, the arts and media. Through lectures and film viewings, readings, discussions, and individual research, students explore fashion as a crucial aspect of culture and how the fashion system evolved from roots in Parisian couture to become a global phenomenon. Liberal Arts Core/MAP Equivalent - satisfies the requirement for Expressive Cultures for Steinhardt students.

title: Fashion Exhibitions and Making
description: Fashion exhibitions play a crucial role in preserving cultural heritage, showcasing design innovation, and fostering creativity. They expand knowledge and offer insight into historical, social, and political contexts and illustrate how fashion reflects and influences society. This course offers students tools for interpreting fashion exhibitions and a behind-the-scenes lens into making them. It also prompts students to think about different sites for fashion curation and display: from art museums, to commercial galleries, to store windows.

sections.notes: Open to all undergraduate students. | Prerequisites: How to Analyze Fashion (ARCS-UE 1098) OR Fashion in Context (ARCS-UE 1088). Please email artadvising@nyu.edu with questions regarding class information or issues with registration.

title: How to: (analyze) Fashion
description: This course is a how-to manual for students who are interested in fashion, but don’t know how to explore it. It offers a toolbox of theoretical concepts, interdisciplinary scholarship, and historical and contemporary case studies. Students learn to ask questions like: How is taste mapped onto bodies in social space? Who works in fashion, and how is this work classified? How do images and clothes (both new and old) circulate around the globe? What does the science of sustainability look like? And, where is the body in fashion’s new digital imaginaries? Meets Steinhardt Lib Arts Core for Expressive Cultures

title: Art Money
description: This course explores different ways artists have interacted with money, in choosing a subject, dealing with the marketplace, and formulating life choices. The course combines theory and studio practice with lecture and discussion and includes art critiques with an active critical engagement. For each of the seven topic units, students may do art projects as well as present or write responses. Open to studio artists in any discipline, those interested in critical theory or art history, and those engaged in arts administration.

title: Arts in Sickness and in Health
description: This course explores bodily transitions across the lifespan through art, writing, performance, and ritual alongside medical and public health perspectives. Students examine the medical gaze, illness narratives, stigma, and the politics of visibility. The course also studies pregnancy, disability, aging, and dying as moments of new embodied knowledge. Through analysis and creative work, students learn how cultural forms can challenge medical authority and restore agency and dignity to lived bodily experience.

title: Interdisciplinary Projects: Articulating The Visual Arts
description: Articulating Visual Arts is designed to help students express & sharpen their thinking & writing about visual art. Topics will include how to write an artist’s statement, exhibit reviews as well as catalog essays. Additionally students will explore how artists apply creativity, in thinking & writing, as part of their practice in visual arts & other media. Readings include texts by contemporary & past visual arts masters such as Frieda Kahlo, Richard Prince, Robert Smithson, Andy Warhol, Barbara Kruger, among others.

title: Interdisciplinary Projects: Contemporary Art Practice
description: This course is constructed around the belief that artists are highly adaptable & flexible, & that their role in an arts community (& the community at large) is fundamental to their practice. To that end, this intensive MFA-only course will serve as a communal laboratory investigating the meaning of “contemporary practice.” The course will pose the question: how does a young artist find community in the art world? As a result, the course is cursory experiment in community building.

title: What is Art?
description: This introductory class explores the nature and value of the arts through an examination of aesthetic theory, select art movements and their context and through hands-on projects that acquaint students, in an embodied fashion, with how artists make meaning. It considers art’s powers and limits, its benefits and potential dangers, the nature of artistic mediums and unpacks the mechanisms through which art communicates a particular vision. At the end of this course, students will be able to define and utilize key terms and concepts particular to the visual arts, and able to create compelling and researched arguments that synthesize theoretical, historical, iconographical and technical frameworks. They will also be able to perform in-depth analysis of artworks and visual media and create and defend their own artworks. Prerequisite: None. title: Foundations in Visual Arts
description: Foundations in Visual Arts introduces students to the basic elements of art making and visual art terminology through hands-on experimentation with materials supplemented by tutorials, workshops, and lectures. Students will work on various projects that explore line, shape, form, space, light/value, color, texture, across 2D and 3D forms. In the process, they will also examine artistic media and genres through a conceptual and critical lens. Foundations in Visual Arts gives students an overview of how basic principles in concert with different media, subjects, ideas and techniques, create meaning in the visual arts. After completing this course students will be able to: demonstrate basic proficiency in drawing and painting using graphite, pen, and acrylic, gain a basic knowledge of color, and be able to plan and execute simple 3D constructions using casting methods, cardboard, wire and paper-mache. Prerequisite: None. Anti-requisite: ART-SHU 310/9210 Introduction to Studio Art Fulfillment: General Elective.

title: Actions and Gestures - Embodied Media as Performance Art
description: What is performance? How do we make embodied art in our technologically mediated world? These questions will guide us as we create performance art in conversation with archival theory, film, new media, and scientific research. Students will encounter the works of Yoko Ono, Marina Abramovic, Joseph Beuys, Laurie Anderson, Adrian Piper, Robert Wilson, Tehching Hsieh, Chris Burden and other pioneers of the genre of performance art. This course will delve deeply into investigating the cultural and technological contexts that inform contemporary performative practices. Students will create their own works using bodies in spaces, archival collection methods, image-capture technologies, and post-production tools to explore the art of performance in the phygital realm. At the end of semester students will organize a performance festival to share their final projects with the campus community. No performance or technological experience necessary. Prerequisite: None. Fulfillment: general elective

title: Foundations in Painting: Painting in Practice and Theory
description: Painting is a remarkable medium whose dynamic evolution across cultures and through millennia continues up until the present. In this class, students will get an introduction to the basic technical, formal, and conceptual principles of painting while exploring how contemporary practitioners are utilizing the medium to address contemporary concerns. Using watercolor, gouache, and acrylic, students will learn about color theory, composition, texture, form, and surface. Through select readings, students will also examine the theoretical questions and historical precedents that have informed painting’s development, analyze the work of historical and contemporary painters and be able to see how their own practice connects to larger art historical and societal concerns. In addition to acquiring basic technical skills and conceptual know-how, students will also gain competency in art critiques and writing artist statements. Prerequisite: None. Fulfillment: general elective

description: This two-point course introduces the fundamental concepts of contemporary dance. Through movement exploration, imitation, and memorization based on Graham technique, students gain an appreciation for the expressive and dynamic capacity of the body. In addition to body work, students learn and perform contemporary dances. It is highly suggested that one has previous dance experience before enrolling. Prerequisite: None. description: This two-point introductory class explores and builds foundational skills for different genres of dance. Through movement sequences, short dances and creative activities, students build up muscle strength, increase coordination, flexibility, balance, and stamina as well as improve their kinesthetic memory, musicality, and knowledge of their own bodies. In addition, imagery and visualization prompts will be used to foster creative experimentation in movement. Prerequisite: None. Fulfillment: General Elective. Repeat rule: Non-Repeatable. description: No prerequisite. The purpose of this studio course is to fully participate in the creative process through movement exploration, setting choreography and engaging in live performance. With a focus on space, quality, aesthetics, alignment, and musicality as well as practicing learning strategies within a duet/group context, students apply their understanding and utilize their training in personal, artistic expression. Students who have had one or more dance classes are encouraged to enroll. Fulfillment: This course counts toward the Cross-School Dance Minor hosted by Tisch School of the Arts at NYU. title: Dances of Northern China
description: This course focuses, through dance, on the embodiment of the minority folk cultures of Northern China. Each semester, students will focus on two folk dances from Yanbian, Xinjiang, or Inner Mongolia. These dances were created by Korean, Uyghur, and Mongolian people. Students will explore the forms of these dances as well as the culture, religion, history influencing the creation of these dance forms. Students with previous dance experience are encouraged to enroll. Prerequisite: None. Fulfillment: This course counts toward the Cross-School Dance Minor hosted by Tisch School of the Arts at NYU. title: Chinese Woodblock Printmaking: A Socially Engaged Graphic Art Form
description: Woodblock printmaking in China occupies a unique and profound place in the history of Chinese visual culture – both reflective of and linked to various political, social, and cultural movements. In this transdisciplinary course, we will explore making our own woodblock prints while investigating the historical conditions that led to the emergence of woodcut as a modern and socially engaged graphic art from the early 20th century to our contemporary time. Students will learn foundational techniques, forms, and applications of relief prints (stamps and woodblock prints) as well as contemporary approaches (using digital tools and equipment) in order to gain a deeper understanding of the art form. This hands-on approach and artistic experimentation will be accompanied by research into woodblock printmaking history, focusing on its revaluation and development in Shanghai, between 1927 and 1932 – directly supported by the writer Lu Xun 魯迅 – through applications during the Cultural Revolution, 1968-76, to the second wave of renewal starting in the 1980s. Prerequisite: None Fulfillment: IMA elective; IMB major IMA/B elective; GCS Major elective Chinese Media, Arts, and Literature elective.

title: Photography 1: Framing Reality
description: We are constantly engaged with photographic images in our contemporary lives, both from a production and a consumption perspective. During this course, we will unpack the various layers of affect hidden within the act of image making with lens based media. In this project-based course students can expect to gain an introduction to photography as an artistic medium through hands-on technical and conceptual experimentation. Students will learn to shoot, edit, and print digital photographs using professional photographic equipment and softwares. Additionally, the course will help students develop critical perspectives by engaging theoretical texts that inform the study of photography as a contemporary artform. During group critiques, students will also learn how to articulate and iterate on conceptual ideas based on peer feedback – by the end of the course, students will have developed a small body of work grounded in critical thought and historical knowledge of contemporary photography. Prerequisite: None. Fulfillment: general elective

description: Few art forms exert as much influence today as comics and graphic novels as visual culture is becoming increasingly flattened, demolishing long-established boundaries between high and low. Incorporating figuration, narrative, complex spatial and cinematic strategies, and forms also pioneered by the avant-gardes, sequential art has risen to a level of unprecedented complexity. But what can it teach painting? This class seeks to establish a dialogue between these connected but mostly disparate disciplines, cross-pollinating their formal and conceptual concerns.

description: This course serves to familiarize the student with the fundamentals of typography. Typography forms the basis of our contemporary communication. Students will gain design abilities based on analogue techniques as well as digital software. The class explores letterform design & moves subsequently to typesetting exercises performed using the letterpress printer & computer. Compositions exploring typography as color, form, & image will be examined for visual impact as well as meaning. The history of typography is incorporated beginning with Guttenberg in the 1400’s through the classic designers of the 17th & 18th centuries, type-design through Russian Constructivism, the Bauhaus, & Modernism to contemporary digital type design.

Students gain the skills and confidence to express their artistic objectives in critical writing, art making, and verbal analysis through presentations, works of art generated through research, and written statements about their artistic objectives.

title: Drawing I for Non-Majors
description: A process-oriented studio art class that takes place in and around Villa LaPietra. Perception and gaze are the fundamentals for the production and reception of drawings. Students will learn to differentiate between ‘customary perception’ (what one thinks he sees) and aesthetic perception’ (what one actually sees). Students will develop basic drawing skills including the use of line, proportion, contrast and perspective while exploring mark-making with different drawing mediums such as pencil, charcoal and ink. Along with the production of drawings, students will discuss their own work as well as the artworks of fellow students. Readings, slide shows and museum visits support the studio practice and enhance critical reception. Groundwork for the development of an individual drawing style will be set. Regular drawing exercises and attendance are crucial to succeeding in the class.

description: The course is focused on photography as an art and photography as a means of communication. It includes aspects of history and the theory of photography and practical photographic education of classic analog/wet darkroom process — i.e. black and white photographic image making and printing. The goal is to develop a new way of seeing through the viewfinder of the camera and to hone critical thinking about photography. This course aims to teach students to experience the photographic works of art and reflect on that experience. Importance is laid on students’ understanding of the photographic image as a means of expressing an individual artistic attitude towards the world.

school: Steinhardt School of Culture, Education, and Human Development - Undergraduate
title: Art: Practice & Ideas
description: 'Art: Practice and Ideas' examines key developments in the visual arts from modernity to the present. Focusing on the ways in which representations both create and reflect the values of a society, the course introduces students to the full range of expressive possibilities within the visual arts, covering painting and sculpture, as well as photography, film, video, conceptual art, and computer media. Topics to be covered include classical, modern, and postmodern relationships to politics, vision, the mind, the body, psychology, gender, difference, and technological innovation. Students will see and understand how artists have integrated perceptions of their historical moment, as well as physical and social space, into creative practices that have, in turn, had a significant impact on the culture of the time. The course is structured around group discussions and in-class writing, beginning with an exploration of artist writings and personal essays, focusing on voice, description, structure, and research. Students learn to distinguish between an essay and an academic paper, examining how personal experience can inform critical discussions around art, culture, society, and politics. Students draft and revise their thesis essays.

Emphasizing how contemporary art is experienced across various contexts, the class features meetings with artists, curators, directors, and other professionals working in the New York art world.

description: This course examines the current developments in contemporary art over the past decade – the art of ‘now’ – from the viewpoint of an artist’s practice & working ideas, looking at current global art production in aesthetic, economic, & social contexts. The major movements in painting, photography, sculpture, installation & performance are examined. Readings will be drawn from first hand interviews & point-of-view accounts, reviews, & critique; a major emphasis on interviews & online studio visits will accompany the texts. Guest artist lectures & off-site museum & gallery viewings will complement the weekly visual presentations & theory conversations. title: Global Histories of Art
description: Designed for art students, this lecture course spans a range of histories from across the globe and challenges how we view, understand, and approach concepts of time, globality, and history. We examine canons, works, and phenomena traditionally excluded from art history focusing on key concepts like image, space, material, text, and ritual in artistic practice. Weekly studies of diverse objects and practices explore cultural, historical, and social contexts that shape art. Draws on multiple disciplines, aiming to connect historical periods with contemporary art.

title: Foundations of Art History
description: This course introduces students to the skills and concepts they will need in order to develop a meaningful engagement with the visual arts and art history as a global discipline. Rather than providing a chronological survey of great works, it covers examples and perspectives from a wide array of regions, periods, and societies. title: Roman Art/Art Under Roman Occupation
description: The history of the people who lived in Rome and under Roman occupation spans over 1500 years, from ca. 750 BCE to 750 CE. It covers creative communities documented in archaeological and textual remains spread across three continents (Europe, Africa and Asia), crisscrossing lands and riding the currents of multiple rivers, seas and the eastern Atlantic Ocean. The Colosseum, the Pantheon, the marble and gilt bronze statuary of empire and much more testify to an extraordinary period and geography of visual, material and spatial creativity. In part for these reasons, the study of “Roman art” has itself held a central place in the humanities generally and in the discipline of Art History specifically. Yet the field is fraught; Roman art is tainted with imperialism and colonialism, and its promulgation in European and American curricula has fostered supremacist tendencies as much as it has underpinned aesthetics and philosophy. So, we must ask, what does it mean for something to be Roman, and what does a canon of Roman art look like? How can we reach beyond the politics of empire-building to see what people in these places and moments experienced as they created and activated the materials of daily life in such a world? This is a survey, but it is not an ordinary survey of Roman art. We will take 20 specific object—from small silver cups to colossal marble temples—and pull them apart to uncover the people they touched, the ways their presences ramified and what they may reveal about being Roman…and not being Roman.

sections.topic: Portable Luxuries in the Medieval World
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Portable Luxuries in the Medieval World. No prerequisites. This lecture course focuses on small, lightweight, or otherwise moveable materials and objects considered expensive or costly by the interconnected societies of Afro-Eurasia during the Middle Ages: gold, silver, and copper; enamelwork; ivory; silk and wool textiles; ceramics; gemstones; glass and rock crystal; and miniature paintings. Intersecting art and economic history, it traces how medieval objects were treated as both art and commodities; how medieval artists were linked by and dependent upon long-distance trade routes; and how medieval patrons manifested their wealth and power through the materiality of images. Throughout the term, we will reflect upon the different ways materials are assigned value (their specific cultural significance, through exchange, and/or the need for skillful artistic manipulation); how luxury wealth and art-making are moralized; and the relationship of luxury and portability to practices of diplomatic gift-giving. Readings will include theoretical texts and secondary scholarship paired with short primary sources. Museum visits will provide the opportunity to discuss objects firsthand.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Raphael Reimagined. No prerequisites. Recommended Prerequisite: Completion of ARTH-UA 10 (Foundations of Art History) and/or ARTH-UA 5 (Renaissance Art) are recommended as a valuable introduction. The School of Athens, The Triumph of Galatea, his divine Madonnas – Raphael’s painted visions create the illusion of the suspension of earthly time. While his works hardly show their age, Raphael (1483–1520) had his life cut short at the age of thirty-seven. The year 2020 marked the 500th anniversary of his death and inspired a series of international exhibitions (in his hometown of Urbino, Berlin, Rome, Washington, and London) celebrating a prolific artistic output that belies its maker’s all-too-brief career. Our class will take advantage of Raphael’s quincentenary celebration here in New York, in the form of a once-in-a-lifetime Raphael exhibition at The Met from March 29 to June 28, 2026. The Met’s Raphael: Sublime Poetry takes new stock of his career as painter, draftsman, architect, archaeologist, tapestry designer, and poet. We will do the same in our course with an eye to reevaluating Raphael’s most important artistic relationships, friendships, and rivalries – including a remarkable exchange of art works with Albrecht Dürer. Among our discussion topics will be Raphael’s artistic roots and the roles played by older Umbrian masters such as Pietro Perugino and Luca Signorelli (and Leonardo and Michelangelo in Florence) on his artistic formation; his collaborations with Bramante, Marcantonio Raimondi, Raffaellino del Colle, Giulio Romano, Perino del Vaga and Polidoro da Caravaggio; and his artistic legacy in Rome during and following the papacies of Julius II and Leo X. Throughout, we will attempt to situate Raphael’s’ life and career within their broader socio-political, economic, sacred, and historical contexts. To this end, our readings and discussions will address related topics, such as: the possibilities of printmaking to disseminate an artist’s inventions and fame; the study of ancient art as impetus for a new modern style; aspects of antiquarianism; theories and concepts of urbanism; and Raphael and Michelangelo as understood through the double-lens of veneration and competition. Issues of representation will be examined within the frameworks of a variety of critical approaches, ranging from iconography and reception to visual poetics and material culture. *** Students are strongly encouraged to take advantage of The Met’s unprecedented Raphael exhibition (March 29–June 28, 2026) as the ideal introduction to and preparation for the course. A number of objects traveling for the show will be seen in the U.S. for the first time in their history.

title: Medieval Art in Europe and the Transcultural Mediterranean
description: This course offers a broad introduction to the architecture, pictorial arts, and visual and material culture of the European Middle Ages in the Greek-speaking East, Latin West, and transcultural Mediterranean c. 250–1450 CE. It provides an overview of the concepts, developments, and vocabulary necessary for analyzing and understanding the arts of the medieval period in light of the historical, religious, social, cultural, conceptual, and esthetic contexts and of their production and reception. Topics to be examined include the creation of a vocabulary of medieval imagery and architectural forms; uses of and attitudes toward the classical tradition; art and its makers, patrons, and audiences; materials and techniques of medieval art-making; the arts of religious and devotional practice; the relationships of word and image; the imaginative, multisensory, and performative dimensions of medieval art and architecture; medieval cultural exchange and colonization; art and ideologies; the relationship between art and nature; and the functions of and controversies concerning images in the medieval world. Readings include significant primary sources as well as secondary sources that offer a range of approaches to the interpretation and analysis of medieval art, architecture, and visual culture. Museum visits will provide the opportunity to discuss objects firsthand.

title: Modern Architecture
description: This course offers a historical survey of the built environment from 1800 to the present. Starting with the intensification of global interconnectivity in the 19th century, we will explore the role of architecture and urbanism since 1800 through themes such as industrialization, colonialism, orientalism, nationalism, fascism, post-colonialism, imperialism, and war. Rather than a Eurocentric reading of the past two centuries, which offers a narrative of modernity as an invention of the West that was then adopted by the rest of the world, we will recognize modernity as a global condition and a way of understanding the human condition and the built environment of the past two centuries. Global in scope, the course provides a chronological and thematic account of the technologies, socio-economic forces, aesthetic impulses and collective desires that have shaped the built environment. Particular attention will be given to the fraught relationship between modernity and imperialism; the rise and fall of ‘modernism’ as a specific set of design methods and discursive strategies; non-Western modernisms; and interfaces between architecture and other artistic disciplines. Furthermore, this course traces the interactions and exchanges of architectural styles and ideas in a highly connected modern world, in order to understand the ways in which diverse societies translated ideas, appropriated forms and styles from distant geographies and cultures, and used architecture and design to respond to socio-political changes.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Social History of Photography. Prerequisite: ARTH-UA 10 Foundations of Art History; or ARTH-UA 2 History of Western Art II; or ARTH-UA 6 Modern Art; or a score of 5 on the AP Art History exam; or permission of the instructor. Students who do not have the prerequisite, but who have taken other art history courses or courses in relevant fields are encouraged to contact the instructor directly. This class is not a "typical" chronological survey of the history of photography, or a discussion of photography as an art form. Although we all acknowledge that photographers can be artists, any vision of the medium that limits its function strictly to an aesthetic arena is missing the Big Picture. Photography’s various forms and functions permeate all levels of modern society, shaping and reflecting our understanding of the world and thus influencing every aspect of our daily lives. The camera is an image-making tool that has transformed the nature of all modern perception and communication, most recently in this digital age. These premises are the basic assumptions underlying this course, and my lectures will aim at opening your eyes to the range and influence of photographic imagery, both "high" and "low" art, in modern visual culture. The year-long sequence is divided into two parts. Part I (Social History of Photography), taught in the Fall semester, emphasizes the ways in which various kinds of photographic images have changed our perceptions of ourselves, our society and the world in which we live. The lecture topics have been planned thematically rather than chronologically, a format that emphasizes certain ideas that I feel are particularly important. Part II (Aesthetic History of Photography), which will be offered in the Spring, is a chronological survey of "art" photography, and the lectures will describe the ways in which the aesthetic tradition has developed in relation to other fine art forms like painting, sculpture and film. Taken together, Parts I and II offer a broad and rich overview of the various forms and functions of photography in modern society.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Abex to Pop. No prerequisites. Chronologically, this course covers the time period from the rise of Abstract Expressionism in the 1940s through the development of Pop Art and Minimalism in the 1960s and early 1970s. In North America, this evolution is complicated by a renewal of geometric abstraction concurrent with Abstract Expressionism and by the catalytic role of Neo-Dada (especially the work of Jasper Johns) as a starting point for both Pop Art and Minimalism. Twenty years ago, it seemed reasonable to assume that the important art of this period was mostly made in the United States. Since then, however, numerous exhibitions and publications have demonstrated that the European, Latin American, East Asian and South Asian avant-gardes of this era demand attention on par with art from the United States. This course will therefore follow the intertwined art histories of all of these regions. It will also examine the long-overlooked contributions of Black and women artists.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Environments, Situations, Spaces: Neo-Avantgarde Models (Re-)Cast in the Present. Prerequisite: ARTH-UA 10 Foundations of Art History; or ARTH-UA 2 History of Western Art II; or ARTH-UA 6 Modern Art; or a score of 5 on the AP Art History exam; or permission of the instructor. Students who do not have the prerequisite, but who have taken other art history courses or courses in relevant fields are encouraged to contact the instructor directly. Taking the view that intelligent, dynamic exhibition concepts have the potential to provoke innovation for artists, curators, and audiences alike, this course focuses on game-changing propositions, definitions, exhibitions, and installations from past and recent decades. Examining the first breaks away from the discrete art object—that is, paintings and sculptures, understood as individual entities—room-scale projects have progressed outward, into the streets, thence to other, radically diverse sites, and, still more recently, to multiple platforms generated by and in cyberspace, we trace a history that continually redefines the conceptual, physical, as well as political/ideological scope of what we consider to be art. Our course research and learning will run the gamut of scholarly and curatorial activity, from visiting permanent installations and current exhibitions in New York, viewing documentary footage of landmark shows, and reading analytical texts by artists and curators on different models/approaches. We will be considering how the exponential expansion of art into unprecedented spaces, actual or virtual, and how such spheres of innovation are often accompanied by methodological revision. A combination of reading and active fieldwork will help us visualize the kaleidoscopic shifting of ideas that have so often rendered art’s incremental formal breakthroughs harbingers of a broader grasp of the visual “reality” of (a) given time—past and present. A key project/assignment includes stepping into the role of curator and using the course readings and site visits to conceive of an exhibition of your own.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Intro to African American Art. No prerequisites. This course will examine the major concepts and themes central to the study of African American art and the visual culture of the larger African Diaspora from the late 18th century to the contemporary moment. The African Diaspora refers to subjects of African descent outside of the continent of Africa and the various factors that inform our understanding of this cultural construction. We will investigate the fashioning of African Diasporic subjects across various artistic practices including the decorative arts, works on paper, painting, sculpture, photography, and installation. The major issues addressed will include the Black Atlantic, syncretism, the New Negro, Black modernism, and the limits of visibility. Case studies will focus on works that show how the visual represents, regulates, and generates African American and African Diasporic identities of the past and present.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: History of Spanish Art 1898-Present. No prerequisites. This class will survey the major artists, movements, and institutions that shaped Spanish art from the end of the nineteenth century to the present. Centered around some of Spain's most prominent artists and architects, including Antoni Gaudí, Pablo Picasso, Joan Miró, Luis Buñuel, Salvador Dalí, Maruja Mallo, Antoni Tàpies, Equipo Crónica, Pedro Almodóvar, and Ocaña, we will explore such issues as: the reception of European avant-gardes, the debate between "pure" and "social" art, the use of history and myth in the construction of national artistic styles, notions of “center” and “periphery,” the impact of political shifts including the Spanish Civil War, Dictatorship and transition to democracy, and recent work by contemporary artists and activists. The contexts in which artists trained and showed their works will be explored including art academies, galleries, exhibitions, museums, and cafés which were spaces for the formation of artistic identities. This class will be a combination of lecture and discussion. Much of the material presented in the lectures will not appear in your readings, so it is absolutely vital that you come to class and take notes. Discussion is equally important since many of the artists and concepts that we study may be unfamiliar to you and are not usually included in surveys of modern art or Iberian literature.

It will examine how Asian and diaspora artists work between local, regional and global currents to broaden the narrative of art history. The subject of study includes a range of media including painting, printmaking, photography, video, installations, sculpture and new media.

title: Modern Art in Europe and America
description: Art in the Western world from the late 18th century to the present. Content includes the neoclassicism and romanticism of David, Goya, Ingres, Turner, Delacroix; the realism of Courbet; the impressionists; parallel developments in architecture; the new sculptural tradition of Rodin; post-impressionism to fauvism, expressionism, futurism, cubism, geometric abstraction in sculpture and painting, modernism in architecture in the 20th century, and after the First World War, dadaism and surrealism. Also covers developments since 1945, such as action painting, pop art, minimal art, and numerous strands of postmodernism. Study of the collections of the Metropolitan Museum of Art, the Museum of Modern Art, the Guggenheim Museum, and the Whitney Museum of American Art is included.

title: History of Architecture: Antiquity to Present
description: Introduction to the history of Western architecture, emphasizing the formal, structural, programmatic, and contextual aspects of selected major monuments from ancient times to the present. Monuments discussed include the Parthenon, the Roman Pantheon, Hagia Sophia, the cathedral at Chartres, St. Peter's, Palladio's Villa Rotonda, St. Paul's Cathedral, Versailles, the London Crystal Palace, Frank Lloyd Wright's Fallingwater, Le Corbusier's Villa Savoye, the Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao, Mies van der Rohe's Barcelona Pavilion, and others. Lectures analyze monuments within their contexts of time and place. Also considers aspects of city planning in relation to certain monuments and to the culture and events of their time.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Affordable Housing. PERMISSION OF PROFESSOR MOSETTE BRODERICK OR PROFESSOR JON RITTER IS MANDATORY FOR ENROLLMENT. Prerequisite: ARTH-UA 601 History of Architecture: Antiquity to Present AND ARTH-UA 661 Shaping the Urban Environment. This course counts for Seminar credit for Urban Design and Architecture Studies majors. Housing is shelter and much more. It is the basic building block of neighborhoods, communities and cities. The creation of Affordable Housing, Sustainable Communities and Livable Cities has been the topic of numerous books, worldwide conferences, and serious research and study by architects, urban designers, planners, environmental psychologists, sociologists, real estate professionals, economists and legal professionals in universities, governmental institutes, professional organizations and the United Nations. The architect’s role in the creation of housing today is an important one. Achieving truly affordable housing however, requires a complex team of real estate professionals and government, along with private and public participation and cooperation. The course will look at Affordable Housing through a combination of illustrated lectures, Guest lecturers, and site visits in an attempt to understand not only the planning and architecture of Affordable Housing, but also the history, new technology, culture, humanity and opportunities in the creation of Housing, Neighborhoods, Sustainable Communities and Livable Cities. Most importantly, it will demonstrate the enormous commitment required to participate in the solution of the housing problem in our communities, our cities, our nation and the world.

title: Shaping The Urban Environment

Special attention is given to real estate development, landmark preservation, city planning, and community participation in New York City.

title: Urban Design: Infrastructure
description: Serves as a laboratory for the investigation of New York City's infrastructure, using the definition of the word as a point of departure. In what ways can the city be perceived as a collective undertaking, with intricate components interwoven in continuous strands? What systems and forces give the city and its neighborhoods their current form, and what influences their future shape? Can these systems be dissected? What do these analyses tell us about the relationship of the city to its inhabitants and to the wider environment? Through lectures, reading assignments, discussions, and field trips, we investigate some of the major components of the city's infrastructure, such as the street grid, water supply, waste disposal, and subway system.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Prime Media: The diagrammatic, the ‘indeterminate’ score, events and other post-musical/linguistic composition models . DEPARTMENTAL CONSENT REQUIRED TO ENROLL. Open only to departmental majors who have completed five 4-credit art history courses. Students who do not have the prerequisite, but who have taken other art history courses or courses in relevant fields are encouraged to contact the instructor directly. In many ways the 1960s clarified the historical criteria for the 20th/21st century. Introducing text-, instruction-, and information-based strategies, along with a pivotal deployment of real-time, rupturing the single medium through a field of radical multiplicity. In this course, we will examine the crystallization of these ideas through what I call “prime media:” formal matrices of mediation, that are not the art itself, but which imply that art no longer coincides with a single object, but instead, procedures through which a perceiver-initiated realization comes into being. A major point of departure is the compendium by composer La Monte Young, An Anthology of chance operations (1963). In this landmark collection, 27 composers, poets, artists, choreographers, and other largely uncategorizable figures presented work articulated almost entirely in textual form. We will trace how this actively exploratory field would extend through key initiatives of sixties/seventies art—now integral to the art-historical canon that has come to constitute those decades—Fluxus, Minimalism, Conceptual Art, and Institutional Critique, among others.

sections.topic: The Complex Career of Agnes Varda
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: The Complex Career of Agnes Varda. INSTRUCTOR CONSENT REQUIRED TO ENROLL. Open only to departmental majors who have completed five 4-credit art history courses. Students who do not have the prerequisite, but who have taken other art history courses or courses in relevant fields are encouraged to contact the instructor directly. All interested students MUST send a message (at least one paragraph) via email to Professor Rice PRIOR TO REGISTERING FOR THIS SEMINAR containing a rationale for your wanting to take the course, any courses that you have had in the past that qualify you for admission as well as any other relevant experiences. NO STUDENT MAY MATRICULATE WITHOUT THE PERMISSION OF THE INSTRUCTOR. This seminar will be a study of the complex career of French filmmaker Agnes Varda (1928-2019), one of the most celebrated and original filmmakers of the 20th and 21st centuries. Beginning as a still photographer, she explored various ways to expand the frozen image in time and space and then moved on to film. Having seen few movies and having had no education in the medium, she was nevertheless quickly recognized as one of the first and defining artists of the French New Wave by the 1950s. Focusing often on women’s issues, on social stresses embedded in the most mundane aspects of daily life, and on political problems like homelessness, global consumption and hunger, she created narratives that explored the lived experiences of characters caught in the web of history. Moving between documentary, fiction and autobiography, she demolished the barriers between these genres as well as the barriers between the public and the private, the objective and the subjective. Late in life, needing a new challenge, she moved into the visual arts – she became a “plasticienne” and created installations, sculptures, filmic tableaux and everything in between, showing her work in museums, in galleries and at festivals worldwide. This class will examine the tri-part career of this extraordinary woman, focusing on her astonishing originality, her recurring themes and the singular creative vision that managed, in spite of the diversity of her work, to breathe life into everything that she did.

sections.topic: By Herself: Women Artists in Early Modern Europe
sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: By Herself: Women Artists in Early Modern Europe. DEPARTMENTAL CONSENT REQUIRED TO ENROLL. Open only to departmental majors who have completed five 4-credit art history courses. Students who do not have the prerequisite, but who have taken other art history courses or courses in relevant fields are encouraged to contact the instructor directly. This discussion-driven seminar aims to trace the lives and careers of pioneering women artists working north and south of the Alps, from the late fifteenth to the seventeenth centuries. Our main protagonists will include celebrated virtuose such as Sofonisba Anguissola, Lavinia Fontana, Artemisia Gentileschi, and Judith Leyster alongside perhaps less familiar names such as Properzia de’Rossi; Plautilla Nelli; Catharina van Hemessen; Fede Galizia; Giovanna Garzoni; Elisabetta Sirani; Maria Sibylla Merian; and Luisa Roldán. In addition to our study of these exceptional figures’ artistic production, we will range broadly to address themes that include notions of fame; entrepreneurship and the business of art; the history of science and medicine; sexuality, gender, and the human body; motherhood, art, and the rituals of childbirth; the lives of wives and widows; female patrons, collectors, and connoisseurs; and women’s agency and self-fashioning in the early modern period.

Requires Department Consent
Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Art, Empire, and Colonialism. DEPARTMENTAL CONSENT REQUIRED TO ENROLL. Open only to departmental majors who have completed five 4-credit art history courses. Students who do not have the prerequisite, but who have taken other art history courses or courses in relevant fields are encouraged to contact the instructor directly. Focusing on art’s capacity to reveal stories of protagonists and places often less visible in textual archives, this seminar explores the role of representation, artistic agency, embodied knowledge, and critical imagination in writing histories of empire-building and European colonialisms in South Asia. From the seventeenth-century Mughal empire to the establishment of British colonial rule in the nineteenth century, shifting political and artistic formations both shaped and were shaped by the emergence of new visualities, aesthetic values, and technological experiments. Challenging the teleology of European Enlightenment that has long structured interpretations of this period, art historians have emphasized the circulation of people, objects, and associated knowledge across court workshops, city bazaars, port towns, religious establishments, and colonial networks. Alongside reconsiderations of periodization, art, and modernity, contemporary artists have contributed critical fabulations grounded in archival research that illuminate the epistemic erasures, including laboring bodies that produced material worlds. Drawing together these methodological approaches, weekly seminar meetings will examine the relationship between aesthetic forms and power; knowledge and art; empiricism and enchantment; servitude and enslavement; Orientalism and exoticism; and diplomacy and portraiture. Study sessions at the Metropolitan Museum of Art and the Yale Center for British Art with curators and conservators will support student research through close engagement with primary sources, including illustrated manuscripts, sumptuous albums, venerated calendars, fabulous maps, storied textiles, and painted photographs. Concurrently, we will debate how demands of reparations and provenance research animate–and silence–the presentation of public histories in these museums. If repairing the legacy of past colonialisms highlights the urgency of art historical learning, then how do violent ethno-nationalisms in present-day South Asia and United States undermine its potential?

sections.topic: Shifting Perspectives in Art History of African Di
sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Shifting Perspectives in the Art History of the African Diaspora. DEPARTMENTAL CONSENT REQUIRED TO ENROLL. Open only to departmental majors who have completed five 4-credit art history courses. Students who do not have the prerequisite, but who have taken other art history courses or courses in relevant fields are encouraged to contact the instructor directly. This course examines the major concepts and themes central to the study of African American art and the visual culture of the African Diaspora by foregrounding shifting perspectives from the nineteenth century to the present day. Weekly readings illustrate the divergent ways scholars approach the same keyword, work of art, institution, or archive of materials. We will investigate important debates on the fashioning of African Diasporic subjects across various artistic practices including painting, sculpture, photography, and installation. Case studies focus on scholarship that reframes how the visual generates Black identities of the past and present. Such a reflective look at African American art and the visual culture of the African Diaspora will encourage students to contribute, revise or upend this burgeoning subfield of art history.

Requires Department Consent
Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Approaching Art History. DEPARTMENTAL CONSENT REQUIRED TO ENROLL. Open only to departmental majors who have completed five 4-credit art history courses. Students who do not have the prerequisite, but who have taken other art history courses or courses in relevant fields are encouraged to contact the instructor directly. Art history as an academic field emerges in the late 19th century. This seminar will offer an introduction to some of the ideas and methods that art historians have used since then to describe, analyze, and evaluate works of art. These methods can be divided into a few basic categories such as formal analysis, social history, iconography, and philosophical interpretation (or “critical theory”). The problem is that very different kinds of art history are lumped together within each category. The formal analysis of Renaissance art requires different tools than the formal analysis of Abstract Expressionism. The social history of Baroque art utilizes different categories than the social history of Impressionism. The theological iconography of Medieval art is different from the secular iconography of Romanticism. It might be argued that art historical methodologies, at any given moment, have more to do with the Zeitgeist and the contemporary art of their own time than with the earlier work that historians say that they are studying. This course will therefore be organized as a series of case studies, examining the diverse methods that have been applied to the Western art of different periods (Ancient, Medieval, Renaissance, Baroque, 19th -century and 20th -century). For purpose of comparison, some attention (but not enough) will be given to the aesthetics of South Asian and/or East Asian art. Contemporary art, which requires a new set of critical approaches, will not be included. The class will be conducted as a colloquium—that is, as a series of weekly discussions of shared readings. Students will give two or three brief presentations and will write two papers. But the main goal is well-informed, thoughtful discussion.

sections.topic: What Was Conceptualism, and Why Won't It Go Away?
sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: What Was Conceptualism, and Why Won't It Go Away?. DEPARTMENTAL CONSENT REQUIRED TO ENROLL. This course examines the conceptual art movement, the hopes that shaped its political and aesthetic stratagems, and its legacy. We will begin by revisiting some of the major assumptions and conditions that catalyzed conceptualism, including the cultural climate of the 1960s, the critique of the object-status of art, concerns about the broader social function of the artist, as well as commodity culture. We will then take up our topic from various thematic vantages: the historical and philosophical question of language; the notions of “dematerialization” and documentation, particularly as aesthetic strategies aimed at “suppressing the beholder”; the practice of institutional critique and the broader idea of the world as system; the relationship between art, “information,” and the technological imaginary of the times. A few seminar meetings will be dedicated to focusing on a single artist or artwork. As we proceed we will also keep an eye on the question of why and in what ways conceptualism has persisted beyond its founding moment in the late 1960s, and what its more recent iterations in artistic production—as ‘global-’, ‘neo-’, and ‘post-conceptualisms’—have to offer.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Art and Law. No prerequisites. Art Crime and the Law will provide students with an overview of art law by examining the intersection of art and international legal systems. The art world is a complex array of individuals, institutions, and artworks, thus the proposed course will explore some of the legal issues associated with those relationships. The course will examine art world participants including artists, patrons and consumers, dealers and auction houses, government officials, art experts such as museums, historians, and critics, in addition to forgers, thieves, and looters. Students will analyze the relationships between art institutions and this cast of characters. The course will also explore the international movement of art in times of peace and war, as well as the protection of cultural heritage. In addition to class meetings, a select few trips to arts institutions in NYC will be hosted during the course of the semester. Evaluation will be based on a midterm exam, a term paper, and class participation. Art Crime and the Law will help students to develop practical skills to be used in successful art careers.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Art of the Pacific Islands. No prerequisites. Art of the Pacific Islands is an introductory lecture course on the traditional art and architecture of the peoples of Melanesia, Micronesia, Polynesia, and tribal Indonesia in the Pacific. At least 26 distinct art traditions from these four regions will be covered focusing on their styles, functions, and contextual cultural meanings.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Introduction to Himalayan Art. No prerequisites. This course is an introduction to the art and culture of the Himalayan region, from the 4th century to today, with special emphasis on Western Tibet, Central Tibet, and the Kathmandu valley. Through a chronological and thematic approach, it examines the historical development of the region’s artistic production, both Hindu and Buddhist, and delves into the connections with neighboring regions, primarily India and China. The course outlines the main phases of artistic forms in Nepal and Tibet, and covers how to interpret Himalayan materials in terms of iconography, style, technique, religious meaning, function, and historical context. Includes sessions at the Rubin Museum of Art.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Intro to Archaeology. No prerequisites. This course presents an introduction to the Archaeology of the Mediterranean World, examining the history and context of sites and monuments as well as the methods, practices, and research models through which they have been excavated and studied. From the Bronze Age palaces of the Aegean, to the Athenian Acropolis, to the eastern cities founded by Alexander the Great, the Roman Forum, Pompeii, and the Roman provinces, we consider the ways in which art, archaeology, architecture, everyday objects, landscape, urbanism, technology, and ritual teach us about ancient Greek and Roman societies.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Topic: Bad Art. No prerequisites. How do we know when art is bad? Does bad art suffer from too much or too little technique? Is bad art a moral problem, an aesthetic one, or both? What does bad art reveal about the ways we live and discipline ourselves? This interdisciplinary course thoughtfully engages various kinds of bad art in literature, film and television, painting, music, architecture, and theater—as well as art about bad art—with an emphasis on the formal predicaments they present. We will question the translatability of bad art across time and space: does the “badness” of a work of art come across in other historical, cultural, and geopolitical contexts? We will also productively sit with the feelings of discomfort, difficulty, embarrassment, and outrage that bad art evokes in us to examine the ethical demands we place on aesthetic experience. Towards this end, our critical discussions on negative aesthetic judgments (including terms like kitsch, camp, totalitarian, gimmick, guilty pleasure, and cringe) will be attentive to questions of race, gender and sexuality, political economy, and empire. Our secondary texts come from a range of theoretical and philosophical traditions and will include works by T.W. Adorno, Roland Barthes, Lauren Berlant, Pierre Bourdieu, Natalia Cecire, Boris Groys, bell hooks, Fredric Jameson, Julia Kristeva, Karl Marx, Kobena Mercer, Sianne Ngai, Michele Wallace, and Slavoj Žižek.

title: Renaissance Art
description: This course is an introduction to Renaissance Art by exploring in depth the historical, political and cultural evolution of Italy and Europe between the 14th and the 15th centuries. This overview will be not confined to works of art but will include social and patronage issues - i.e. the role of the guilds, the differences in private, civic and church patronage - that affected the style, form and content of the Italian rich artistic output, which reached a peak often nostalgically referred to by later generations as the “golden age”. Themes such as patronage, humanism, interpretations of antiquity, and Italian civic ideals form a framework for understanding the works of art beyond style, iconography, technique and preservation. The course analyzes the historical and social background of the beginning of the Renaissance during the 14th century and the impact of patronage on art. It then focuses on the early 15th century art in Italy and Europe and deals with the Medici Family’s age. Lastly it analyzes the ‘golden Age’ of the Renaissance, specifically focusing on Verrocchio, Botticelli, Perugino and Ghirlandaio. By the end of this course, students gain a thorough knowledge of the Italian and European Renaissance Age, developing practical perception and a confident grasp of the material, understanding the relationship between both historical and artistic events and valuing the importance of patronage. As the Renaissance works are often still in their original physical settings, during field-studies to museums and churches in Florence students will have a unique opportunity to experience the works as their original viewers did and as their creators intended.

title: British Art in London
description: The principal aim of this course is to familiarize students with the history of British art from the Stuarts to the early Victorian era. Teaching will be conducted entirely on sites in London or its immediate vicinity. The course will begin with the elite patronage of the Stuart court and end with the development of public institutions of art from the mid-eighteenth century. The social significance of portraiture, the cult of antiquity, the art market and the rise of landscape will all be studied as themes. There will be a strong emphasis on the European sources of British visual culture and the emergence of a distinctive national tradition of painting from Hogarth through to Turner.

title: Special Topics: Medieval Art in Europe
description: This course examines medieval art and architecture of France through an exploration of the monuments and moments that define our understanding of the period. The course moves from the Early Christian Church to late Gothic to help students gain an understanding of medieval France through an analysis of monuments in their historic and cultural contexts. From the portals of Notre-Dame of Paris to the collections of the Musée de Cluny, we will seek to decode the symbolic language of medieval sculpture and architecture. Pairing texts and monuments, we will consider the writings of authors such as the Abbot Suger as we inspect his church of Saint-Denis, or as we study liturgical objects in the collections of the Louvre. Throughout the course we will consider how visual art during the Middles Ages helped shape cultural identity and express the political and religious agendas of the age. The course ends with a study of E.E. Viollet-le-Duc’s work during the 19th century, together with his legacy and role in constructing our notions of medieval art and architecture. Conducted in English.

title: Early Masters of Italian Renaissance Painting
description: This course is conceived as a series of selected studies on early Renaissance painting, offering in depth analysis of the historical, political and cultural evolution of Italy and Europe between the 14th and the 15th centuries. This overview will be not confined to works of painting but will include social and patronage issues - i.e. the role of the guilds, the differences in private, civic and church patronage - that affected the style, form and content of the Italian rich artistic output, which reached a peak often nostalgically referred to by later generations as the “dawn of the Golden Age”. Themes such as patronage, humanism, interpretations of antiquity, and Italian civic ideals form a framework for understanding the works of art beyond style, iconography, technique and preservation. Special attention will be given to the phenomenon of collecting as an active force shaping the development of artistic forms and genres. By the end of this course, students gain a thorough knowledge of the Italian and European early Renaissance age, developing practical perception and a confident grasp of the material, understanding the relationship between both historical and artistic events and valuing the importance of patronage. As the early Renaissance works are often still in their original physical settings, during field-studies to museums and churches in Florence, Venice and Milan students will have a unique opportunity to experience the works as their original viewers did and as their creators intended.

title: Masterpieces in The Prado Museum II
description: The aim of this course is to offer an introduction to Spanish Art from The Golden Age to the early Nineteenth Century, with special emphasis on El Greco, Diego Velázquez and Francisco de Goya. Given its position as a primary depository for Spanish art, the collection of El Museo del Prado will be a major focus of the course, with regular class visits to the museum and related institutions. The artistic relationship artists of the Spanish School maintained with foreign artists (Bosch, Titian, and Rubens) will be considered in depth. Contemporary readings in art history are incorporated as relevant to the subject. The intention of the course is to teach students how to approach the formal analysis of paintings within a rich context-based interpretative framework, including the social and historical conditions surrounding artistic production.

title: Impressionism to Post-Impressionism
description: Begins by considering how impressionism refined and redirected the artistic aims of 19th-century realism, then follows the development of progressive art to the brink of cubism and pure abstraction in the first years of the 20th century. Following impressionism and post-impressionism, close attention is paid to symbolism, aestheticism, art nouveau, the Arts and Crafts movement, fauvism, and expressionism. The aesthetic aims of these movements are analyzed in tandem with the social and cultural conditions that generated them.

title: Place-Building-Time:The Architecture of Berlin
description: Berlin is a unique modern Metropolis. Its alternating history with often drastic changes offers a comprehensive background to explore and investigate the nature of architecture in correlation to the various developmental processes of urban life and culture. Architecture is embedded in the urban fabric in which place and time serve as the main threads, constantly changing their multifaceted and layered relationships. This urban fabric provides the fertile soil for urban life and culture, which literally takes place in various scales between the public and the private realm, two further threads intertwined in the urban fabric. Experiencing the city through walking is essential for learning how to observe, see and read "Place, Building and Time" in Berlin. Tours will alternate with classroom discussions and workshops.

title: Special Topics
description: Prague is a unique city, in which all architectural styles combine: from the pre-Romanesque, to Romanesque and Gothic, Renaissance, Baroque and Classicist styles, to the modern ones that include Historicism, Art Nouveau, the original Cubism in architecture, Art Deco, Constructivism and Functionalism, even the post-war Stalinist architecture, and contemporary trends. The city did not undergo extensive renewals such as occurred in other European metropolises, and thus fragments of various epochs have been left standing here side by side, and partially, there is also the medieval urban layout to be seen. Architects and master builders from many European countries worked here and local architects and artists were also influenced by foreign models. The city is in fact an ideal textbook of architecture from the Middle Ages to the present day. The course should take the students through this development chronologically, in lectures accompanied by projections of pictures and short films, but also in visits to typical buildings, including their interiors. The main emphasis will be put on the period of the 19th and 20th centuries, in which the lecturer specializes. Architecture is linked to other fields, such as fine arts, urban planning, national heritage care, industrial design, and others. Teaching will thus also focus on these. During the course, each of the students will present an independent study of one chosen building: they will analyze the building, place it within a broader context of European architecture and supply it with their own illustrations. They will defend the work. At the end of the term they will sit for a test. There is compulsory and recommended specialist literature in English available for them, and they are expected to supplement the information gained at lectures and excursions by self-study. By the end of the term the student should have acquired some knowledge of the complex development of Central-European architecture, of the most significant figures, and be fairly well informed in related fields.

title: Czech Art & Architecture
description: This course presents a survey of art and architecture in Prague and its environs – from the Middle Ages to the modern era – with an emphasis on key periods in Czech history, and placed within the context of the main periods and movements of Western art history. The course is rooted in a discussion of the city of Prague, and students are encouraged, through excursions and assignments, to become acquainted with the city’s architecture, monuments and urban design. Students learn to analyse formal aspects of art and architectural styles, and are encouraged to investigate their sources and theoretical foundations.Emphasis is given to the historical and cultural context of art styles and movements. We also look at art patronage in some key periods of Czech history to see how this reflects political, cultural and ideological change.
