title: Site­ Specific to Immersive Dance Theater: Choreographing for Unconventional Formats and Spaces
description: This movement and performance course fosters the creation of interactive experiences that blur the lines between performers and audience, utilizing unconventional spaces for site-specific choreographic structures. Throughout the semester we will immerse ourselves in time-based performance art, emphasizing embodied choreography that challenges the confines of the traditional proscenium stage. Students will be expected to engage confidently in physically demanding movement vocabularies, bolstered by frequent performance opportunities. Set against the backdrop of New York City's rich cultural legacy, the course takes place in outdoor settings at various landmarks. With the inclusion of guest artists, students will collaboratively craft public performances, which will be documented on video. Our goal will be to probe the role of public spaces in articulating social commentary, melding choreography, activism, and performance art, and offering a unique opportunity for students to enhance their movement skills in notable urban locations, honing their performance capabilities within an ensemble. The desire and passion to participate and engage in movement and performance as an ensemble is required.

sections.notes: Restriction: UTCOARBFA This section is only open to Collaborative Arts majors. All non-majors can register for this course under Tisch Open Arts using the course code OART-UT 810.

title: The Collaborative Arts Theatre Experience
description: Experimental makers have exploded the traditional structures of collaboration in theater. And yet, a completely egalitarian process - the image often associated with the words “collaborative” or “devised” - is a myth. “Liberation paves the way for new power relationships,” Foucault writes, “which must be controlled by practices of freedom.” How do we work together: with an auteur, with a chaos agent, with a friend, with a stranger? In this class, you will have the chance to write and make theater, and your classmates will be your collaborators, audience members, responders and peers. Throughout the semester, you will engage with the work of American experimental theater artists and make work of your own. During the first half of the course, we will be reading and watching a variety of experimental work that has been performed in NYC in the last 50 years. Each week, you will be given a prompt inspired by the texts we have been engaging with, and you will write a 5-7 minute play in response, to be shared with classmates the following week (they will offer comprehensive feedback.) In the second half of the course, you will rehearse with your classmates to eventually present either a mini-festival of your work, or one longer piece made collectively. In practice, you will have the opportunity to stage your work, and experiment with devising and directing as well as writing.

sections.notes: This section is only open to Collaborative Arts majors who have completed the first year BFA core acting classes. All non-majors can register for this course under Tisch Open Arts using the course code OART-UT 1917.

title: Choreography
description: The purpose of this course is to enable the student to gain a heightened awareness, appreciation, and knowledge of dance through movement and performance. We focus on the foundations of dance such as control, aesthetics, alignment, dynamics, athleticism, musicality, use of space, development of learning strategies within a group context, and personal, artistic expression. The students exploration of their creativity, expression and concepts, as well as their work on other dancer's bodies is part of the work of this course. Through individual and collective kinesthetic participation in unfamiliar patterns, the student is physically and conceptually challenged and informed. Students will be asked to problem solve as homework assignment and in-class composition exercises. Dance experience is recommended, but formal dance training is not required.

sections.notes: This section is only open to Collaborative Arts majors. All non-majors can register for this course under Tisch Open Arts using the course code OART-UT 805.

title: Live in New York City
description: We will explore the tension between the live and the scripted, the performed and the texted--almost entirely in the field of theatre but also in some other genres of performed events. A series of productions will be carefully curated to see different artists' renderings of these two aspects of the live event, and we will sustain an interest in other dualities, including the tension between the virtual and the real, the rehearsed and the improvised, etc.

title: Abrupt Climate Change
description: Combining science and the art of storytelling, this course will tackle one of the most pressing issues facing the future of humanity: Abrupt Climate Change. In a unique collaboration with NYU physical climate scientist Professor David Holland, students will research and create work that bridges the divide between science and the public through accurate, creative science-based storytelling. This highly multidisciplinary, hands-on course welcomes students from all backgrounds and fields of study to imagine and invent creative ways of telling stories about this global phenomenon and to investigate solutions. Weekly assignments will lead to a final collaborative project and an exhibition open to the public.

title: Art on the Edge
description: Taking off from the practices of medium-based art categories, this course is structured across key topics in contemporary art - “art of today, produced by artists who are living in the twenty-first century”. During the semester, via the framework of readings, projects and assignments, we will consider the importance of the visual arts in the larger context of society. Each week we will look at a different topic, which will be organized around key concepts, artists and artwork examples. The main goal is to allow us to contemplate the process of interaction between visual art, history, cultural, socio-economical, and technological forces. The stress of our gatherings will be on the artist as a thinker and a maker.

sections.notes: Restriction: UTCOARBFA This section is only open to Collaborative Arts majors. All non-majors can register for this course under Tisch Open Arts using the course code OART-UT 1019.

title: Multi-disciplinary Arts Practice with Community Groups: Theories and Practice of Group Work in Arts
description: Whether you are a filmmaker looking to better understand how to build a cohesive and productive film crew; a theatre maker excited about building a performance project or theatre company; a multi-media artist looking for ways to innovate your ideas for artistic work in collaboration with others; an artist looking for tools for building an artistic ensemble, or a multi-disciplinary artist looking to take your creative work out into communities as social practice, this combination lecture/activity-based class provides you with tools for better understanding how to enter into and engage others in collective creative work of purpose. Multi-Disciplinary Arts Practice with Community Groups: Theories and Practice explores the challenges and benefits of making artistic work with others and the tools needed to create meaningful collaborative projects. In this class we interrogate definitions of community and group, explore the balance between group process and producing an artistically excellent project, and examine the processes of creating artistic work with others to strengthen our own artistic voices while helping raise the creative voices of others. With its focus on social practice, this course provides a foundation for working with small group structures in a variety of community settings and professional creative work environments. The course satisfies a CA major requirement as well as a social science requirement for all other Tisch students.

sections.notes: Restriction: UTCOARBFA This section is only open to Collaborative Arts majors. All non-majors can register for this course under Tisch Open Arts using the course code OART-UT 1017.

title: The Villain
description: What makes a villain and who decides? In this course, we will track the evolution of the villain across the globe and through the ages, exploring representations of evil in mythology, literature, and art history, as well as on the stage and screen. We'll identify the origins of iconic imagery, interrogate the scapegoating of characters and populations in popular narratives, and question our own perceptions of villainy in art and culture. Our material will include sacred text, global performance traditions, political documents, psychological studies, essential works of early cinema, and relevant works of today from Disney to Jordan Peele. Assignments will take the form of textual analysis and research as well as artistic responses in a variety of mediums, all seeking to understand new perspectives on those we label "villain."

sections.notes: This section is only open to Collaborative Arts majors who have completed the first year BFA core acting classes. All non-majors can register for this course under Tisch Open Arts using the course code OART-UT 1024.

title: Cinematic Narratives
description: Filmmaking, photography, and the basics of visual imagery are explored through a hands-on studio art experience, which provides an overview of the development of visual storytelling throughout history. From the first creation of early hand drawn cave paintings to modern film production, all the essential elements of visual representation, visual imagery, visual grammar, and visual narrative are explored. Lectures introduce and explain a variety of methods used to capture a visual image and how imagery, both with and without words, is used to convey meaning. In class painting, etching, drawing, film, and photo assignments are given for students to create their own visual imagery, using these several different artistic formats. Technical training on cameras and editing software accompanies these practical assignments. Students also complete photo and short film projects throughout the course, as they explore the essential nature of visual storytelling, pre-visualization, and practical production. The course examines how the basic tools of traditional narrative storytelling are also used in purely visual storytelling - to create a secondary world and to maintain a suspension of disbelief in order to inform, entertain, and affect the audience. In spring 2021, cellphones and gimbals will be employed for film and photo work and additional asynchronous DSLR photo and video camera training will be provided over the course of the semester. Hands-on studio work will be accomplished in-person, in-class, following social distancing protocols - and any needs for remote work should be arranged for in advance so that remote based art supplies can be provided as necessary.

title: Contemporary Music Applications
description: Contemporary music applications is an intermediate music production and computer music class. The course will encourage a creative approach to using recording software as a tool that can be applied to music making for a wide range of interdisciplinary practices. Students will be introduced to mixing, sound design, advanced audio/MIDI editing, and production techniques for composing music. It will explore concepts and questions such as how does sound re/de/contextualize an image and how are dynamics created through mixing and effects processing? This class will encourage students to step outside of their musical comfort zones to further their technical skills in composing and producing music with software.

title: Musical Theatre Writing Workshop
description: This is a team-taught workshop that encourages you to find your own voice and learn to merge your unique artistic vision with those of other collaborative artists to create exciting new musical theater. The course will start by covering the basics of songwriting for the theater, but it is not a music theory class; we’ll be focusing more on using music to tell stories than on compositional techniques. Together we’ll examine theater songwriting craft, issues of communication between artists of different disciplines, and storytelling through music and text. Poets, playwrights, and writers from other genres, and composers from a wide variety of stylistic backgrounds ranging from pop to classical, country to hip-hop, rap to jazz to fusion—all are welcome to participate, regardless of experience or lack thereof. We aim to create a supportive environment in which you feel free to experiment and to explore both what musical theater has been and what it can become. Note: most of your homework will be done in collaboration with one or more of your classmates, so expect to spend a significant amount of time working with others.

title: Composing Music with Max
description: The foundations of Max, a powerful visual programming language for music and multimedia, will be covered in this course. We will examine how computers can be utilized to create situations for music creation, performance, and collaborative improvisation as well as applied to building interactive, generative music. In addition to learning Max's fundamental building blocks, we will also use fundamental music theory as a tool to better understand music making. We will create programs that examine rhythm, melodies, chords, scales, and recognize other qualities of music like timbre, texture, and dynamics while taking into consideration the principles of harmony, melody, and rhythm defined in basic music theory. The final will require you to develop a collaborative piece of interactive computer music, a collaborative performance environment, or another final project that has been discussed and agreed upon together. This class does not require any prerequisite programming skills or prior music theory knowledge.

title: Dance: Movement and Performance
description: This foundational dance course introduces students to the building blocks of movement practice in the service of self-expression and group collaboration, and the body as a frame for practicing physical performance and movement. The class encourages a sensory as well as a mechanical experience for students to build an individualized movement practice in a group setting. These fundamental movement skills will support the sharing of a common movement-based vocabulary: Walking, falling, skipping, jumping, giving and taking weight, and partnering will be among the elements of this embodied practice. Through maintaining the dual focus on creating and learning movement, students will enter the world of physical gestures, movement material, and choreography with an understanding of their importance in all artistic and creative contexts. The course also introduces students to notions of space, time, shape, rhythm, and composition, as components that can be applied to an ensemble, or individual physical practice.

title: Experiments in Art and Technology
description: All art uses technology, yet technology alone isn't art—it is the burning spark of imagination and personal vision that rips time, space, and the ordinary apart, harnessing tools and bending materials to create a manifestation born from the mind's eye, and in this course, you will explore the relationships between art, imagination, and technology, paying homage to pioneering engineer-artists of the late 20th and early 21st centuries by reconstructing historic work and learning to embrace the spark, bang, buzz, and smoke that often arise at the periphery of the known. Through research, field trips, discussions, and hands-on projects, you will celebrate past achievements, challenge boundaries, and embark on a personal journey between invention and art.

title: Playful Performance Props
description: TouchDesigner is a powerful software hub for live audiovisual performance and installation art. With a cutting-edge buffet of inputs and outputs at our disposal, what new, evolved, or remixed types of art can we create? If you’re a musician, you’ll make and play an instrument that didn’t exist before. If you’re a dancer, your movements will become the music and visuals, instead of the other way around. If you’re a visual artist, you’ll collage with code, sculpt with magic, and create installations that respond to your audience instantly. If you’re all of the above, you’ll have fun in this class. The course starts with video art — live camera feeds, visual effects, and projection mapping — then weaves in audio reactivity and sound generation for DJ/VJing. We will use the MediaPipe plugin to detect our faces, bodies, and objects and use that data to make music, control systems, and modulate visual effects. We will scan objects, people, and environments with our phones to create virtual scenes and 3D animations rendered live. We will learn communication protocols — MIDI to send input and receive output from MIDI controllers or DAWs such as Ableton; OSC to wirelessly connect to other computers, software, and livecode environments; and NDI to send high-resolution and low-latency video feeds between devices. By the end of the course, students will be able to use TouchDesigner to connect and control any modern art/performance/game software. Assignments are time-intensive: creating original work to be shown in class and watching recorded lessons of the next week’s concepts. Classtime is a mix of homework performances, collaborative exercises, concept walkthroughs, and studio time. The final is a small group performance or interactive installation that is a part of a public show. No previous coding, fabrication, or performance experience necessary. Note: There is no longer mandatory use of Arduino in this course, though students with interest in Arduino microcontrollers can still create custom hardware interfaces that send sensor input or receive command signals and turn TouchDesigner into a hub for interactive installations or performance props.

title: Virtual Performance and Unreal Interactions
description: What types of performance can we create if we’re not limited to a physical stage or even a physical body? How much more can we communicate with video once our audience has the power to directly interact with the content, not just passively observe? We can create dynamic, digital experiences and innovative, virtual performances using Unreal Engine, a game engine and powerful suite of development tools. Students will learn the fundamentals of Unreal Engine, including 3D environments and assets, lighting, cameras, animations, audio, basic VFX, and programming interactivity using visual scripting blueprints. Then, we will incorporate external hardware such as depth cameras, LiDAR scanners, and motion capture suits to create our own digital assets, including virtual avatars of ourselves. Students will use this foundation in virtual production to create projects ranging from 3D music videos to choose-your-own-adventure memoirs to Performances with puppet avatars in an online 3D environment. The final assignment will be a part of a public show.

title: Universe in a Blender
description: Blender is a dynamic tool that can be used to design real world sets, physical objects and virtual assets for various media and live performance. It can render robust animations and impose visual effects on recorded video. It has the capacity to interface easily with interactive softwares like Unity and Unreal, while having the potential to output hi-fidelity renders for print. But beyond that it’s just a software. The ability to create any believable world comes from you. In this class we will explore a variety of techniques to create living, breathing fictional worlds while honing the skills in Blender to bring them to life. Students will be asked to create food, buildings, clothing, people and traffic signs from their fictional universe - building consistency of aesthetic, narrative allusion, and the fine details that make any world “believable”. The class will involve dissecting and discussing media on this world building, technical tutorials and instruction in Blender, and hands on workshops that tackle the conceptual questions of world building while exploring how to interface Blender with an outside medium: (3D printing, Pattern Making, Asset Development, Unity, Unreal, After Effects, recorded video). Students will be expected to watch technical tutorials and read short pieces on these topics for homework. Students will also complete weekly deliverable assignments.

title: Small Lights at the End of the World
description: In this course students will develop foundational skills of lighting design for live performance. In small teams, students will work both as lead artist for their own time based, live, human centered event, and as lighting designers for fellow classmates and collaborative projects. Small Lights at the End of the World will center on hands-on exercises, including programming of the ETC EOS family of lighting consoles in Collaborative Art's Studio G performance studio, presentation of visual research, electrical safety and basic wiring, best practices for technical documentation, safe hanging of lighting fixtures, and the visual standards of "professional" lighting design. We will also build DIY lighting objects that can be adapted to any scale of production opportunity, yet stored under the bed of your studio apartment. Because lighting is a rapidly evolving, ever changing field, students will develop the research skills to self-teach new techniques on a project by project basis. Collaborating in light requires comfort with conceptual abstraction. Short writing assignments and classroom discussions will help us form our own language for light as a medium of perception. We will engage the ethical quandaries of working in hierarchical collaboration, and carbon intensive artistic practices in the age of human driven ecological collapse. Working together, we will push at the boundaries of form and perception, questioning deeply held assumptions, and moving towards radical integrations of light and performance.

title: Powder Room
description: Powder Room empowers artists to become architects of their own creative infrastructure. Using large language models and AI coding assistants, with a focus on Claude.ai, students will design and build custom software tools tailored to their individual artistic practices, without requiring a traditional programming background. Rather than adapting work to fit existing platforms, students will learn to articulate their creative vision and translate it into functional software: generative video processors, live performance controllers, custom editing pipelines, interactive installation engines, experimental notation systems, and beyond. In the Powder Room we will treat AI not as a creative collaborator, but as a fabrication partner - a means by which artists can build the exact tool or machine they need, on their own terms. Through hands-on projects spanning performance, video, emerging media, and cross-disciplinary work, students will develop fluency in prompt-driven development, rapid prototyping, and iterative tool-building. Critical discussion will examine what it means for artists to own and author their own technical means of production. Our goal will also be to open source our tools, contributing to a growing commons of artist-built software freely available to other artists and the general public.

title: Collaborative Screenwriting: The Writers' Room
description: Always thought you had that perfect concept for a streaming TV show? Curious about what makes those shows tick, and to see if you have what it takes to collaborate on a show that works? Focused on the development of the half-hour streaming ‘prestige' TV series, The Writers’ Room is an Intermediate and Collaborative TV Screenwriting class that addresses the latest forms of shows that sell, on the platforms that dominate the market. Shows like The Mandalorian, Ted Lasso and The Bear are 'binge-worthy' because along with dynamic stand-alone episodes they present connected dramatic arcs stretching over seasons. Often these shows are developed with multiple writers, in a format known as the 'Writers’ Room.' Along with conceptualizing a show, the class is intended as a practicum in collaboration, modeling the Writers Room to prepare the future screenwriter for one of the central forms of commercial storytelling. In this class we will cover what it actually takes to break into TV writing and create a roadmap to developing not only a great TV episode but conceptualizing its entire first season. What will sell a great show? Great premises, fulsome outlines, dynamic pitches, engaging decks, etc. How do you 'break' an episode and build provocative story arcs? Students will emerge with a group-conceptualized deck for an original show as well as that show’s original pilot--all done in the form of a structured workshop environment, with the last half of the class modeling the writers room. Our main texts are current shows that fit within this context. Note: this is a rigorous, collaborative class that requires significant out-of-class meetups with your group colleagues, so please be aware of the time commitment.

title: Auto Performance Lab
description: This is a creative workshop designed for playwrights who yearn to act and actors who have an itch to write. Using one’s self as material, participants create a short solo performance for an end-of-semester presentation. The lab combines physical work (both group and solo) with in-class/out-of-class writing exercises aimed at enhancing students’ capacities to transform the stuff of their real lives into mimetic fiction. The final composition may stand alone as a finished, self-contained piece or may be an extended monologue planned as part of a full- length play, given the creator’s primary interest (solo-performance vs. playwriting). In-class exercises, group critiques (though the instructor prefers the word “responses”) as well as analysis of other artists’ solo performances are used to shape students’ final compositions.

title: Intermediate Screenwriting
description: A continuation of the training presented in Making a Scene: Screenwriting and Intro to Screenwriting. Required work in the class includes extensive scene work. Guided by their screenwriting instructor, students will complete the screenplay begun in Intro to Screenwriting and then do a rewrite or they may begin, complete, and rewrite a new full-length screenplay. The focus in this class will be on story structure and development and the completion of a full-length screenplay. If you plan to do a new work, you must come to the first class with three ideas for full-length screenplays. Each idea can be described in one or two paragraphs.

title: Experimental RISO
description: The death of printed matter has been predicted for more than half a century. Meanwhile, artists have been busy continually proving that print media—and the nimble RISO, in particular—offers vital new possibilities for experimentation. With a capacity to layer pure spot color, like silkscreen, and output quickly, like digital processes, the Risograph duplicator has revolutionized visual culture over the past decade. RISO aesthetics have made their way into animation and film, into mainstream digital design culture, and has flooded independent art book publishing. Because the process engages and serves niche communities of artists, it has given voice to groups traditionally excluded from mainstream publishing. It is the machine largely responsible for the thriving, international small press movement, which challenges both the traditional scarcity-based economy of the art market, and the myth of the lone artist. Experimental RISO will take this spirit as a starting point, as our class works together as a small community to push the RISO into more experimental territory. We will explore a myriad of “off label” uses for RISO printmaking. We will design non-digital publications using exquisite corpse methods and learn how to translate film and animation into RISO. Avant-garde publishing has a long history of cutting through the so-called dichotomy between paper and electronics, so we will use conditional design “codes” to design programmatically. We will investigate the RISO’s potential to produce performance-based art—looking to Bruno Munari and Victorian Troublewit performance for possible inroads.

title: Artist Studio Practice
description: This course will engage students directly in the discourse of contemporary art and in the hugely diverse practices of artists in their studios in New York. Framed predominantly around studio visits, the course will expose students to hybrid mediums and working strategies that will complicate, not facilitate, systems of categorization. Meeting outside of the physical classroom for the majority of the semester, students will be expected to be prepared to navigate the city independently to various locations across Manhattan, Brooklyn and Queens for site visits. Each week, we will sharpen our abilities of seeing, questioning and understanding not only physical spaces of creativity but also mental strategies of production across a wide variety of media. Supplementing the visual feast of these weekly adventures, students will participate in material workshops at a number of artist’s studios and will build a record of influences, ideas, research and modes of making in individual sketchbooks that will be compiled during the semester and which will help inform the class’s collaborative project at the culmination of the semester – a Studio Guide to assist in oblique strategies of creating. Weekly readings, videos and podcasts will introduce elements of art criticism, theory, philosophy and history and will inform our understanding of what we see and how we approach making in the studio. Prior experience in object-making is recommended, however, it is not required. This class is best suited to Collaborative Arts BFA students as well as NYU students through the Open Arts program.

title: Progressive Art Studios, Neurodiversity, and Living Creatively
description: Progressive art studios are radical art collectives where artists with intellectual and developmental disabilities make art. Finally catching the attention of the mainstream art world, these art utopias yield some of the most unorthodox artwork of our time – sometimes (imperfectly) labelled as “outsider art.” In the words of critic Lyle Rexer, this artwork “tends to be all present tense and to reinvent the wheel in terms of visual forms.” Progressive studios offer all artists – with and without disabilities – a new model for living creatively, one that prioritizes collaboration over competition and accessibility over elitism. This course will introduce students to the values and daily practices of the progressive art studio, a place where disability justice and artistic experimentation intersect. Students will work closely with artists from YAI Arts, a progressive studio in Manhattan, to bring the progressive studio to the NYU classroom. Together students and artists will explore different modes of mentorship, communication, and artistic collaboration, encouraging free-flowing creativity and self expression in a supported environment. Students will form relationships with neurodiverse artists, learning from one another while creating a flourishing creative oasis. For their final project, students will mount an exhibition in collaboration with YAI Arts, featuring artwork by students alongside studio artists, organizing and curating the exhibition according to the studio artists’ desires.

title: Wood: Structures and Stages
description: This course situates wood within the context of Collaborative Arts' interdisciplinary environment where making, performance, and critical inquiry intersect. Taking on a DIY approach, students will engage with wood on a hands-on level, confronting its material resistance and learning from its demands. Working with wood cultivates decision-making, adaptability, and sensitivity to material feedback - skills that are essential not only in art-making but also in live performance. The goal is to expand students' perception of wood and its potential for creating various constructions and objects in relation to our bodies. We will explore structural building form and how its scale, shape, and removal creates various weight-bearing structures - from chairs and tables to shelves, stages, lofts, and houses. We will learn to cut straight, curved, holes, and internal shapes utilizing tools such as hand saw, band saw, jig saw, chop saw, drill press, and circular saw. We will learn to join materials together with nail, screw, hardware, lamination techniques using drills, hammers, and clamps. The semester culminates in a final performance that synthesizes learned techniques with individual artistic inquiry, and emphasizes the inseparable relationship between form, concept, and content through self-made wooden structures and stages.

title: Art Palace
description: Art Palace is a series of weekly talks/events presented by working artists with noteworthy careers in the greater New York area. The course's purpose is to introduce Collaborative Arts BFA students to a disparate variety of multi- and inter-disciplinary practitioners, allowing students to listen to, learn from and - in many cases - collaborate with visiting artists. Conceived as an addendum to the first-year core Collaborative Interdisciplinary Practice class, it is required of all incoming students in their first (fall) semester, however each evening's event is open to all Collaborative Arts majors who would like to participate.

sections.notes: This section is only open to Collaborative Arts majors.

title: Performing Emerging Forms
description: New technology is changing the way we work, perform, make, and present. It is also creating extraordinary new opportunities for new art forms and emerging practices. In this course we will offer students of all disciplines a stage for the exploration of new forms of creation. In this hands-on course students will work collaboratively to conceive of, develop, design, rehearse, and perform new multidisciplinary work with a focus on performance, in combination with technologies such as virtual production and extended reality (AR, XR, VR). Students will have the opportunity to hear from and explore the amazing work of artists and technologists throughout London who are in residence at 180 Studios.

title: | COHRT-UA 9010 First-Year Cohort: Authoring your NYU Story
description: First-Year Cohort: Authoring your NYU Story is designed to help CAS students connect to their story and cultivate a sense of purpose and direction by weaving together an understanding of how they got here, how they can build on where they are, and how they can be the author of their lives moving forward. Combining self-reflection, group discussion, and exploration of professional development and interpersonal theory, the course helps students make sense of the lived experiences that have brought them to this point, shape how they can intentionally use their time at CAS and NYU, and identify the contributions they will make to our community and our world. The meetings will encourage knowledge sharing, establish a network, and explore the four themes of the College Cohort Program: Academic Success, Personal & Career Development, Community Engagement, and Leadership Experience.

Combining self-reflection, group discussion, and exploration of professional development and interpersonal theory, the course helps students make sense of the lived experiences that have brought them to this point, shape how they can intentionally use their time at CAS and NYU, and identify the contributions they will make to our community and our world. The meetings will encourage knowledge sharing, establish a network, and explore the four themes of the College Cohort Program: Academic Success, Personal & Career Development, Community Engagement, and Leadership Experience.

Reading Alain Locke: This seminar explores the writings of philosopher and critic Alain Locke (1885-1954), making use of them as avenues into histories of racial formation, American empire, and twentieth-century theory. Focusing on the moment of The New Negro anthology but, equally, on prior and later phases of Locke’s work, the seminar examines the ways he intervened in debates in education, political science, literary studies and art history. Along the way, we will discuss works by Locke’s contemporaries, including Jessie Fauset, Wallace Thurman, W. E. B. Du Bois, Randolph Bourne, Jean Toomer, and Melville Herskovits, as well by those who in different ways influenced his thought, including Georg Simmel and William James. Finally, students will evaluate recent reconsiderations of Locke and his place in 20th-century letters undertaken by critics, comparatists, and biographers.

sections.topic: Ancient Materialisms: Matter & Gender in Class Ant
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Revisiting the Western Classics: Ancient Materialisms: Matter and Gender in Classical Antiquity - In the wake of the recent “new materialist” turn, this class examines the emergence of the notion of “matter” in classical antiquity. In short, matter, from the Latin ‘materia’ (related to mater, mother) is transmitted from Aristotle’s Greek innovation hulê (literally, wood). We will undertake close readings of key ancient philosophical texts, including various Presocratics, Plato’s Timaeus, Aristotle’s Physics, Metaphysics, and Generation of Animals, and Lucretius’ De Rerum Natura, tracing the discourses of materiality that arise in concert with tropes of sex and gender. The guiding question here is: what can matter’s genealogical ties to the feminine tell us about the materialization of bodies and genders? At the same time, we will attend to the topographies and texture of ancient thinking about nature and materiality in the context of the emergence of metaphysics more broadly. Alongside a narrative of “emergence” we will also consider hermeneutic questions – what are the ethico-political stakes of a “retrieval” of antiquity and how can we determine our relationship to these distant texts? And how does a consideration of ancient modes of thought help to enrich contemporary discourses of matter, gender, and the poetics thereof? To help orient our study we will draw on contemporary thinkers including Irigaray, Kristeva, Sallis, Cavarero, as well as critically engaging 19th century theories of archaic matriarchy. Some background knowledge of psychoanalytic theory is advised, as is knowledge of Greek, however all readings will be in translation. Counts for Pre-1800 req.

description: Introduces recent developments in Comparative Literature, harnessing energies of Area Studies (Middle Eastern Studies, African Studies, and so forth) in order to extend its scope geographically.

sections.notes: CALAMEGS PROSEMINAR: Concepts of the Global South: This course pursues the “global south” as concept, tracing how the term becomes differently meaningful in varying contexts of its articulation since the mid-twentieth century. Our approach extends in two directions: accounting for prefigurations of the “global south” in discourses of Third Worldism, Afro-Asianism, and others; and at the same time, exceeding a geographic understanding of the term by examining instead its capacity to site intellection and relation. Along the way, we will consider what conceptualizing the “global south” reveals about life under the logics of capitalism, how thinking the “global south” can re-form what we understand as “theory,” and how we might theorize majority and majorness (alongside notions of the “commons,” “multitude,” collectivity, and solidarity) in the face of and against majoritarianism. The syllabus pairs benchmark readings on the “global south” and its contexts with theoretical writings by Gramsci, Deleuze & Guattari, Hardt & Negri, and others.This seminar counts as the required introductory course for the “Advanced Certificate in Comparative Approaches to the Literatures of Africa, the Middle East, and the Global South” (CALAMEGS). It is also open to students not enrolled in CALAMEGS. *counts for Non-Euro req

Title: "Being at Home in the Unhomely/Uncanny: Freud, Heidegger, Derrida" Description: The seminar will consist of a comparative study of the way Freud, Heidegger and Derrida approach the question of the Unheimlichen – Uncanny. Of particular interest will be the role played by literature (or Dichtung) in these different approaches. An underlying question that will accompany the discussion is whether theorizing the uncanny is also a way of domesticating it. In German (a knowledge of which is desirable but not a prerequisite), this can be expressed as the relationship between two words that sound almost the same but have quite different connotations: heimisch (homey) and heimlich (secret). Meets Sept 2 through Nov 25, 2026. (Two sessions will meet off-schedule). Taught in English by Prof. Samuel Weber.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Title: Alienation and Freedom in 20th Century French Psychoanalysis, Psychiatry and Psychology Description: A significant proportion of the most interesting and intriguing French “theorists” of the later 20th century, such as Georges Canguilhem, Frantz Fanon, Félix Guattari, Michel Foucault, Jacques Lacan, Francesc Tosquelles, emerged from a broadly common medical and political disciplinary background which drew on what in the English-speaking world are regarded as the separate and distinct “p-disciplines” of philosophy, psychiatry, psychoanalysis and psychology. In this course we will attempt to reconstitute the dynamic interactions within this intermingling milieu both historically and philosophically. Will be looking at work originally conceived within a Marxist framework that developed into the anti-psychiatries of the later 20th century. The course will entail a close reading of texts by those named above along with other related intellectuals such as Gaston Bachelard, Franco Basaglia, Gilles Deleuze, Fyodor Dostoevsky, R. D. Laing, Jean-Paul Sartre and Maurice Merleau-Ponty, with a focus on the issues of existential alienation and freedom that characterized the thinking of this era.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Course Title: Introduction to Literary Theory This course introduces graduate students to literary theory. It offers a chronological outline of the major intellectual developments in the broader field since the end of the nineteenth century. Meetings combine faculty and guest mini-lectures, student presentations, and discussion. Analysis and discussion of the weekly reading assignments is the seminar's centerpiece. Participants are encouraged to regard theory and criticism as praxis, that is, as something you do—rather than as an abstract, fixed object of study. Readings include: Saussure, Derrida, Foucault, Butler, Sedgwick, Ngai. Readings and discussion in English.

Title: “Freud and the Cinematic Imagination" Description: From the onset, the dream factory cinema drew into focus the proximity between this new medium and psychoanalysis. The aim of this block seminar is to explore how a set of articulations of the unconscious – be it dreamwork, neurotic and psychotic symptoms, trauma, repetition compulsion and the death drive – have not only inspired screenplays but can, in themselves, be reconceived in cinematic terms. Meets Sept 4 - Oct 9, (2 classes meet in last week). It is possible to enroll in GERM-GA2222 Bronfen and also GERM-GA2224 Malabou's 7-week course with no time conflict. Taught in English.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Title: "Negativity and the Unconscious: Hegel, Freud, Bergson" Description: This seminar explores the philosophical and psychic dimensions of negativity as the force that shapes both thought and life. Beginning with Hegel’s dialectical notion of negation as the motor of becoming, we will trace how this concept transforms in Freud’s discovery of the unconscious and in Bergson’s philosophy of duration and creative evolution. The course examines how negativity moves from logical contradiction to psychic repression to temporal differentiation — from the structure of Spirit to the work of mourning to the élan vital. We will ask whether negativity is destructive or productive, reactive or generative, and whether contemporary thought can still think transformation without the negative. By reading Phenomenology of Spirit (selected sections), Freud’s “Negation” and 'Beyond the Pleasure Principle', and Bergson’s 'Creative Evolution', we will test the hypothesis that the unconscious is not merely the site of repression, but a 'plastic power of differentiation', where negation becomes the very form of life. Meets 7 weeks from Oct 16 - Dec 4, 2026. It is possible to enroll in GERM-GA2222 Bronfen for the first 7 weeks and also GERM-GA2224 Malabou in last 7 weeks with no time conflict. Taught in English.

Title: Historical Representation and Critical Theory: The “Global South” and New York Description: This course aims to rethink cultural materialism and historical representation to develop a toolkit for critically examining contemporary dynamics, with a primary focus on the “Global South.” In a world characterized by rapid shifts—from the rise of AI and modern warfare to narratives of humanity in crisis and the mobilization of culture to galvanize nationalism and racialism—this seminar takes a productive pause to reconsider our frames of analysis. If our present moment is one where 19th- and earlier 20th-century paradigms are being reconfigured to seek legitimacy for contemporary political and economic agendas, what critical toolkits do we need? How can the "Global South" help us explore, understand, and examine this process? Our course will deploy cultural materialism as one of the many analytical lenses to examine these dynamics. Drawing on Raymond Williams’ definition of culture as a "productive process" of political, economic, and social conditions, we will approach culture as a terrain directly involved in the material production of public life and explore the significance of public humanities within this context. In that vein, we will engage with New York City’s material cultural landscape (including but not limited to the Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York Public Library Archives and Collections, NYU’s Grey Art Museum and Special Collections, neighborhoods like the now-demolished “Little Syria,” or commemoration sites like the 9/11 Memorial and Museum), raising methodological questions about historical representation and the “public.” Students will develop projects (some examples include but are not limited to, digital maps, archives, or exhibitions; physical exhibits; or public policy proposals) that materialize and reconfigure the critical theoretical frameworks studied. No prerequisite is necessary. *CALAMEGS elective, Public Humanities elective

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Course Title: Politics of fire ! : Arts, fiction and theory in Africa and the diasporas Parmi les quatre éléments que sont la terre, l’eau, l’air, le feu, ce dernier se distingue en ce qu’il convoque de multiples métaphores du pouvoir, de la création et de la vie qui circulent sur le continent africain et dans ses multiples diasporas. Il peut renvoyer aux cosmovisions anciennes – comme Kalûnga, l’étincelle de feu qui remplit le vide premier, origine de toute création dans les cosmologies Bakongo. Il symbolise, encore, la puissance de transformation de la matière par les forgerons, analogue à l’exercice du pouvoir souverain, dans de nombreuses sociétés africaines avant les vagues de colonisations modernes. Il décrit aussi la fureur, le désir, la révolte et la volonté de justice dans les mouvements africains-américains tout-au-long du 20e siècle. Le « feu » dans ce cours, n’est pas traité comme un « objet scientifique », pour reprendre le philosophe Bachelard, mais comme un objet symbolique qui traverse les arts, la culture, les imaginaires sociaux, mentaux et spirituels sur le continent et dans ses diasporas. Comment l’image du feu, son symbole et ses représentations circulent-ils dans ces espaces de circulation libre ou contrainte des humains, des biens et des idées depuis l’époque moderne ? Peut-on tracer des affinités symboliques ou des continuités géographiques et historiques entre ces représentations ? Quels types d’imaginaires politiques et/ ou métaphysiques sont produits par cette poétique du feu? L’enjeu de ce cours ne consiste pas à compiler des représentations du feu, en les juxtaposant pour former un catalogue de références. Il entend plutôt saisir comment la puissance de l’imagination nourrit des représentations psychiques et sociales dont les symboles et les métaphores, loin d’être insignifiants, sont coordonnés les uns avec les autres. Ce qui nous permet de repenser sur un mode symbolique, culturel et poétique les liens entre l’Afrique et ses diasporas. Dans ce cours, les géographies privilégiées pour cette poétique des éléments sont l’Afrique Centrale (univers Bakongos, RDC), l’Amérique latine (Brésil) et l’Amérique du Nord (USA). Les matériaux utilisés et travaillés en classe sont artistiques (arts visuels contemporains), cinématographiques et textuels (fiction, théorie).

Title: Dante and Medieval Thought: Prose Works and Lyric Poetry Description: Dante and Medieval Thought examines the evolution of Dante Alighieri’s intellectual profile, tracing its trajectory from his youth in the Vita Nuova through the development of his mature thought in works such as De Vulgari Eloquentia, Convivio, Monarchia, Questio de Aqua et Terra, and his lyric corpus. As a poet and philosopher aware of heterodox temptations, Dante engages deeply with the European debates of his era. His prose and lyric output, while revealing the tormented nature of his reflection—often tortured by doubt—contribute an indelible chapter to the intellectual history of his generation and his precursors. Starting with the Vita Nuova—which invents autobiography in the Italian vernacular (la lingua del sì)—this course explores key themes of medieval debate. We will examine the invention of "interior writing," theories on the origins of language, and the power of the human intellect. This final theme is inextricably linked to the pursuit of earthly happiness and, as proposed in the Monarchia, the possibility of a terrestrial paradise realized within time and space. The course includes selected readings from, the works of Plato and Aristotle, as well as pagan and Christian Neoplatonic texts (Plotinus, Proclus, the Liber de Causis, Pseudo- Dionysius, and Augustine). It further examines the influence of scholastic and medieval thinkers such as Bonaventure, Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, Averroes, Siger of Brabant. While these readings are essential for a rigorous understanding of the Commedia, they also serve a broader purpose. They provide the interpretive key to the ancient and medieval traditions of rhetoric, philosophy, science and theology, as well as to Dante’s own universe.

Topics in African Literature: Africa--In Theory - Recently there has been an explosion in “theory from the South.” Some of the most exciting interventions have come from African theorists such as Ato Quayson, Achille Mbembe, and Mahmood Mamdani. Taking recent works by these theorists as our starting point, we will explore the application and adaptation of metropolitan thinkers such as Benjamin, Foucault, Derrida, and Schmitt, in order to theorize violence (“necropolitics,” genocide, xenophobia), among other burning issues. We will also take stock of earlier endeavors by Africanist and Afro-Americanist thinkers such as Du Bois, Senghor, Mudimbe, and Ngũgĩ to define critically Africa’s specific contributions to the making (and making sense of) the world that all of us inhabit. Since a number of these thinkers are also writers and/or literary theorists, we shall also be analyzing key texts by Yambo Ouologuem, Abdulrazak Gurnah, Thando Mgqolozana, Zoë Wicomb, Phaswane Mpe, and Antjie Krog. *counts for 20th c. sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Worlding Comparison: Is comparison a useful critical lens through which to understand our present world? This course questions the meanings and uses of “comparison” – an intellectual practice that seemingly issues a connective drive – in a world rife with divisions, inequity, exploitation, and extraction. Against what are often considered the Eurocentric origins of “comparison” as an analytic category, we will explore what the task of world-ing comparison could entail in terms of both shaping an intellectual practice capacious enough to grasp the totality of the world, and, at the same time, specific enough to attend to the particular demands of differently lived conditions. In so doing, the course will provide a theoretical foundation to key debates in Comparative Literature, including on disciplinarity, commensurability, translatability, relationality, and the value of literature in a rapidly evolving mediascape. Critical perspectives from postcolonial, Global South, and world literary theories (Glissant, Melas, Menon, Cheah) among others, will be placed in conversation with literary texts (Kafka, Borges, Lahiri, Xi Xi) in order to probe the capacity of comparison – and of literature – to transform “world” from a noun into an active verb, from an object of inquiry into a powerful practice of meaning-making.

title: Translation Theory: Comparative Approaches and Case Studies
description: The aim of this course is to introduce students to some key texts and issues in the history of translation theory that help us situate translation in an expanded field of comparative literary studies, cross-cultural analysis, world-making, epistemological borders, ecologies of language, politics, and media theory. Topics include: the figure of the translator/interpreter/mediator as a go-between or suspected traitor in key literary works; a brief history of translation theory; translational afterlife: questions of survival and cultural memory; debates in translation studies relating to the politics of difference and untranslatability in world literature; the politics of translation in relation to questions of nationalism, cultural appropriation, linguistic apartheid, accent tests (linguistic passporting), and outlaw dialects; the emerging field of linguistic ecology, with a focus on vocabularies of nature, planet, cosmos, ecocide, and extraction; and translation studies in the era of AI, machine translation, and computational humanities (what is a unit of translatability? How are concepts of what a language is changing? Are memes a new media language? Can algorithms be considered a language?)

sections.notes: This course will examine theories and practices of translation across languages and media as a repertoire of interpretive, expressive, and artistic techniques. We will attend to close syntactic and semantic translations of poetic and philosophical texts and learn about the technical and metaphoric uses of translation in fields like linguistics, psychoanalysis, law, artificial and machine translation, and interpretation. Students will have the possibility to test their own understanding of inter and intra-linguistic transfer through various exercises and experiments.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS V95.0951 Gramsci in the Americas : This seminar introduces students to key themes in the work of the Italian organizer and theorist Antonio Gramsci (1891-1937), with the aim of developing familiarity with pivotal terms in his corpus, including “hegemony,” the “national-popular,” “common sense,” and the “subaltern,” among several others. We examine Gramsci’s contributions to what he called a “philosophy of praxis.” The seminar subsequently turns to the ways critics in both North and South America who were part of Gramsci’s same generation developed lines of inquiry and promoted theoretical innovations comparable to his. A portion of the seminar concentrates on the work of later writers who have made use of Gramscian thought, utilizing it to think about distinct social and political situations, extending in this way Gramscian concerns throughout the twentieth and twenty-first century. Readings may include works by W. E. B. Du Bois, Carlos Nelson Coutinho, Gayatri Spivak, Randolph Bourne, and José Carlos Mariátegui.

sections.topic: Drama of Internal Alterity & Political Compromise
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Autobiographical Crash Sites: The Drama of Internal Alterity and Political Compromise: We shall examine a wide range of texts that confront a history of self in a compromised world where the very premises of selfhood must be constantly discarded and reinvented, part of a shattering linked to difficult growth spurts, politically stunted. Readings span from Rousseau and Goethe to James Baldwin, Walter Benjamin, Freud, Hannah Arendt, Kafka, Chantal Akerman, Werner Herzog and Sandy Stone, whose pathbreaking Post-Transsexual Manifesto provides some of the theoretical groundwork for establishing a hermeneutics of Bildung and transition, a recast of autobiographical theories and crucial psychoanalytic checkpoints. The failure of self-appropriation is a theme driven by Nietzsche in a number of morphs dependent on the often repressed inclusion of “the woman in Nietzsche.” Participants will be encouraged to work on their own projects that use this course as a jumping-off point for theoretical engagements with the frustrated development of self and history in an era of incessant traumatization. *Sponsored by the Department of German. Contact: lindsay.oconnor@nyu.edu

Benjamin L. Robinson | COLIT-UA 244 / GERM-UA 244 Topics: The German Intellectual Tradition: Theaters of Revolution: Politics, Theory, Drama | W 2-4:30p 4 credits |SEM Taught in English |This course investigates the relationship between revolution – as a political concept and a historical event – and modern theater. We will engage a selection of revolutionary plays alongside key theoretical writings that grapple with political change. We will practice "critical interpretation" in an expansive sense: Students will not only analyze texts through short written essays and reflections but also develop creative, performance-based responses in collaboration with peers. Readings in critical theory and the history of political thought will supplement interpretations of theatrical works by Kleist, Büchner, Brecht, Müller, Weiss, Özdamar, Jelinek, Holzinger. **This is a crosslisted course originating in another department and does not count towards the Comp Lit major or minor core requirements.

sections.topic: Coal, Oil, and Nuclear Novels and Films
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS V95.0550005 Energy Aesthetics: Coal, Oil, and Nuclear Novels and Films: This course explores the relationship between energy regimes and aesthetic production. It considers the distinctive qualities of artworks made in eras shaped by coal, oil, and nuclear energy as well as the role writers, filmmakers, and other artists have played in public debates about industrialization from the late nineteenth century to the present. Readings and films center the experiences of marginalized peoples who have been disproportionately affected by energy extraction and nuclear armament in the United States and the former Soviet space. They also confirm the power of storytelling for exposing injustice and mobilizing the public against it.

Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS V33.0300 This course will survey literature produced at various points in the tumult of modern Chinese history, from the early Twentieth Century through to the present day. While the time period will be broad, we will hope to engage in close, critical readings of significant works of fiction from a selection of major authors writing in Chinese. Most of the course will focus on writers from Mainland China, with the inclusion of several examples of works from the broader Sinosphere. How do certain concerns of modernity arise in different texts, at different times, and for different writers in different places? What different relationships do we see being shaped between literature, life, and politics, and how does fiction negotiate certain tensions and anxieties about modern and contemporary life? By exploring a variety of engaging novels and short stories, we will hope to gain a more nuanced understanding of modern writing in Chinese, and the role that fiction has played as both an agent of modernity and a reflection of modern “Chinese” life, broadly conceived. *This is a crosslisted course originating in another department and does not count towards the Comp Lit major or minor core requirements.

GADBERRY| COLIT-UA.800 / IDSEM-UG 2257: The Witch (in Theory) | M/W 9:30AM - 10:45AM|Silver RM 508| In this class, we will study the infamous witch-hunts and witch trials of early modern Europe alongside twentieth- and twenty-first-century attempts to grasp the conditions that led to them. Just what do the notorious witch-hunts and femicides of renaissance Europe have to do with the emergence of capitalism and the constitution of “secular modernity”? How do witches, witchcraft, and witch-hunts represent a challenge for explanation or interpretation, and what do witches have to do with the production and theorization of knowledge, with accounts of intimacy and individuation? How might explanations of witchcraft amount to theories about how words work, about linguistic efficacy or the limits of language? Our course arrives shortly after the twentieth anniversary of an important theoretical work on our topic, namely, Silvia Federici’s Caliban and the Witch (2004); we will follow Federici’s cue to ask what the witch has to do with theories of history, language, and knowledge. Our approach will be selective rather than exhaustive: we will study early modern works alongside political philosophical and feminist recuperations of the witch, and we will likewise examine historical, anthropological, and sociological treatments of the witch in relationship to social explanation. Along the way, we will read comparatively on witchcraft, sorcery, and magic.*sponsored by Gallatin Contact: Jason Yi: jason.yi@nyu.edu Note: these courses do count as core courses toward the Major or Minor .

sections.topic: Eros and Sexuality in Modern Jewish Lit
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. What’s love got to do with it? This question has been debated by Jewish writers since the inception of modern Jewish literature. For decades, Jewish authors, artists, and intellectuals negotiated the status of romantic and sexual love within Judaism, often as a troubling, at times alien, subject matter in the context of Jewishness and the Jewish tradition. With the rise of modern Yiddish and Hebrew literatures in the beginning of the twentieth century, writers articulated new modes of conceiving desire, love, sex, and gender, especially as they related to Jewish society and politics, and these issues continue to be debated within the different avenues of Jewish culture today. This course is devoted to exploring the transforming status of eros and sexuality in Jewish culture by focusing on a diverse selection of literary works, alongside drama, film, and academic essays. Building on feminist and queer theory, our discussions will revolve around issues such as sexual politics and nationalism, love and religion, border-crossing, constructions of femininity and masculinity, and queer love. All materials are available in English translation. Sponsored by the Department of Hebrew & Judaic Studies. Contact: kln2049@nyu.edu. *This is a crosslisted course originating in another department and does not count towards the Comp Lit major or minor core requirements.

title: Studies in Prose Genres
description: In this course we focus on four contemporary novels in which the world of the character, the narrator, or the author, is read through the lens of a literary classic. In each case, the reading and rewriting of the primary text involves temporal and spatial displacements (from the 18th to the 20th century, from Europe to the Caribbean and to the South Pacific) that generate shifting perspectives and a constant reshuffling of center and periphery. Between a reverential affiliation to the past and a creative misreading and rewriting of it, these intertextual encounters with « great » Western literary works insistently raise the questions of identity, originality, and “writing back”. Exploring these questions will therefore also involve drawing on comparative, translation, and postcolonial studies.

title: Kafka and His Contexts
description: The course is focused on exploring Franz Kafka’s work – stories, novels, diaries and letters – in the context of fin de siècle Prague and the birth of modernism. We will take a closer look at the cultural and social context of Central Europe (literature and the arts, but also the Modernist architecture of Adolf Loos, Simmel’s sociology of the metropolitan life, Freud’s analysis of the unconscious, Brentano’s psychology, the resonance of Nietzsche’s philosophy, or the emergence of new media like phonograph and silent film) in the first two decades of the 20th century. In addition, we will discuss the adaptations of Kafka’s work and its impact on later art, fiction and film (Borges, Welles, Kundera, Roth, Švankmajer). The topics discussed through Kafka’s writings and other related works include: man and metropolis, family, estrangement, authorship, time, writing and media, travelling, territories and identities, languages, animals, art and pain. We will be especially interested in how these phenomena transform when represented in and through the medium of literary fiction.

title: Topics in 19th Century Lit
description: Romantic, Victorian, and Modernist writers in both Britain and the United States were fascinated by Italy. Shelly and Byron were inspired by the hope of a new political dawn in the Italian Risorgimento. Robert Browning, George Eliot, and E. M. Forster saw the transition from Medieval to Renaissance culture in Florence as mirroring and offering an example for their own struggles to free themselves from the repression and religious orthodoxy of Victorian England. Henry James and Edith Wharton saw Italy as beautiful and dangerous in equal measure and used it as the setting of stories about the clash of old world and new world cultures. T. S. Eliot and Ezra Pound were both profoundly influenced by Dante. As you can see, the "Italy and Italians" of the title refers not only to images and characters in the works of the British and American authors we will be reading but also to the influences of Italian literature on literature in English. Recurring themes in the course will be history and its uses in literature, gender and sexuality, democracy and aristocracy, language and power, and religion as an instrument of sexual repression. There will also be theoretical components, introducing you to various critical approaches to literature: psychoanalytic criticism, gender studies, post-colonial studies, and Harold Bloom's theory of the anxiety of influence.

EAST-UA 950-001 – Topics in Asian Studies: Gender, Revolution, Livelihood: Modern and Contemporary Chinese Women Writers | Crosslisted with: Comparative Literature (COLIT-UA 950) | Time: MW 9:30–10:45 |The goals of this course are two-fold: it surveys and introduces the representative works of moder Chinese women writers on the one hand and, on the other, examines and tackles general problems, such as equality and liberation, desire, and subjectivity. We ask the following questions: What do patriarchy, the new marriage law, and revolution mean for modern Chinese women? What are their responses to the unprecedented historical and social changes during the 20th century? How do the problems of gender challenge and complicate our understanding of colonization, revolution, modernity, and identity? This course explores the above questions mainly through the novels and short stories written by modern Chinese women writers. *Sponsored by the Department of East Asian Studies. Contact: Keyssa Reyes. *This is a crosslisted course originating in another department and does not count towards the Comp Lit major or minor core requirements.

title: African Women Playwrights
description: African Women Playwrights is a reading-intensive course that focuses on the structural and narrative diversification of the theatrical texts written by women from the continent in the 20th and 21st century. We’ll critique the plays as both literature and dramatic texts intended for production. What is clearly evident in African women playwrights’ writing is its focus on women’s agency; generational legacies; tensions among tradition, colonialism, and modernism; unresolved issues between tribal and national identities; family relationships; intimacy and commitment; the spiritual conflicts set from among the worlds of rituals, polytheism and monotheism; the challenging coexistence among Christianity, Islam and Judaism; the impact of the global diaspora on African identity; and the intersecting issues of blackness, Africanness and womanhood.

title: Proseminar: Theory and Methods in the Social Sciences: Interdisciplinary Perspectives
description: This seminar, designed for incoming M.A. students, provides a broad introduction to theories and methods that have shaped the interdisciplinary terrain of the social sciences. The course emphasizes the reading of classic and more contemporary works of social theory and methodology, with a focus on key concepts and thinkers. How does one define a society? What is culture? How have social and cultural processes been understood? What is the relationship between a society or culture and a social group, an institution, or an individual? What is the nature of power, difference and identity? How do such foundational questions generate theories of modernity, capitalism, nationalism and globalization? How do such foundational questions orient the variety of disciplines within the social sciences? The course also surveys qualitative and quantitative methodologies, exploring the relationship between theory, methods, and the broader goals of research within the social sciences. Empirically grounded writings will explore the links between research frameworks, methodologies, data collection and theoretical claims. Readings will include classic texts by Karl Marx and Max Weber and more contemporary theorists such as Michel Foucault, David Harvey and Judith Butler, among others. Guest lectures by Gallatin faculty will introduce students to a range of methodologies (ethnography, quantitative data sets, the case study method, documentary analysis, interviewing and survey methods) and interdisciplinary research frameworks.

sections.notes: Open to Gallatin MA students only.

title: Proseminar in the Arts: Why Do You Want to Make It, and How Can You Make It Better?
description: This course is intended for Gallatin graduate students in their first or second semester who will be pursuing an artistic thesis. Students who have advanced past their second semester are encouraged to contact the professor in advance of taking the class to be sure the parameters of the class will be appropriate. The class aims to pose difficult and productive questions that will help you understand your tendencies and priorities as an artist, the methods you employ, and where these are in the service of the work as opposed to where they stand in the way. The class requires rigorous and individualized research into your sources of artistic influence with an emphasis on analytical thinking about the methods and strategies employed by those artists or thinkers you consider key influences. The course includes assignments that explore your existing strategies and subject matter in order to understand what has motivated and generated the work thus far. Other assignments push students to work against the grain of their usual modes in order to discover new ways of working and to undermine default strategies. Towards the end of the term, the accumulated insights will be channeled into writing about your work that will be useful in the future context of an artist’s statement or artistic aims essay. In the personal and lab-like atmosphere that this course hopes to cultivate, the class also aims to connect Gallatin graduate students to each other’s work and practice, and to take advantage of the enormous importance that peer input and critique can have on work in progress. Possible side effects include: focused engagement, enhanced motivation, collaboration.

title: Proseminar in the Humanities: Culture and Globalization
description: This proseminar explores how to do interdisciplinary research in the humanities. To exemplify this approach, our subject is Africa-China relations. China’s controversial investment in Africa causes reactions ranging from accusations of a “new colonialism” to celebrations of a collaborative “win-win” for development. Also, immigration both by Africans to China and by Chinese to Africa signals a shift in global power dynamics and an opening of a new era of multi-polar globalization. Through an analysis of media, history, literature, political economy, sociology, film, and art this seminar examines the interdisciplinary nature of these relations. We ask what are the connections between the longue durée of history and the contemporary moment? How do different actors at state and individual levels engage with Africa-China relations? What are the symbolic dimensions of these relations? And finally, how does this shift to multi-polarity impact theories of globalization across disciplines?

title: Proseminar: Creative Writing Across Genres
description: This course is for Gallatin MA students who will be pursuing an artistic thesis that incorporates creative or dramatic writing (novel, poetry, screenplay, drama, memoir, cultural criticism, etc.) The class helps students understand and develop the genres, methods, and research practices that they will employ in writing and in situating their work within literary traditions. By close reading across genres, students will learn to identify and critique their own sources of writerly influence with an emphasis on thinking about the methods and strategies employed by these writers. This course’s workshop structure aims to connect Gallatin MA graduate students with each other through sharing their work and practice. Students will then draw on these frameworks and approaches as they draft the Thesis Proposal during the Thesis Proposal Seminar.

sections.notes: Open to Gallatin MA students only.

title: Proseminar: Interpretation and Textual Analysis
description: This interdisciplinary seminar for incoming MA students introduces a series of key theoretical debates about interpretation and textual analysis. Beginning with thinkers like Marx and Freud whose work underpinned theories of interpretation in the early part of the twentieth century, we will then move into debates about the location of meaning that challenged the ways in which scholars, artists, and critics conceived of their work. The course continues with close analysis of the “high theory” of the 1970s and 80s, such as New Historicism, structuralism, deconstruction, and cultural studies which both reflected and fomented broader shifts within the contemporary Western world. We will conclude our survey with twenty-first century approaches to interpretation, including material culture, postcolonialism, feminist and queer theory. A portion of each class will be devoted to applying the readings to students’ own research projects. Students will emerge from the course with a strong understanding of the interpretive theories of the past century and will be encouraged to use the course's introductory framework to further develop the theoretical underpinnings of their own work in the Thesis Proposal Seminar.

title: Master's Thesis I
description: Master's Thesis I Registration Form: https://forms.gallatin.nyu.edu/node/377 In Master's Thesis I, students work under the supervision of the adviser and independently on the thesis research, project, or artistic work described in their thesis proposals. While students and advisers each work in their own ways, Master's Thesis I typically involves activities such as mapping the academic field, compiling an annotated bibliography, creating a draft outline, and completing a chapter draft or some equivalent portion of an artistic work. The goal for MT I is for students to advance significantly from the proposal stage into the drafting and execution stage of their project. Student and adviser (the grading instructor for this class) should plan to meet at least four times during the semester and students should plan to submit at least 15-20 pages of draft material to their adviser by semester's end. Students creating an artistic thesis should aim to have 15-20 pages of draft material of the research essay and to have made a firm start on the artistic work by the end of MTI. Master's Thesis I culminates in the RAW Forum (Research and Writing Forum) and the Works in Progress (for performance based theses) where students present their work on panels for comments from faculty. Participation in the RAW Forum and Works in Progress is optional but strongly recommended. Students will receive information about Raw Forum scheduling later in the semester. All students are required to attend a mandatory information session for Master's Thesis I during the first week of classes. For more information about registering for this course, see https://gallatin.nyu.edu/academics/registration/graduate/MTI-registration-instructions.html

school: Robert F. Wagner Graduate School of Public Service
title: Statistical Methods I
description: This course introduces students to basic statistical methods and their application to management, policy, and financial decision-making. The course covers the essential elements of descriptive statistics, univariate and bivariate statistical inference, and introduces multivariate analysis. In addition to covering statistical theory the course emphasizes applied statistics and data analysis, using the software package, Stata. The course has several "audiences" and goals. For all Wagner students, the course develops basic skills and encourages a critical approach to reviewing statistical findings and using statistical reasoning in decision making. For those planning to continue studying statistics (often those in policy and finance concentrations) this course additionally provides the foundation for that further work.
