title: Writing Narrative
description: This course is for graduate students who wish to strengthen their creative writing skills or acquire more experience in narrative prose: stories and novels, of course, but also memoirs, essays, biographies, travel narratives, first-person journalism and any form where story is a structural element. It's a foundational course, covering basic concepts such as structure, point of view, dialogue, character development, modes of realism, figurative language, and narrative drive, but it will also serve as a refresher for students returning to the writing process. One primary goal is to provide a firm head start on creative projects, though for some, this will also be a chance to assess commitment before getting in too deep. Assignments will include short weekly writing exercises, responses to Brightspace discussion boards, and at least one longer piece to be discussed workshop-style and significantly revised as a final. Readings in various genres will alternate with essays on craft; assignments will include works by Alice Munro, Stephen Millhauser, Edward P. Jones , Louise Erdrich, Haruki Murakami, Annie Dillard, John Gardner, Francine Prose, David Foster Wallace, Italo Calvino, Joan Didion, Janet Malcolm and Zadie Smith, among others.

sections.notes: Open to MA and PhD students. Advanced undergraduates require instructor permission.

title: Trauma, Communities, and the Politics of Suffering
description: Diagnoses and discussions of individual trauma have become all but ubiquitous. And yet collective trauma has not received the same level of public attention or disciplinary development. This course seeks to track the emergent field of Collective Trauma over the last several decades. We will explore the ways in which forms of social suffering and trauma have been theorized, examined, and "treated," while critically engaging the psychological, cultural, and political implications thereof. Collective or cultural trauma is thought to emanate from cultural upheaval and formidable challenges to the social and moral order. In class and in our readings, we will attempt to map key contours of this multivalent disciplinary field and its related practices. We will explore a variety of theoretical and empirical sources, as well as case studies on topics such as: Truth commissions and reparations; intergenerational and epigenetic trauma; the Covid pandemic and mental health crises among teens; atrocity and indigenous modes of healing; memorials and the politics of memory; activism and communal healing linked to gun violence; displacement and foced migration; PTSD and sexual violence; art-based therapeutic methods; racialized modes of structural violence; climate change and community trauma, to name a few. Some of the authors/artists/activists we will explore include Didier Fassin, Gloria Anzaldua, Yael Danieli, Paul Farmer, Ta Nehisi Coates, Stef Craps, Susan Sontag, Jefferey Alexander, Franz Fanon, Gloria Anzaldua, and Judith Butler.

sections.notes: equal to MA OR equal to PhD Open to MA and PhD students. Advanced undergraduates require instructor permission.

title: Black/Human
description: As part of ongoing struggle against police brutality, environmental injustice, mass incarceration and white supremacist violence, activists, artists, academics and everyday folk are wondering aloud about how antiblackness shapes the world we live in. Both plea and protest, the insistence that black lives matter activates and animates an older, yet enduring concern that centers the vexed relationship between blackness and the (properly) human. In this course we will consider what it means to treat the question of the relation between the black and the human as a radically open one. We will read widely in black studies, with an emphasis on recent literature that forwards urgent and profound critiques of humanism. Our readings--which include essays by Sylvia Wynter, Hortense Spillers, Saidiya Hartman and Frank Wilderson, Jared Sexton, Fred Moten, Joao Vargas and Zakiyyah Jackson--provide us with an occasion to consider what modes of being, politics, aesthetics and sociality are enabled or dis-abled by thinking blackness outside of the category of the human. Some of the inquiries to be foregrounded here are: What are the stakes in decoupling our study of blackness from humanism? Do the models of thinking "beyond" the human offered by post-humanism, new materialism, and animal studies inadequately incorporate a racial history that posits blacks as sub- or inhuman? What do we make of new works that rethink this history of black life alongside the live(lines)s of objects, machines and animals? Over the course of the semester we will devote much time to exploring the intricacies of this new and exciting literature, thereby deepening our awareness of why it has sparked such intense and lively discussion and debate.

sections.notes: Open to MA and PhD students. Advanced undergraduates require instructor permission.

title: Graphic Histories
description: How do we represent historical events graphically? How can we use drawing to practice paying attention to historical images? How do we generate new perspectives when telling histories with multiple narratives? Similar to the impact that The 1619 Project has had by reaching a broader audience, could graphic histories raise the visibility of previously marginalized stories and allow us to rethink long-held beliefs about our past? In this methods-focused course, we will read and analyze historical scholarship and graphic histories in a case- study approach in order to determine how best to work with primary sources to create our own graphic histories with diverse representation. This course relies on the philosophy and techniques of Lynda Barry and Ivan Brunetti with the underlying belief that anyone can draw. No prior drawing experience is required. Readings may include works by Kyle Baker, Meg-John Barker, Jason Eaglespeaker, Ebony Flowers, Rebecca Hall, Ken Krimstein, Nora Krug, John Lewis, Scott McCloud, Eric Orner, Frank “Big Black” Smith, Anna Veltfort, and Gene Leun Yang. Guest speakers may include authors, illustrators, historians, publishers, and visual storytellers.

title: Deans' Service Scholars: Language & Power
description: Linguist James Paul Gee has described English language teachers as standing ‚ “at the heart of the most crucial educational, cultural, and political issues of our time.” This Deans’ Service Scholars course places students at the intersection of service learning, English language teaching, and critical applied linguistics. It is designed to integrate experiential learning with an exploration of the broader forces which influence educational settings. The course is both a study and application of service-learning, a pedagogy combining academic inquiry and engagement with a community outside the university. In the fall semester, with the support of faculty and in partnership with a local volunteer organization, Scholars will teach English at a local school for migrant communities in Shanghai. At the same time, through discussion seminars, readings, and reflective writing, Scholars will explore the social, cultural, and political factors which often intersect with language teaching, and consider how these factors operate in the context of their service learning project. Seminar topics will include linguistic imperialism, language stigma and status, English as a lingua franca, and the recent rise of global Englishes. In the spring semester, Scholars will organize a community engagement project which is based on their experiential and course learning in the fall. Through coursework, volunteer teaching, and community engagement, Scholars will also gain experience in the pedagogical and service approaches of Project-Based Learning (PBL) and Participatory Action Research (PAR). Notes: Application is required for course enrollment. The link can be accessed on the course webpage. Language and Power course webpage, https://shanghai.nyu.edu/page/language-and-power. Prerequisite: None. Fulfillment: General Elective.

title: Literature of Modern Ireland I

sections.notes: SAME AS G58.1083 & G65.1086. Literature of Modern Ireland I, “Republicanism” is a complex term across a broad range of scholarship in Politics, History, Philosophy and Literature. This course will examine how the various strands of republicanism that emerge in the Renaissance in England took on different and yet more complex meanings in Ireland. We will read first a range of English Renaissance texts for their implications about the application of English power in Ireland. We will then consider how the 17th century Republican revolution in England established a set of ideas about Ireland and Irish culture that impacted the emergence of an Irish literature in the eighteenth century. We will then survey how Irish writers sustained and developed republican political ideas in the wake of the American and French Revolutions into the United Irish movement of the 1790s. Lastly, we will consider how the Act of Union, passed as a response to the 1798 Rebellion, had enormous and long-lasting implications for the shape and tenor of Irish writing in the 19th century and beyond. The course will conclude with a consideration of how republicanism evolved in response to the political crisis of the state form in 20th and 21st century Ireland. Authors read on the course include Spenser, Shakespeare, Milton, Swift, Burke, Edgeworth, and a wide range of Irish writers working across multiple genres. These literary texts will be read alongside select debates in political theory and Atlantic history.

title: Topics in Medieval Lit
description: Topics within the field of Medieval literature vary from semester to semester, depending on the instructor.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. The Medieval Miscellany This course will focus on a series of manuscripts produced in late-medieval England that have been grouped by scholars in the loose and highly permeable category of “miscellanies”: a “provisional term,” as Georg N. Knauer has put it, “for a manuscript of mixed contents.” Indeed, given the rich variety of these manuscripts’ inclusions--everything from romances and lyrics to prayers, charms, lists, recipes, and prognostications--one aim of the course will be to explore a broad spectrum of texts that usually fall outside the scope of surveys of medieval literature. On another level, our aim will be to investigate the very idea of miscelleneity: are these manuscripts considered miscellaneous simply because to modern scholars they appear to be a hodge-podge of everything but the proverbial kitchen sink? Or do they exhibit methods of organization that have not so far been discerned? Or do they exemplify an “order” that may properly be termed “miscellaneous” and thus attest to an aesthetic of miscelleneity? In considering these questions, we’ll examine the material facts of each of our miscellanies in detail and undertake a study of medieval “literacies” and modes of textual production and transmission in late-medieval England (in this way the course will also serve as an introduction to manuscript studies). In addition, we’ll put the terms miscellany and miscelleneity in dialogue with their more orderly twins--the anthology and monumentality--and, in turn, with the concepts and categories that underwrite them, including genre, the author, the scribe, the reader, and the book. This dialogue will be aided by our readings of a range of scholars and critics--from Hugh of St. Victor to Deleuze and Guatari--and by our consideration of such contemporary phenomena as blogging and scrapbooking. Finally, we’ll bring our study to bear on the question of how best to make these “miscellanies” available to students and scholars; this thread of the course will entail transcribing texts from medieval manuscripts (either from digital or photographic facsimiles) and a trip to Columbia University’s Rare Books and Manuscripts Library to see a selection of real “live” miscellanies.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Course Description: Dante and Medieval Thought: Prose Works and Lyric Poetry examines the evolution of Dante Alighieri’s intellectual profile, tracing its trajectory from his youth in the Vita Nuova through the development of his mature thought in works such as De Vulgari Eloquentia, Convivio, Monarchia, Questio de Aqua et Terra, and his lyric corpus. As a poet and philosopher aware of heterodox temptations, Dante engages deeply with the European debates of his era. His prose and lyric output, while revealing the tormented nature of his reflection—often tortured by doubt—contribute an indelible chapter to the intellectual history of his generation and his precursors. Starting with the Vita Nuova—which invents autobiography in the Italian vernacular (la lingua del sì)—this course explores key themes of medieval debate. We will examine the invention of "interior writing," theories on the origins of language, and the power of the human intellect. This final theme is inextricably linked to the pursuit of earthly happiness and, as proposed in the Monarchia, the possibility of a terrestrial paradise realized within time and space. The course includes selected readings from the works of Plato and Aristotle, as well as pagan and Christian Neoplatonic texts (Plotinus, Proclus, the Liber de Causis, Pseudo-Dionysius, and Augustine). It further examines the influence of scholastic and medieval thinkers such as Bonaventure, Albertus Magnus, Thomas Aquinas, Averroes, Siger of Brabant. While these readings are essential for a rigorous understanding of the Commedia, they also serve a broader purpose. They provide the interpretive key to the ancient and medieval traditions of rhetoric, philosophy, science and theology, as well as to Dante’s own universe.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS DRAP-GA 2323. This graduate seminar offers an intensive exploration of Montaigne’s Essais (1580-95) as a work that invents a new form of experimental and exploratory prose. Over the course of the semester we will read substantial portions of this huge work, often honing in on specific passages, in order to attend closely not to Montaigne’s thought but to his thinking. Montaigne talks about many topics, from the seemingly insignificant (for example, thumbs!) to the obviously consequential (such as death, civil war, the ontological similarities between humans and non-humans, or the devastating impact of European colonialism in the Americas), so we shall also cover many topics – but throughout, we will pay particular attention to Montaigne’s writing as writing and to the ways in which the Essais, even when dealing with the toughest of questions, always remain hesitant, open, uncertain. Montaigne himself often interrupts his thinking to comment on his writing. In one chapter (III.13), Montaigne writes how we often “fail to recognize the natural sickness of [our] minds, which does nothing but range and ferret about, ceaselessly twisting and contriving and, like our silkworms, becoming entangled in its own works,” which is also a fair description of his prose style. At another point (III.9), he says that his writings are nothing but “the excrements of an old mind.” To take the Essais seriously, then, is not to extract from them any stable doctrine or position on any given topic, but to inhabit this movement of mind as it unfolds and re-folds on each and every page. This seminar will thus ask ultimately to compose a self that is provisional, digressive, and perpetually revised. Students may read in French (Villey-Saulnier edition) or English (Screech’s translation). Class discussion will be in English. We will have several guest lecturers.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS DRAP-GA .2661. First Person Narratives: Victorian and Contemporary Novels with Professor Robson. This seminar will examine two groups of novels. In the first half of the semester we will conduct an intensive study of four mid-Victorian works of fiction (Charlotte Bronte's Jane Eyre and Villette; Emily Bronte's Wuthering Heights; and Charles Dickens's David Copperfield); in the second half, we will analyze a number of British and American novels published since 2000 (Zoe Heller's Notes on a Scandal/What Was She Thinking?; Lionel Shriver's We Need To Talk About Kevin; Kazuo Ishiguro's Never Let Me Go; Julian Barnes's The Sense of an Ending; Barbara Kingsolver’s Demon Copperhead; and Julia May Jonas’s Vladimir.) We will have two driving concerns throughout. The first is formal. After becoming familiar with narratological terminology and concepts, we'll aim to define key differences in affect and world-view between novels in which the narrator is the protagonist and those in which he or she is peripheral to the central story. The second is thematic. All of our novels, nineteenth-and twenty-first century, concern themselves one way or another with schools, universities, scenes of learning, pedagogical moments, and so forth. We'll consider the very close links that are thereby forged between educational structures and ideas of properly-ordered selves; we'll also be considering the relationships between these two normative forms and the acts of violence and desire that are graphically depicted in our novels. Expect our readings to be supported by critical texts by theorists Jan Starobinski, Robyn Warhol; D. A. Miller; Galen Strawson; Fredric Jameson; Anna Kornbluh, and others.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS DRAP-GA 2838. Writing the modern city with Professor Augst. This graduate seminar explores the aesthetics, ethics, and politics of identity in modern and contemporary American literature, tracing the continuous remaking of the self against the backdrops of urbanization, mass culture, and rapid media change. Taking up the relation between historical experience and artistic form, it samples the literary imagination of identity and community as they evolve alongside transformations in American society from the late nineteenth century to the present. How did the American novel greet the changes of the 20th century, and how did ordinary experience itself become a character in larger stories about modern and postmodern life in the United States, ranging from the experiences of immigration and racial conflict, mass consumption and social alienation, personal liberation and cultural innovation? What resources of perspective and scale, character and setting, temporality and fragmentation have the novel, life-writing, poetry, and autofiction furnished for writers and readers as they seek to map emergent geographies of race, gender, class, and sexuality? What do literary representations of authenticity and immediacy tell us about the local and global horizons of the self in our contemporary digital moment? Tentative readings include Theodore Dreiser's Sister Carrie, John Dos Passos's Manhattan Transfer, James Baldwin’s Another Country, Toni Morrison's The Bluest Eye, David Wojanrowicz's Close to the Knives, Karen Tei Yamashita's Tropic of Orange, Patricia Lockwood's Nobody is Talking About This, selected poetry by Ginsberg and O'Hara, among other works. The course will also survey a variety of critical and theoretical perspectives [Simmel, Kracauer, Foucault, Baudrillard, Chun, Kornbluh, Zuboff, etc.]. Requirements include active participation in course discussions and class presentations, as well as analytical writing.

Borders and Diaspora This seminar examines borders and diasporas as material realities and conceptual practices, specifically as they are deployed, recalibrated, visualized, and reimagined by scholars, writers, artists, archivists, activists, cultural workers, and others in and beyond the interdisciplinary field of Latinx Studies. Paying particular attention to questions of colonization, slavery, genocide, state violence, and multiple relocations and dislocations within and in excess of a national frame of reference, we will discuss how the entanglement of border formation and diasporic movement can both expand and challenge the parameters of theory and public practice, subaltern and imperial histories, and community and institutional transformation under conditions of corporatized research university systems. In addition to readings of classic and contemporary texts from Latinx and cultural studies (potentially including authors such as Juan Flores, Gloria Anzaldúa, Lorgia García Peña, Emma Pérez, Stuart Hall, Paul Gilroy, Norma Alarcón, Alán Pelaez Lopez, Kency Cornejo, and others), the class will feature interactive guest presentations by and/or visits with practitioners whose work is remapping our understanding of borders and diasporas in and beyond literary and cultural studies. While this seminar approaches borders and diasporas largely through the field of Latinx Studies, students are welcome and encouraged to engage borders and diasporas in ways that align with their own research. Students will have the option of undertaking a final project in lieu of a research paper, and the course syllabus, discussions, and programming will make room for emerging modes of public engagement, including community archives and activism.

Narrative Theory/Novel Theory-- This course will be a dynamic, multi-faceted, creatively challenging introduction to theories of narrative and the novel. In addition to canonical sources (Auerbach, Watt, Bakhtin, Shklovsky, Said, Bhabha, Jakobson, Lukacs, Barthes) we will read a selection of works of fiction about fiction: Montes’s The Time of the Novel, Franketienne’s Ready to Burst, Calvino’s If on a winter’s night a traveler, Barth’s “Lost in the Funhouse.” There will be creative weekly assignments and experiments, and students will have the option of writing a research paper or their own work of metafiction as a final project.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS G65.2917 Gender on Display: Image and Ideology in Modern Culture: This seminar examines the making of modern gender in the age of images. As modern systems of sex, sexuality, and racial difference were consolidated in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries, new visual technologies were transforming everyday life and reshaping the conditions of visibility itself. In the United States, these developments coincided with the consolidation of modern state power and an expanding global presence, giving gendered images unusual force in organizing social and political life. What emerged was a new culture of gender in which masculinity and femininity could be staged, circulated, and politicized with unprecedented force. Treating gender as an ideological construction and a powerful engine of political feeling, the seminar explores how new ways of seeing reshaped gendered life and became entangled with race, nationalism, consumer culture, and the aesthetic appeal of fascism. Our theoretical itinerary will move through accounts of ideology (Marx, Althusser, Williams), visuality and mediation (Feuerbach, Crary, Sontag), modern gender and sexuality systems (Laqueur, Chauncey, Canaday), race and representation (hooks, Dyer, Campt), and commodity culture and fascist aesthetics (Benjamin, Mosse, Halberstam, Gil’Adí). Readings in theory and criticism will be paired with literary and visual works from modernity into the digital present, allowing us to trace how gender moves between page and screen, body and image, and aesthetic form and political life.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS G65.2917 The long twentieth century saw the decline of the inversion model of understanding queer desire (the idea that a person has a psychological sex at odds with their assigned sex) and the rise of the same-sex model that shapes scientific and popular understanding to this day. Ultimately this development scripted the severing of homosexuality from transsexuality in both the psychiatric manuals for mental disorders and in the headlines of tabloids. But whereas these organs of two very different kinds of bourgeois social power increasingly distinguished a gay person from a trans person, the gritty, working-class spaces in which LGBT life flourished did not view these lines as bright and fast. These parallel historical processes, distinguished by class register, shaped gay sociality and literature as they emerged as genres unto themselves in the twentieth century. This course studies the social history and literary reflection of this dual process: the solidarities forged, antagonisms stoked, and aesthetic forms invented to address this recontouring of the landscape of gender and sexuality. Our literary readings will begin with early depictions of fairies and inverts in works by Proust, fin-de-sieclé sexologists, and Claude McKay. Then we will move to the mid-century when gay and trans identities had permeated bourgeois notice with works by Truman Capote, Thomas Savage, and Leslie Feinberg. Finally we’ll consider recent works that emerge from trans writers who are finally able to write without assuming the cisness of their audience; writers include Akwaeke Emezi, Jules Gill-Peterson, and Torrey Peters.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. In this seminar we will read (and occasionally listen to) poems, books, and other works by and about some contemporary poets, mainly in English, some in translation. While most will be 21st-C. works, some readings will come from elsewhere—17th C. Japan, 18th C. Scotland, 19th C. Britain, 19th C. USA. Among the questions we will keep open: what might be (and has been) configured as poetry, and what might be configured as “contemporary.” (As David Hockney has said, “If it’s speaking to you now, it’s contemporary.” Or consider Ezra Pound: “All ages are contemporaneous.” Or Gertrude Stein: “Now./Not now./And now./Now.”) En route we will read some works in poetics and theory, with particular attention to ecological, formal, historical, socio-political, and linguistic concerns. Seminarians will present on critical readings; all will undertake experimental as well as critical writing. Readings may include works by anonymous balladeers, Mosab Abu Toha, Theodor Adorno, Giorgio Agamben, Roland Barthes, Matsuo Bashō, Emile Benveniste, Sean Bonney, Anne Boyer, Inger Christensen, Tonya Foster, Annelyse Gelman, Terrance Hayes, Robin Coste Lewis, Harryette Mullen, Claude Rankine, Paisley Rekdal, Lisa Robertson, Margaret Ronda, Robyn Schiff, Juliana Spahr, Gertrude Stein, Donna Stonecipher, Brian Teare, William Wordsworth, Monica Youn. Walt Whitman’s Song of Myself will companion us throughout, as will Jennifer Chang Crandall’s documentary video project, “Whitman, Alabama.”

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. This course is based in critical traditions and theories of care tied to twentieth and twenty-first century social movements across North America. Our understanding of theory will be broadly construed: we’ll be studying scholarship, organizing materials, manifestos, documentary film, memoir, poetry, zines, etc. We’ll be thinking with texts that recognize care, the everyday reproduction of life, as profoundly valuable – from disability justice to queer and trans care networks to Black, Indigenous, migrant, and Marxist feminisms to mutual aid and to the world-building work of blockades and encampments. This is a recognition of care’s value pitted against an overwhelming culture of carelessness, itself thriving on invisibilized and devalued care labor. How has care been theorized from sites of neglect, abandonment, and crisis? To what ends has the promise of “care” been leveraged, and how do we care for each other outside the state and the nuclear family? What does an attention to care make possible on a rapidly changing planet? We’ll study movements and collectives like: Wages for Housework, The Young Lords, The Combahee River Collective, ACT UP, Sins Invalid, NoDAPL, and Mutual Aid Disaster Relief. Likely care theorists on the syllabus include: Kathi Weeks, Nancy Fraser, Mierle Laderman Ukeles, Audre Lorde, Saidiya Hartman, Sandy Grande, Michelle Murphy, Samuel R. Delany, Hil Malatino, Dean Spade, Sunaura Taylor, and many others.

Alienation and Freedom in 20th Century French Psychoanalysis, Psychiatry and Psychology A significant proportion of the most interesting and intriguing French “theorists” of the later 20th century, such as Georges Canguilhem, Frantz Fanon, Félix Guattari, Michel Foucault, Jacques Lacan, Francesc Tosquelles, emerged from a broadly common medical and political disciplinary background which drew on what in the English-speaking world are regarded as the separate and distinct “p-disciplines” of philosophy, psychiatry, psychoanalysis and psychology. In this course we will attempt to reconstitute the dynamic interactions within this intermingling milieu both historically and philosophically. Will be looking at work originally conceived within a Marxist framework that developed into the anti-psychiatries of the later 20th century. The course will entail a close reading of texts by those named above along with other related intellectuals such as Gaston Bachelard, Franco Basaglia, Gilles Deleuze, Fyodor Dostoevsky, R. D. Laing, Jean-Paul Sartre and Maurice Merleau-Ponty, with a focus on the issues of existential alienation and freedom that characterized the thinking of this era.

title: Introduction to the Study of Literature
description: Open to English majors and minors only. Conducted in a seminar format. Introduces students to the demands and pleasures of university-level investigation of English literature. Students develop the tools necessary for advanced criticism, including close-reading skills, knowledge of generic conventions, mastery of critical terminology, and skill at a variety of modes of analysis, from the formal to the historical. Also emphasizes the writing process, with the production of four to five formal papers.

sections.notes: Designed for English majors and minors, this course focuses on the practice of reading literature. We will examine the set of following questions: What are literary texts and why are they important? How have different historical developments and cultural communities shaped the reading of literature? What is useful or vital about such reading practices? Our specific aim will be to cultivate close-reading and writing skills through the study of various forms and genres of writing. This course offers students a richer understanding of critical reading practices and the implications of different interpretive approaches. This course is restricted to declared majors/minors. To declare, click here: https://forms.gle/XTqYwaRswokpQax77

This course, designed for English majors, investigates the specificity of literature and the “literary” as readerly and writerly practices. We will read widely across genres and historical periods to understand the formal elements, textual strategies, and historical developments that make literature a distinctive category of cultural production, capable of creating complex worlds through the medium of language. We will also consider how and why we read, drawing on the resources of literary criticism to consider reading as a creative, historically changeable and socially experimental practice. We will pay close attention throughout to the political life of literature; this will entail asking about the kinds of cultural communities organized by race, nation, empire, and gender/sexuality that shape what we read and what counts as literature. It will also lead us to consider the way that literature represents and mediates the world and--sometimes—seeks to transform it. This course will emphasize skills of close reading and writing-as-revision. You must be a declared English major or minor to take this class. If you need to declare, please do so here: https://forms.gle/JRG1N1wtptgQRH9s7

title: Literatures in English III: American Literatures to 1900
description: This course surveys the evolution of literary themes and forms from the period of European exploration of the Americas through the Civil War, tracing distinctive traditions of writing and thinking that have shaped the development of modern literature and thought in the United States. How, in particular, did this writing and thought address religious, political and economic conflict? How was it shaped by encounters between European and native American cultures; the arts of religious devotion and cosmopolitan enlightenment; the cultural politics of revolution and modern nationalism; responses to the expansion of capitalism and slavery; the development of print media and modern literary values; and the philosophy and aesthetics of American transcendentalism and sentimentalism?

sections.notes: $PREREQ: V41.0100 ENGL-UA 113: American Literature to 1900 - This course surveys the evolution of literary themes and forms from the European invasion and colonial settlements through the late 19thc entry. Exploring major works of early American writing in historical and social contexts, we will analyze encounters between European, Native American, and African cultures; the poetics of religious devotion and cosmopolitan enlightenment; the cultural politics of revolution and modern nationalism; responses to the expansion of capitalism and slavery; the spread of literacy and the expansion of print culture. Throughout this course, we will seek to place diverse texts in critical dialogue with each other, interpret changes in American literature over time, and test the resonance of historical writings for our contemporary moment. How do literary texts help us to think about questions of identity and difference that have shaped American culture? How might we situate the literature of what would eventually become the United States in relation to the development of literature more broadly? Students will learn to read American literature with attention both to history (the study of change over time) and to genre (poetry, fiction, letters, religious and political texts, and autobiography). Writing exercises, collaborations, discussions, lectures and exams will develop particular themes in the development of literary form and processes of cultural change. In this course our aims are both to introduce you to a body of writing often collected under the heading "American literature" and to practice and develop methods of literary study appropriate to that work. Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Difference and Power, Literature from 1640-1900

title: Reading as a Writer
description: 4 points, discussion/seminar. First offered spring 2016, and every semester thereafter. Prerequisite (or co-requisite): Literary Interpretation (ENGL-UA 200). This seminar is a class in creative as well as critical reading. This class posits reading as an activity and explores reading and writing as reciprocal activities: no strong writers are not also strong readers. What can we learn from a text's forms, modes, codes, and affects? What can we also learn from theories of literature (of poetry and poetics, or drama, of the novel or narrative in general)? How can we read both with and against the grain? And how can a profound engagement with criticism, commentary, and theory help us become better “makers” ourselves? This course assumes that writing is an effect of, and in a feedback loop with, reading: thus this seminar aims to strengthen your capacities for pattern recognition – i.e. sophistication about genre, style, mode. Regular assignments aim to provide a space for critical experiments in reading and writing; the syllabus offers models and goads for reflection and response. Students will direct and distill their inquiries into a substantial final paper (or project). Open only to English majors.

sections.notes: *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Genre, Difference and Power

Reading as a Writer: Time | Given the intense pressures of living in 2026, the notion that “there’s no time to read” is easily conceded to. How can we read in a society where reading a book seems, simply, to take too long — let alone write one? This course is an opportunity to examine the pernicious idea that we’re always out of time. What makes up this understanding of time as “money,” of which we never have enough? How can we experience time differently? We will not only read representations of time and its passing but also write it anew through embodied exercises. We’ll read contemporary literature including speculative fiction about time travel by Octavia Butler; a book-length poem written in one day by Bernadette Mayer; oral histories of radioactive time by Svetlana Alexievich; and investigations of the time of incarceration by Brandon Shimoda. We’ll also go on field trips to live performance and museum exhibitions, and write experiments alongside all of these. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Genre, Difference and Power

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Since 2000: Contemporary Graphic Narratives - Comics, as a narrative form, first gained prominence in America in the pages of early twentieth-century newspapers, where they appeared as gag-a-day strips meant to provide readers with a quick laugh at the breakfast table. In the 1980s and 1990s, comics began to be seen as a literary medium, and this stemmed from the publication of works such as: Maus, Watchmen, Batman:The Dark Knight Returns, Ghost World, and the Hernandez brothers’ Love and Rockets series. The critical and commercial success of these classic works has, in the twenty-first century, established comics as a medium associated with some of the most inventive literary narratives. In this course, we will focus on formally innovative comics that have been published in the past fifteen years. This has been a particularly rich period for long form comics, and my hope is that students will gain an appreciation for these complex and visually engaging narratives Toward that end, we will consider how the distinctive narrative capacities of comics contribute to texts that align with conventional literary genres – short stories, memoirs, novels, dystopian fiction, bildungsroman (coming-of-age) – and those that are specific to the medium: superhero comics and graphic journalism. Because materiality has been an important component of comics’ history, we will examine both print and web comics. This is a general elective course open to anyone interested in learning more about contemporary comics; no prior knowledge is expected. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Genre, Difference and Power, Literature from post-1900

Course Repeatable for Credit. Contemporary Post-Apocalypticism - In this course we’ll study novels, movies, video games, and short stories from the first three decades of this millennium to figure out the speculative genre of post- apocalypticism right now, albeit in light of the genre’s (extremely) long and rich history. How do we make sense of the kinds of “apocalyptic events” that dominate the cultural imagination today – like zombies, asteroids, pandemics, nuclear armageddons, energy breakdowns, and climate catastrophes? What qualifies as an apocalyptic event and what does the notion of “apocalypse” presume about historical experience and figurations of race, gender, class, and sexuality? To what degree do contemporary texts echo the etymological root of “apocalypse,” meaning revelation and new-found knowledge? To answer these questions the class will incorporate a range of secondary materials from literary and cultural criticism, genre studies, environmental criticism, and critical theory. We’ll be concerned not just with the nature of a post-apocalyptic genre or aesthetic, but also the cultural ripples or reception of an apocalyptic cultural event and the activation of an “apocalyptic” framework for interpretation. Which is to say, we’ll want to know how the genres of apocalypse/post-apocalypse have a bearing on fields of possibility for environmental and political action – or, alternatively, might result in resigned inaction. Via the critical and creative traditions of Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurism, we’ll ask how social positionality shapes understandings of apocalypse and its afterlives. Finally, we’ll contextualize the genre of contemporary post-apocalyptic fiction alongside a long history of post-apocalyptic thought – thinking for example the genre of flood fiction today in the tradition of Noah’s Ark – and interrogate the seductive appeal of survivalism, redemption narratives, and clean slates. The syllabus may include: Emily St. John Mandel’s Station Eleven (and the tv adaptation), Ling Ma’s Severance, Colson Whitehead’s Zone One, the movie A Quiet Place, The Last of Us franchise, and short stories by Paolo Bacigalupi, Richard Van Camp, and N.K. Jemisin. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Genre, Difference and Power, Literature from post-1900

Course Repeatable for Credit. The Ethics of Pastoral | From antiquity (Theocritus and Virgil) to contemporary versions of pastoral (Brokeback Mountain and Jez Butterworth’s Jerusalem), with special attention to early modern English, Italian, and Spanish works (Petrarch, Shakespeare, Spenser, Cervantes, Andreini), this course will examine pastoral in poetry, drama and painting (Poussin) with an interest in how pastoral intersects with environmental and eco-critical questions. The seminar will consider the critical tradition that has taken up pastoral as a model for critical and ethical inquiry (William Empson, Harry Berger, John Berger, Gayatri Spivak, Erwin Panofsky, Paul Alpers), and will focus on some of the critical questions – aesthetic, ethical, ecological, political - generated by pastoral. Readings: Selections from Petrarch, Spenser (Shepheardes Calender and The Faerie Queene Book 6, cantos 9-11), Tasso, Aminta; Isabella Andreini, La Mirtilla; Shakespeare, As You Like It, and The Winter's Tale; Cervantes, the Marcela episode from Don Quixote, Lope de Vega, Fuenteovejuna (1612-1614) and contemporary ecological writing. Among the problems we’ll be puzzling over: to what extent does the poet have the right to speak for the shepherd or peasant – those who "cannot represent themselves"? How does the space of the idyll or pastoral retreat come to mirror the space of literature itself? Why does early modernity engage with pastoral in so many forms – dramatic, lyric, the novel, painting, etc. – and what is the lasting legacy of that engagement? *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Critical Theory, Genre, Literature from pre-1640

Course Repeatable for Credit. ALSO ITAL-UA 285 - Queer Love in Premodern Literature | Course Description: This course explores representations of same-sex desire and gender ambiguity in literary traditions from classical antiquity to the early modern period. Far from being a modern invention, homoerotic love—and the anxieties, aspirations, and pleasures surrounding it—has long shaped Western literature, even as its presence has been alternately celebrated, contested, denied, or overwritten across centuries. We will trace these shifting attitudes by reading authors who either explicitly evoke same-sex desire or encode it through indirection, metaphor, and gender play. Beginning with antiquity, we examine Sappho’s lyric fragments, Plato’s Symposium, Ovid’s narratives of transformation, and Martial’s epigrams, alongside moments of gender ambiguity in myth and epic. In the medieval and early modern periods, we turn to Shakespeare’s sonnets, Ariosto’s elusive treatments of homoerotic desire, and the exploration of gender in the Roman de Silence. We also consider lesser-known works, including Giulia Bigolina’s Urania, an unpublished prose narrative that stages complex bonds among women; Immanuel of Rome, a Jewish-Italian poet often compared to Dante; and the poetic Latin letters exchanged between medieval women (the so-called Tegernsee letters, interpreted by Peter Dronke). Throughout the semester, we will investigate how authors encode desire, disguise it, or articulate it openly; how same-sex affection intersects with friendship, politics, and spirituality; and how gender variance and emotional intimacy challenge the boundaries of literary representation. The course welcomes students from all backgrounds and requires no prior knowledge of classical or early modern literature.

Course Repeatable for Credit. ALSO ITAL-UA 285 - The Young Dante: Inventing a New Life | Course Description: The Young Dante: Inventing a New Life examines Alighieri’s formative years tracing his sentimental, intellectual, and poetic evolution within the socio-cultural landscape of Florence. The course is structured around the narrative arc of Dante’s inaugural work, the Vita Nuova. Composed in the vernacular through a hybrid of prose and verse, this “idealized autobiography” signifies the emergence of a new cultural sensibility by pioneering the use of interior discourse in the vernacular tongue. This story of an education shaped by love synthesizes influences from Provençal and Sicilian lyricism, classical and medieval Latinity, and early Christian thought. Central to the inquiry is Dante’s engagement with contemporary poets—specifically Guido Guinizzelli and, most crucially, his “first friend” the influential Guido Cavalcanti. While the Vita Nuova underscores their profound intellectual bond, it simultaneously delineates the dialectical tensions that ultimately precipitated their definitive estrangement. The course features primary readings from the Vita Nuova, Dante’s prose work, and his lyric poetry, with consistent analysis of their thematic and stylistic trajectories toward the Divine Comedy.

title: Intro to Old English Language & Literature
description: Study of the language, literature, and culture of the Anglo-Saxons from about AD 500-1066. Oral readings of the original texts and a survey of basic grammar. Representative prose selections are read, but emphasis is on the brilliant short poems: Caedmon's Hymn, The Battle of Maldon, The Seafarer, The Wanderer, and The Dream of the Rood, that prepare the reader for the epic Beowulf.

sections.notes: This course introduces students to Old English language and literature and also to the culture and history in which this language thrived. It will also use J. R. R. Tolkien’s work, both academic and creative, as an entry point to consider all of these aspects. It will be divided into three parts. In the first part, we will go over basic Old English grammar and read, with the help of translations, passages from Old English prose in various genres. Since Old English is different from its descendant Modern English in many aspects, we will study basic grammar and core vocabulary. In the second part, we will read shorter Old English poems such as elegies, battle poems, and riddles. We will also consider how Tolkien uses some of these poems in his creative work. In the last section we will read excerpts from Beowulf while comparing translations of these passages by Tolkien, Seamus Heaney, and others, and also examining various adaptations (e.g., novels, films). Satisfies: Literature from pre-1640

title: Shakespeare
description: Why is Shakespeare still a vital cultural force 400 years after his death? How was he able to speak both to us and to audiences of his own day? This course will survey Shakespeare’s major plays and poems, and will look at their historical, cultural and theatrical contexts. But we will also consider Shakespeare’s afterlife on stage and screen.

sections.notes: Shakespeare and Film | Shakespeare has long been a fixture of highbrow culture, but his works are also continually being reinvented in global popular culture—evident most recently in an explosion of comics, dance, film, radio, television, and new media adaptations. This course will consider the dissemination of Shakespeare’s plays across a range of cultures in the 20th and 21st centuries. We will do so by investigating how certain plays have been adapted and performed, focusing on how various aspects of Shakespeare’s art are transposed to visual media. Our focus will be on Shakespeare’s modern afterlives in different parts of the world, centering questions of race, gender, sexuality, generational conflict, and political intrigue. In addition to acquiring a close understanding of select plays, students will reckon with the theoretical issues attendant on a study of Shakespeare and adaptation. Plays will include The Taming of the Shrew, Romeo and Juliet, Hamlet, Othello, and The Tempest. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Genre, Literature from pre-1640

title: Colloq: Shakespeare
description: Intensive reading of six to eight plays of Shakespeare chosen from among the comedies, tragedies, and histories, with attention to formal, historical, and performance questions. Only open to English majors.

sections.notes: Law and Shakespeare - How can key works by William Shakespeare help introduce us both to the history of law in the Anglo-American and Roman civil-law traditions and to current theories about law and political power? Beginning with legal history and comic drama, our seminar will compare common law and equity in England as rival systems that place competing versions of the public good (inheritance as common wealth, and commonwealth as state power) above particular interests. Then, through a range of tragedies and late tragicomedies, we will consider different versions of “political theology” in the Renaissance, that is, the application of religious categories of thought to the juridico-political sphere of law and government. The historical placement of the sovereign both inside and outside human law was already a theoretical issue in Shakespeare’s drama. We will read a selection of Shakespeare’s works along with a critical article or two each week. The plays include The Comedy of Errors, The Merchant of Venice, Measure for Measure, King Lear, Hamlet, and Coriolanus. Theorists and critics include Giorgio Agamben, Lorna Hutson, Braden Cormack, and Julia Reinhard Lupton. A presentation, term papers, and in-class essays will make up the grade along with informed and lively class participation. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Critical Theory, Genre, Literature from pre-1640

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. PREREQUISITES: V41.0200 & V41.0210. SAME AS V65.0445 Epistolary Act(or)s | The letter is one of the oldest genres of writing, which despite shifts in technologies is still with us today in the form of the email. The academic / professional email is the genre of writing you engage with most frequently as a student at NYU. Indeed, a major part of being a student involves managing correspondence with professors, peers, administrators, and other assorted interlocutors. Oddly, for such a foundational genre, we almost never talk about it in a classroom context. We simply expect you to come to university prepared to read, write, and track countless numbers of emails every week for the duration of your undergraduate studies. This course seeks to address this gap by centering correspondence practices both digital and analog, asking you to consider your own epistolary style as you read classic epistolary (letter) texts from antiquity to the modern period. Beyond their primary purpose to make introductions, narrate circumstances, and/or make requests of the recipient, writers have harnessed epistolary writing to explore complex themes of loss, absence, desire, community, etc.. We will seek to understand epistolarity’s mediational logics, rooted in the formal conceit of a speaking document that is a proxy for an absent speaker, and the ways that this conceit lends itself to these manifold artistic ends. To better understand these artistic ends, we will engage in critical-creative writing assignments that ask you to adopt the persona and epistolary conventions of a given author and reflect on this process in formal writing. You will also have the opportunity to engage in your own (actual) correspondence with faculty members and reflect on that process as well. Readings will include Selections from Sappho, Ovid’s Heroides, The Letters of Abelard and Heloise, Thomas More’s Utopia, Mary Shelley’s Frankenstein, and others. Ultimately, the goal of this course is to allow students to put the texts and ideas of the course into conversation with their own practice—and have some fun doing so. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Genre, Literature pre-1640

title: Colloquium: Milton
description: Emphasis on the major poems (Paradise Lost, Paradise Regained, and Samson Agonistes) with some attention to the early poems and the prose. Traces the poet's sense of vocation, analyzes the gradual development of the Miltonic style, and assesses Milton's position in the history of English literature, politics, and theology.

sections.notes: Milton- The syllabus for this colloquium is designed around a reading of John Milton’s epic poem Paradise Lost in its entirety. Paced so as to allow students sufficient time with the epic book by book, at key moments the course will also encourage you to draw connections between Paradise Lost and Milton’s major lyrics, his pastoral elegy Lycidas, and his dramatic works (A Masque and Samson Agonistes). In addition, we will read one or two major prose texts by Milton that parallel Paradise Lost in key ways. Our concerns will include the development of Milton’s poetic career and his political ideas during a time of civil war, revolution against monarchy, and its restoration. We will consider religious toleration and its limits in Milton’s writing. We will also address the epic claims that Paradise Lost makes on global history amid emerging notions of gendered subjectivity and racial difference in the mid-seventeenth century. Assignments include term papers, weekly writing assignments, and in-class essays. I have ordered two paperback textbooks for the course: Paradise Lost (Oxford World’s Classics) and Milton’s Selected Poetry and Prose (Norton). Satisfies: Literature from 1640-1900

title: Jane Austen
description: This survey of Jane Austen’s work examines her compact oeuvre of fiction, whose critical reception has been formative to the discipline of English literature itself. We will read Persuasion, Pride and Prejudice, Sense and Sensibility and other classics to consider Austen’s deep, virtuosic inheritance of eighteenth-century narrative forms as well as their afterlives in contemporary culture, including popular film adaptations of Austen’s work (Clueless, Love and Friendship). Students will embark on a careful study of an author widely recognized as one of the master stylists of the English language.

sections.notes: *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Genre, Difference and Power, Literature from 1640-1900

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Of Monsters and Medicine | Befriending “monsters” in literature and popular culture, this course will listen to what they can tell us about desire, difference, disability, and death. Examining dialogues between monstrosity and the medicalized body, we will trace how these figures regulate social anxieties around contagion, infection, and ecological collapse. We will also explore how we consume (as readers, listeners, viewers) these “others” to navigate the errancy within: what these monsters help us do to/with our own bodies. Likely texts include: Frankenstein (Mary Shelley, 1818), Dracula (Bram Stoker, 1897), Predator (John McTiernan, 1987), My Neighbor Totoro (Hayao Miyazaki, 1988), Frankenstein in Baghdad (Ahmed Saadawi, 2013), Mongrels (Stephen Graham Jones, 2016), Sinners (Ryan Coogler, 2025). Class participation (frequently collaborative groupwork) will be weighted equally with assignments, which will include written and multimedia options. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Difference and Power, Literature from 1640-1900, Literature from post-1900

title: Contemporary British Lit and Culture
description: Prerequisite: V41.0220. Studies in contemporary British fiction, exploring postwar British culture in an era of profound political and economic change and social upheaval. Examines a range of avant-garde, neorealist, postcolonial, and popular texts that challenge received notions of ?Englishness.? Particular attention is paid to the interaction between literature and other cultural forms, such as cinema, popular music, and sport.

sections.notes: How have British writers responded to the end of empire, Cold War, economic decline and radical changes in racial and sexual politics? This course offers an introduction to contemporary British culture in an era of profound political and economic change and social upheaval. The course will also offer students interdisciplinary approaches to literature and culture through the Medical Humanities by focusing on questions of trauma, healing, and public health. In order to give students a rich sense of context and history, the course will integrate multimedia elements drawn from visual culture, film, art and popular music, with rigorous textual analysis of contemporary British literature. We will explore novels, poetry, music and film profoundly influenced by the shadow of war, by immigration from the former colonies and racial and ethnic diversity, by dramatic shifts in gender relations and sexuality, by class conflict and deindustrialization, environmental catastrophe, and by the potential “break up” of Britain and the aftermath of Brexit. Caught between an ambivalent “special relationship” with America and a technocratic European superstate, how has British culture adapted to its uneasy geopolitical position? How does a nation so obsessed with images of its past traditions, such as the World Wars, Empire and the Monarchy, remain at the cutting edge of music and popular culture? How has British involvement in postcolonial conflicts, the Troubles in Northern Ireland, or in the wars in Iraq and Afghanistan affected its culture? What is Britain’s position in the global cultural economy? We will examine a range of avant-garde, postcolonial and popular texts which challenge received notions of Englishness. Particular attention will be paid to the interaction between literature and other cultural forms such as film and TV, punk music and other popular and independent music, and sport. Texts may include the work of Virginia Woolf, Alexander Baron, George Orwell, Samuel Selvon, John Osborne, Ian Fleming, Muriel Spark, Penelope Fitzgerald, Caryl Churchill, Kazuo Ishiguro, and Zadie Smith. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Genre, Difference and Power, Literature from post-1900

title: Colloquium:
description: Considers the imaginative ?logic? of James Joyce?s career and the extent to which the trajectory of his works constitutes a ?development? of forces posited in the early writings. Readings span the entire oeuvre, from Dubliners to Finnegans Wake, and include Joyce?s poetry and his play, Exiles.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. PREREQUISITES: V41.0100 OR V41.0200 & V41.0220. SAME AS V58.0625. "James Joyce and Modern Ireland" In the context of the centenary of publication of Joyce’s Ulysses, this class will examine how Joyce’s work represented Ireland in the crucible of its uneven modernization. We will read Dubliners, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man, and Ulysses to examine how Joyce understood Irish culture in the context of a world changing in profound but complex ways. One of our central concerns will be the manner in which Joyce’s work, especially Ulysses, has provoked the development and refinement of a broad array of critical and theoretical approaches to literature and culture.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. This course will explore the cultural dynamics of transatlantic modernism as seen through the lens of urban experience. Focusing on London and New York as centers of gravity for modernist culture, we will explore the reciprocal relationship between modernism and the city: how was modernism shaped by the urban experience and how, in turn, did experiments in literature, media, and art help to mold our conception of the modern city? The course will explore the parallels and contrasts among a variety of forms including literature, film, art, music, stressing the uneven developments of the period, with special attention paid to the tension between highbrow and popular forms. We will investigate patterns of migration and diasporic movement from London, to Dublin, to Paris, to New York, and examine the relationship between the modernist metropolis and other modern spaces such as rural areas and underdeveloped regions, the suburbs, and colonial metropolises and territories, and home fronts during two World Wars. The course will read modernist texts as both response to and symptom of the crises of modernity unleashed by urbanization, immigration, war, imperialism, revolution, decolonization, as well as shifts in gender roles, race relations, and class conflict. We will consider the claims of the modernists to represent the dominant cultural response to the age alongside the transformations of literary realism, avant gardism, the rise of mass culture and advertising, and transformations of urban space and in technologies of mass communications like film, documentary, radio and popular music. Readings may include the work of Henry James, Edith Wharton, Stephen Crane, Joseph Conrad, Virginia Woolf, James Joyce, T.S. Eliot, William Carlos Williams, Ernest Hemingway, Langston Hughes, Gwendolyn Brooks, F. Scott Fitzgerald, Claude McKay, Richard Wright, Samuel Selvon, Salman Rushdie, and Zadie Smith. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Genre, Difference and Power, Literature from post-1900

title: Major Texts in Critical Theory
description: Major texts in critical theory from Plato to Derrida, considered in relation to literary practice. The first half of the course focuses on four major types of critical theory: mimetic, ethical, expressive, and formalist. The second half turns to 20th-century critical schools, such as Russian and American formalism, archetypal criticism, structuralism, psychoanalytic criticism, feminism, reader theory, deconstruction, and historicism.

sections.notes: SAME AS V29.0843002

SAME AS V29.0843002 Rather than a salad-bar sampler of disparate theoretical approaches, this course proposes a narrative that begins with Pragmatism and Russian Formalism, and moves into Structuralism, Phenomenology and Post-Structuralism, while integrating the theoretical ideas with literary practice. Theorists will include William James, Victor Shklovsky, Roland Barthes, Maurice Merleau-Ponty, Paul de Man and Gilles Deleuze; writers will include Gertrude Stein, Robert Smithson, Lyn Hejinian and Lisa Robertson. Rather than use literature merely to illustrate theory, we will instead develop methods for staging a lively discussion between the two fields. Satisfies: Critical Theory

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. CENSORSHIP: THEORY AND PRACTICE - In this seminar we will embark on a comparative study of the theory and historical practice of modern censorship, from the passage of the first statutory obscenity laws in the nineteenth century to the resurgence of direct censorship in the US under the Trump administration and on university campuses today, with many stops along the way. Our semester will be organized around three overlapping but nonetheless distinct contexts for thinking about how censorship functions: the regulation and policing of sexuality; political and ideological control and exclusion, in particular through immigration laws and state surveillance; and the erasure of histories of racial discrimination and colonial domination. In each case, we will also structure our studies around three kinds of readings. First, we will read a broad, comparative sampling of literary texts and cultural objects that reflect on or have been subject to specific forms of censorship, ranging from Emma Goldman’s Living My Life to Cuban poet Herberto Padilla’s Fuera del Juego to 2 Live Crew’s hip-hop album As Nasty as They Wanna Be to the record of the FBI’s extensive surveillance of Black authors such as James Baldwin. Second, we will study specific laws, tactics, and legal-political mechanisms that have been used to chill dissent and silence speech. We will also read widely across critical theoretical and philosophical texts that help us to think through and theorize what censorship is. Our principal goals will be to consider how and why societies regulate language and expressive activity in the first place; to refine our research skills by examining concrete instances of modern censorship in their historical context; and to ask how these historical case studies can help us to understand—and to withstand—the intensification of legal, political, and institutional censorship in the present. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Critical Theory, Difference and Power, Literature from 1640-1900, Literature from post-1900

Course Repeatable for Credit. The Red and the Violet: McCarthyism and Academic Freedom at NYU - This course focuses on the stories of three tenured NYU faculty members who were persecuted for their Communist politics in the 1940s and 50s, as a starting point for a more general study of anticommunism, academic freedom, and political activism in higher education during the McCarthy period. The faculty members are Edward Berry Burgum, Associate Professor of English; Margaret Schlauch, Professor of English; and Lyman Bradley, Associate Professor and Chair of the German Department. All three were called to testify before anticommunist congressional committees in the early 1950s. Bradley refused to cooperate and was jailed for contempt, whereas Burgum invoked his Fifth Amendment rights; both Bradley and Burgum were subsequently stripped of tenure and fired from the university. Schlauch was investigated for subversive activities, but rather than testify, face imprisonment, or lose her job, she chose to flee the U.S. for Poland. She resigned from NYU and joined the faculty of the University of Warsaw, where she continued her career in exile. Our course will focus on the events leading up to and following their coerced departure from NYU, including their remarkable accomplishments outside the university—as public educators, Marxist scholars, antifascist and civil rights activists, and union organizers—for which they were persecuted. Through our case study of NYU, we will be examining the specific ways that US institutions of higher learning were pressed into the service of a repressive and authoritarian political agenda during the second Red Scare, while also raising challenging questions about the ideological functions of the modern university. Our course readings will be drawn in large part from primary source materials housed in NYU’s University Archives and the Tamiment Library, many of them unearthed by NYU students in my Spring 2026 course on the topic. We will supplement these archival documents with scholarly readings about the Red Scare, the labor movement, academic freedom and higher education, Marxist theory, and midcentury leftwing politics. We will also read literary and cultural texts from the period by authors such as Richard Wright, Howard Fast, Gwendolyn Bennett, W. E. B. DuBois, Mary McCarthy, Arthur Miller, and others. In addition to opportunities for original archival research, students enrolled in this course will have the option to help mount a public exhibition about Schlauch, Bradley, and Burgum on campus in November 2026, and to participate in related programming and events. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Critical Theory, Difference and Power

Course Repeatable for Credit. Race and the Human - This course will consider the contested status of the human in anticolonial, postcolonial, and diasporic thought and literature, from the turn of the 20th century to the present. For many of the authors we'll study, racism did not just deny humanness to racialized and colonized subjects--it also threatened the moral and political unity implied in the term humanity and cast a long shadow over the promise of humanism, to which many of these thinkers remained committed. We will examine the versions of antiracism our authors articulated, and consider how they reconciled their critiques of enlightenment humanism with visions of radical new humanisms. We will consider how these interrogations of the human emerged out of revolutionary anticolonialism and in dialogue with a host of postwar developments: the rise of the human rights regime, the establishment of new international institutions, the development of a global culture of memory and memorialization, and transformations in the biological and social scientific meaning of race. We will pay close attention to gender and the way it complicates the human and dehumanization. We'll also consider recent challenges to the centrality of the human that ask us to consider ecology, animality, and other non-human forms of materiality or being. Authors may include W. E. B. Du Bois, Frantz Fanon, Aimé Césaire, Hannah Arendt, C. L. R. James, Primo Levi, Charlotte Delbo, Sylvia Wynter, Bessie Head, Toni Morrison, and Adania Shibli, among others. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Critical Theory, Difference and Power, Literature from post-1900

title: Latina/o Literature
description: This course offers an in-depth exploration of the rich and diverse literary traditions of Latina/o writers, spanning a wide range of genres, themes, and historical contexts.

sections.notes: Latinx Prison Writing - This course explores the politics of imprisonment, incarceration, detention, and captivity through the prism of Latinx writing and cultural production. Through a range of literary, poetic, cinematic, and dramatic cultural forms, we will engage with the crisis of US mass incarceration while also attending to the regimes of captivity and detention that animated the Spanish colonial order and continue in regimes of Latin American statecraft. As such, we will ask questions about the interrelation between writing, punishment, literacy, freedom, captivity, justice, abolition, and decolonization. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Difference and Power, Literature from post-1900

title: Intro to Postcolonial Studies
description: This course offers an introduction to the interdisciplinary field of Postcolonial Studies, examining the social, cultural, political, and literary legacies of colonialism and imperialism. Through an exploration of key texts, theories, and historical contexts, students will gain a critical understanding of the complexities surrounding the postcolonial world and its ongoing implications. Only open to English majors.

sections.notes: This course offers a wide-ranging introduction to postcolonial theory and literature and is suitable both for students new to the field and those who have taken other courses in these topics. We will closely consider key historical texts and contexts of imperial culture and anticolonial resistance, and we will examine the central debates that have shaped postcolonial studies over the past 40-plus years. Throughout the course, we will pay attention to how postcolonial studies as an interdisciplinary field of cultural critique challenges the ongoing history of colonial knowledge production, and we will ask whether literature has a special capacity to disrupt such epistemological and representational violence. We will also examine how postcolonial theory helps us understand the ongoing catastrophes of the neocolonial present and the new forms of imperial power that organize our carceral and unequal world. In addition to reading literature and theory, we will watch several films (by Gillo Pontecorvo, Abderrahmane Sissako, Mati Diop, and Larissa Sansour) and consider other works of art and visual culture (by Yinka Shonibare, Wifredo Lam, Pablo Picasso, Ingrid Pollard, and Michael Rakowitz). Authors may include W. E. B. Du Bois, M. K. Gandhi, Aimé Césaire, Frantz Fanon, Edward Said, Assia Djebar, Gayatri Chakravorty Spivak, Chinua Achebe, Stuart Hall, Jamaica Kincaid, Kamila Shamsie, and Isabella Hammad, among others. *Up to 2 of the following satisfied with this class: Critical Theory, Difference and Power, Literature from post-1900
