title: Financial Risk Management
description: This course introduces the techniques and problems of Financial Risk Management and Asset Pricing. It emphasizes risk finance and attitudes; Value at Risk; risk measurement principles; valuation and expected utility and their relevance in the valuation and the pricing of financial investments; insurance; management of derivatives; and risk management. Throughout, risk-management application problems are explored., The course introduces and focuses on the fundamental principles of the Arrow-Debreu state preference theory used to price derivatives and other assets in complete markets. Risk neutral-Binomial models in option pricing; essential elements of Ito calculus; and the Black-Scholes model for pricing options are introduced and applied to practical financial decision making and risk management problems. title: Options Pricing & Stochastic Calculus
description: This course provides the mathematical foundations of Option Pricing models. The techniques covered include arithmetic and geometric Brownian motion, first passage time, the reflection principle, the stochastic Ito integral, Ito differential Calculus, change of probability measure, martingales, Stochastic Differential Equations and Partial Differential Equations. Some of the pricing models considered are the European, Barrier, Asian and American options. These problems are either solved analytically by the martingale approach or numerically, by applying approximation and simulation methods. Since the same techniques allow the treatment of more complex financial products, examples of credit derivatives will be also presented. This course is a requirement in the Computational Finance Track | Prerequisite: FRE-GY 6083 and matriculation into a master or doctoral program

These techniques are analyzed both mathematically and using computer aided software that allows for the solution and the handling of such problems. In addition, the course introduces techniques for Monte Carlo simulation techniques and their use to deal with theoretically complex financial products in a tractable and practical manner. Both self-writing of software as well as using outstanding computer programs routinely used in financial and insurance industries will be used. | Prerequisite: FRE-GY 6083 and Matriculation into a master or doctoral program

title: Econometrics and Time Series Analysis
description: Financial econometrics has matured into a necessary and essential part of financial engineering that provides opportunities to deal with real and practical problems in finance. For example, techniques such as ARCH and GARCH and their subsequent development are used to estimate the volatility of underlying financial processes; the analysis of intra-day trading data that requires particular models and techniques; memory-based and fractal stochastic processes to study complex markets behaviors and copulas applied routinely to model- and estimate-dependent risks. These financial and risk problems require the application of advanced financial-econometric techniques, which the course provides from both theoretical and empirical-applied viewpoints. Selected cases provide a real-world sense of financial engineering when it is faced with financial-market reality and complexity. | Prerequisite: FRE-GY 6083 and Matriculation into a master or doctoral program

title: Fixed Income Securities and Interest Rate Derivatives
description: This course examines the body of analytical tools and measures that constitute modern fixed-income markets. The valuation of interest-rate sensitive cash flows is the unifying theme. Major topics include theories of term structure, institutional aspects of fixed-income markets and analytical techniques for managing interest-rate risk. Bond refunding, defeasance, corporate bonds, forwards, futures, options and interest-rate swaps are discussed. The course gives an overview of the major classes of fixed-income securities and the markets in which they trade. title: Statistical Arbitrage
description: Statistical arbitrage refers to strategies that combine many relatively independent positive expected value trades so that profit, while not guaranteed, becomes very likely. This course prepares students to research and practice in this area by providing the tools and techniques to generate and evaluate individual trading strategies, combine them into a coherent portfolio, manage the resulting risks, and monitor for excess deviations from expected performance. It introduces theoretical concepts such as cointegration, risk capital allocation, proper backtesting, and factor analysis, as well as practical considerations such as data mining, automated systems, and trade execution. Programming languages such as R, Python, or C++ will be used to present applications to data at low, intermediate and high frequency. | Prerequisites: FRE-GY 6123, FRE-GY 6083 and Matriculation into a master or doctoral program

sections.notes: Title: "Negativity and the Unconscious: Hegel, Freud, Bergson" Description: This seminar explores the philosophical and psychic dimensions of negativity as the force that shapes both thought and life. Beginning with Hegel’s dialectical notion of negation as the motor of becoming, we will trace how this concept transforms in Freud’s discovery of the unconscious and in Bergson’s philosophy of duration and creative evolution. The course examines how negativity moves from logical contradiction to psychic repression to temporal differentiation — from the structure of Spirit to the work of mourning to the élan vital. We will ask whether negativity is destructive or productive, reactive or generative, and whether contemporary thought can still think transformation without the negative. By reading Phenomenology of Spirit (selected sections), Freud’s “Negation” and 'Beyond the Pleasure Principle', and Bergson’s 'Creative Evolution', we will test the hypothesis that the unconscious is not merely the site of repression, but a 'plastic power of differentiation', where negation becomes the very form of life. Meets 7 weeks from Oct 16 - Dec 4, 2026. It is possible to enroll in GERM-GA2222 Bronfen for the first 7 weeks and also GERM-GA2224 Malabou in last 7 weeks with no time conflict. Taught in English.

title: Approaches to French Literature
description: This course offers an introduction to central works in French literature, while presenting students with a toolkit for literary analysis. Eschewing a strictly chronological approach, we will explore some of the key lines of thought animating French literary production from the Middle Ages through the twentieth century. Students will have the opportunity to refine their skills in reading and writing through in-class workshops devoted to techniques for close reading, developing a thesis from textual evidence, and identifying arguments in critical texts. Our objectives will be both to understand the diverse functions of literature as a cultural practice and to prepare students to take Discovery courses and other advanced seminars in literature.

title: Approaches to French History
description: This course is an exploration of the forces, ideas, and tensions that have shaped France and the French-speaking world across time. The course examines pivotal moments and developments in the history of France through a range of historical lenses, allowing for varied points of emphasis. Students will analyze the dynamic interrelations between history, literature, society, fine arts, and philosophy, considering how cultural production can both reflect and influence historical change. Students will engage directly with historical texts and scholarly interpretations to develop critical perspectives on the past and better understand its repercussions and reinterpretations in the present. Students will examine major intellectual movements, social transformations, political conflicts, and the relationships between state, nation, and citizenry, all of which have played a role in defining French and Francophone identities and experiences, as they refine their skills in analysis, discussion, and oral and written presentation.

sections.notes: PREREQUISITES: FREN-UA 30 (or an equivalent course - FREN-UA 9030 in NYU Paris and FREN-SHU 30 in NYU Shanghai), an AP French Language and Culture Exam score of 4 or 5, or a score above the level of FREN-UA 30 on the online placement exam. This course traces the dramatic, messy, exciting, and revolutionary story of France from the Middle Ages to the present. We’ll meet queens and kings, revolutionaries, philosophers, artists, and ordinary people while exploring and discussing the ideas, social movements, and historical turning points that helped shape modern France. This course is taught in French.

title: French Novel and Society: The 19th Century
description: Study of Balzac, Stendhal, Flaubert, and Zola as a means of identifying the individual?s changing relationship to the environment and the social, political, and intellectual contexts of his or her epoch. Problems of 19th-century novel, narrative structure, point of view, invention, and observation.

sections.notes: Pourquoi jouons-nous ? Loin d'être un simple divertissement, le jeu constitue une manière privilégiée de comprendre la vie moderne. À travers des œuvres de Balzac, Baudelaire, Hugo, Zola, Huysmans, Rachilde et Gide, ce cours explore comment le roman français du XIXème siècle transforme le jeu en un outil de réflexion sur le désir, le capital, le genre, la performance ainsi que sur la modernité en général. Nous verrons ainsi comment le roman peut être appréhendé comme un laboratoire où s'inventent et se contestent les règles du jeu de la société en France. PREREQUISITES: FREN-UA 30 or equivalent (FREN-UA 9030 in NYU Paris, FREN-SHU 30 in NYU Shanghai) or an AP French Language and Culture Exam score of 4 or 5.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. History of the Romance Languages Why is written French so unintuitive and complicated? Why are there letters you don’t even pronounce? And why does it all sound so prestigious and refined? This course will explore how the French language evolved from its Latin roots to the rich diversity of today’s Francophone world. We will look at the twists and turns of its history—how political power, cultural exchanges, and unexpected linguistic shifts shaped its grammar, sounds, and spelling. By diving into texts, manuscripts, and key moments in history, we will uncover the reasons behind the quirks and complexities of French—and why they continue to fascinate and frustrate us today! This course will be taught in English.

sections.topic: Early Music in Sounds and Songs
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. War cries, bird songs, city noises, nonsense poetry, love laments, and divine invocations—this course explores a thousand years of sound and song from the Middle Ages to the late 1700s. It introduces key idioms, genres, and forms of early Western music while examining how text, music, and space shape rich sonic experiences. No prior musical knowledge required. The course will be taught in English.

title: Race in France: Literature, Film, Theory
description: Course conducted in English. In recent years, France’s complex relationship with race has been the object of intense debates. Traditionally, France has relied on a universalist ideal of color-blindness that does not recognize the existence of race and rejects its use in public discourse and political action. Today, however, a growing number of activists and intellectuals contend that the traditional republican ban on race has not only failed to prevent racism but makes it impossible to fully measure racist discriminations. This course investigates how French and francophone writers, intellectuals, artists and filmmakers, have engaged with these questions. While exploring the historical and political context of these debates, we will ask ourselves how artistic and literary practices can challenge established concepts of identity. In addition to introducing you to important intellectual and artistic debates in contemporary France, this course will also offer you the opportunity to rethink some of the categories that structure U.S. debates on these questions by confronting them to a different cultural context.

sections.notes: At first glance, love is not a political affect. It nullifies tensions, cancels antagonisms, oppositions, and conflicts. Yet, in the 20th- and 21st-century Black France, many thinkers, poets, and artists, from Senghor to Fanon, etc., defended a radical understanding of love. Love can unite those separated by borders, the color line, that is to say, race and racism. It allows for a critique of the power that is exercised as much in public life as within our private lives. It opposes the multiple forms of domination that create hierarchies of rejection. The purpose of this course is to analyze how love was conceived as a transformative force to combat discourses based on race and racism in contemporary Black France. Love is, in this course, understood in its multiple senses: interpersonal, political, and religious. This course will be taught in English.

title: French News in Conversation
description: In this course, students gather once a week for “French news, with coffee.” Before each workshop, students read articles in online French news sources (Le Monde, Le Monde diplomatique, Le Figaro, etc.), research new vocabulary, and consign the most important ideas and their personal reactions in a “news journal.” During the discussion-based workshop, students (in French) will discuss the news, review vocabulary, and generally utilize and improve their fluency and cultural competency. title: French and Francophone Women Writers
description: The rich and diverse literary works by women express their individuality and their important social and cultural role in France from the 12th century to the present. The course studies both the changing sociohistorical context of these writers and the common problems and themes that constitute a female tradition. Writers include Marie de France, Christine de Pisan, Marguerite de Navarre, Mme. de S?vign?, Germaine de Sta?l, George Sand, Colette, Simone de Beauvoir, and Marguerite Duras.

sections.notes: SAME AS SCA-UA 740. “Women writers, women film makers: a contemporary perspective”. Within the broad issue of film adaptations, this course will broach the salient topics of new forms of feminine intimacy with Alice Ferney’s L’Intimité, 2025 (adapted to the screen by Carine Tardieu as L’Attachement, 2025, with Valeria Bruni Tedeschi in the main role), that of being a young Muslim lesbian in today’s France with Fatima Daas’ La Petite dernière, 2020 (adapted to the screen by Hafsia Herzi, 2025), and that of underage girls as objects of males’ predation with Vanessa Springora’s Le Consentement, 2020 (adapted to the screen by Vanessa Filho, 2023). This course is taught in French.

sections.topic: Médias et crises politiques en France aux XXe–XXIe
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. The prerequisite for this course is FREN-UA 30 (French Grammar and Composition). Au croisement de l’histoire des médias et de l’histoire politique française, ce cours vous propose d’examiner le rôle joué par les médias français dans certaines des crises politiques majeures qu’a connu la France au cours du XXème siècle (affaire Dreyfus ; 6 février 1934 ; mai 1968). Il interroge plus généralement la participation décisive des médias à la formation de l’opinion publique et les usages stratégiques faits des médias par les hommes politiques confrontés à une situation de crise. Ce cours se veut aussi être une réflexion sur les évolutions de la démocratie française au cours du XX ème siècle et sur ce que la situation politique actuelle doit aux héritages du passé. Il offre enfin une solide initiation à l’analyse critique des sources médiatiques (archives audiovisuelles et collections de presse écrite). This course is taught in French.

title: French Culture & French Cinema (in French)
description: On December 28th, 1895, cinema was given its official characteristics by the Lumière brothers in Paris. If for over a century, the “Seventh Art” has been an essential element and a vehicle for French culture, the city of Paris has epitomized the evolution and contradictions of the French cinema industry. Focusing on the main tendencies in contemporary French cinema, we will ask the following questions: How do the French filmmakers depict the city of Lights, the City of Love, the City of Horror? How decisive a representation of Paris and its suburbs can be? Why do the images of Paris illustrate the history of French cinema? What do they show about French culture?

title: France and Islam
description: Islam is the second most important religion in France (after Roman Catholicism) and France has the highest Muslim population in Europe. Complex events from the mid-20th century forward have led to continuous heated debate and controversy about the place of Muslim citizens within the secular Republic. France's interwoven history with Islam dates back, however, to the first Umayyad conquests of the Iberian peninsula in the 8th century and then to the period of the Crusades. Through the use of primary sources, literary and filmic texts, and critical readings (notably in history, sociology and cultural studies), this course traces the complexity and heterogeneity of French perceptions of Islam within a broad historical perspective beginning with these early encounters and continuing up to the present day.

title: Lost and Found: Expatriate Writers in Paris
description: This course explores the connections between major French and American expatriate writings of the Modernist period and beyond. As the site of unprecedented cosmopolitanism and creativity, early 20th-century Paris saw the emergence of artistic and intellectual movements that were to have a considerable impact on Western culture to this day. Though a variety of texts (novels, short stories, memoirs, poems, and essays) we explore the questions of inner and outer exile inherent in the modern condition, of living and writing on the margins, of otherness and estrangement in relation to class, gender, sexuality, language, and to Paris as a specific urban environment. Includes texts by, among others, Hemingway, Fitzgerald, Stein, Colette, Apollinaire, Proust, Aragon, Céline and Camus.

title: French Novel: the 20th and 21st Centuries
description: Having become the dominant literary genre in France and in the Francophone world, the novel went through a variety of movements and experimentations from the end of WWI to the middle of the 2020’s. In this course, you will discover how some masterpieces of the genre contributed to the formulation of a new subjectivity, and to the reevaluation of gender definitions; how they related to some of the major collective crises of the times; and how they tested the power of writing through various narratological and stylistic innovations.

title: Studies in Prose Genres: Postcolonial Readings of Classic Texts
description: In this course we focus on four contemporary novels in which the world of the character, the narrator, or the author, is read through the lens of a literary classic. In each case, the reading and rewriting of the primary text involves temporal and spatial displacements (from the 18th to the 20th century, from Europe to the Caribbean and to the South Pacific) that generate shifting perspectives and a constant reshuffling of center and periphery. Between a reverential affiliation to the past and a creative misreading and rewriting of it, these intertextual encounters with « great » Western literary works insistently raise the questions of identity, originality, and “writing back”. Exploring these questions will therefore also involve drawing on comparative, translation, and postcolonial studies.

title: German Occupation in French Literature and Cinema (in French)
description: The course explores how literature and cinema from 1945 to the present have covered the topic of the "Années noires" ("the Dark years"), or the period of German occupation in France. Figured against the backdrop of the events of World War II and the Occupation, the course examines the complexity of questions of identity, memory, and narrative in relation to this complex moment in French history. Includes texts by Sartre, Vercors, Modiano, Perec, Duras. Films include *Les Jeux Interdits (*René Clément), *Lacombe Lucien *(Louis Malle), *Night & Fog *(Alain Resnais). In addition students participate in an overnight trip to visit the D-day beaches and other World War II sites in Normandy. In French.

title: French News in Conversation
description: In this course, students gather once a week for “French news, with coffee.” Before each workshop, students read articles in online French news sources (Le Monde, Le Monde diplomatique, Le Figaro, etc.), research new vocabulary, and consign the most important ideas and their personal reactions in a “news journal.” During the discussion-based workshop, students (in French) will discuss the news, review vocabulary, and generally utilize and improve their fluency and cultural competency. Particular emphasis will be placed on news items relating to diversity and ecology within France and the French-speaking world.

title: French Phonetics Workshop
description: This workshop aims to highlight the specificities of French language pronunciation in order to correct the most frequent errors and to provide students a phonetic correction necessary for a good acquisition of French as a foreign language. We will study the characteristics of French, the specific sounds of French as well as the main difficulties encountered by English speakers. The course will provide both a theoretical as well as practical approach to ensure the acquisition of good aural and oral skills in French. Students will work on listening skills as well as oral production via in-class presentations and exercises to do at home. Through the study of poetry we will work on the relationship between sounds and the spelling of words, rhymes and intonation. In addition, students will learn the international phonetic alphabet as a means to grasping the difference between written and spoken language.

sections.topic: Après la catastrophe : Traces et récits
sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Please contact the department for a permission code for this course. À partir d’études de cas — le génocide des Tutsi du Rwanda, la Shoah, le génocide des Arméniens — ce séminaire examine comment ces événements ont été documentés, racontés et interprétés a posteriori. La réflexion s’étend également à des situations contemporaines (Darfour, Rohingya, Ouïghours, Yézidis, Palestine), où l’usage du terme « génocide » fait débat. Croisant histoire, sciences sociales et études des médias, le cours interroge la production du savoir après la catastrophe et offre une formation aux enjeux politiques, éthiques et épistémologiques liés à l’étude des crimes de masse. title: French-African Relations (in French)
description: A historical and political inquiry into the French system of relations with Francophone Africa from the 'race to Empire' in the 19th century to the current day. The main goals of the course are: to describe the historical development of French-African relations from the colonial to the post-independence era; to investigate the political, economic and cultural mechanisms of French influence in contemporary Francophone Africa; to understand the consequences for France of complex developments subsequent to colonialism, such as African immigration in France. Conducted in French.

description: The French Honors Program is open to all students majoring in French with an overall grade point average of 3.65 and an average of 3.65 in the major. description: An Independent Study is an opportunity for students to work closely with a faculty advisor on a subject or interest related to their area of study. title: Complexities: Ocean
description: The ocean is, obviously, internally complex: marine ecosystems themselves are vast networks of species, down to the microorganism. Marine data science is crucial to measuring environmental change; for instance, polar ice shrinking constitutes key evidence for global warming. The study of oceans also enables the exploration of human migratory patterns, including forced migration and colonialism. Literary and artistic engagement—from Moby-Dick to the photography of the Swahili coast—bring to the fore the challenges confronting representations of oceans and oceanic culture, and reveal dimensions of both that elude empirical methods.Attention to how those who make their lives and livelihoods near and on the ocean—from groups of fishermen in Newark, New Jersey to Māori communities in New Zealand—sheds light on forms of social organizations more generally. Throughout the course, scholars address the ethical challenges of sustainable development, scientific exploration, ethnographic study, and artistic representation, as well as the implications of current decision-making for future generations.

title: Journalism of War, Revolution, Genocide, and Human Rights
description: In this seminar we will read some of the key journalistic works on war, revolution, genocide, and human rights that have been written in the past one hundred years. We will attempt to answer such questions as: How, and why, has the nature of war changed in the past century? Why do some revolutions, such as those in Eastern Europe after the fall of Communism, largely succeed, while others, such as those of the Arab Spring, fail so miserably? How do we understand senseless, sadistic violence—what Primo Levi called “useless cruelty”? Why do sufferers of violence and oppression so often become perpetrators of it? What is the difference between war and genocide, and why did the latter emerge in the 20th century? Why has terrorism re-emerged with such vengeance in the past two decades? What are “human rights”—another invention of the 20th century—and how, if at all, have they become a reality?

sections.notes: This seminar is open to first-year students in CAS only. This seminar will focus on some of the extraordinary political events that made, and changed, the political (and moral) realities of the past century, and that created the world that we now inhabit. Throughout the term we will return to certain questions, including the changing nature of violence and the emergence of disputed concepts such as "crimes against humanity" and "human rights." We'll consider the ways in which "the face of war" in the 20th century (and early 21st) has changed—and the ways in which the journalism that described those wars also changed. We will start with the Russian Revolution and the Spanish Civil War and then study the journalism of, among other events, the Holocaust, the Iranian Revolution, the fall of Communism, the genocide in Rwanda, the war in Bosnia, the Israeli-Palestinian conflict, 9/11, and the Arab Spring.

title: Wiseguys, Spies & Private Eyes: Heroes and Villains in Modern American Culture
description: Through thematic analyses of books and films by topic and genre, this seminar explores the ways in which specific American archetypes and themes are perceived and articulated—from the rugged Old West individualist, to the persevering underdog who becomes a boxing champ, to the evolving perceptions of government, to the Cold War-era uncertainty that spawned a generation of literary and celluloid superspies. We will examine representations of heroes and villains in modern American popular culture and how great films and novels of three particular genres, the Detective, the Gangster, and the Spy, influenced our understanding of these archetypes. From the early influences of Hamlet and Macbeth to Sherlock Holmes, Raymond Chandler’s Phillip Marlowe, Mario Puzo’s (and Francis Ford Coppola’s) The Godfather, James Bond, and Batman, we will look at the mythology and evolution of heroes and villains through popular and high culture icons, the genesis of the genres and how they developed over time, and how great directors, actors, and writers influenced audiences worldwide and were themselves influenced by culture and history.

title: Laboratories for Democracy: Making American Cites Better
description: At a time when many Americans have become increasingly frustrated with what government has produced, there are places that are getting it done right. Cities, states and municipalities serve as what Justice Brandeis called “little laboratories for democracy”—where ideas flourish and problems get solved. From fighting crime in the streets of New York City, to banning smoking in bars and restaurants, to making the power grid more efficient, to encouraging the arts and culture in urban environments, innovations in American cities have spread across the globe. This course examines the intersection of ideas, politics, and action. We study best practices from around the country (and the world), evaluate their effectiveness, and determine whether and how successful programs can be replicated. This course asks students to not only think critically issues of public policy but also to think anew about the role they play in shaping it. Topics for student projects are drawn from current issues and problems facing decision-makers and elected officials in America today.

sections.notes: This course is open to first-year students in CAS only. Examines the intersection of policy, politics, media, and government, focusing on issues including: income inequality, justice, health, education, and the environment as we look for implementable ideas to improve lives and speed our recovery.

title: How We See
description: Do we see the world the way we do because we are the way we are or because the world is the way it is? The ease with which we comprehend the visual world, and recognize objects and events, makes it tempting to think that the world is just the way we see it and to take our perceptual capabilities for granted. But when we comprehend that we cannot process all the information available in the environment, when we try to build machines that can see, or when we encounter people who have lost some specific visual capability—for example, persons who can no longer recognize faces—we realize how extraordinary and intricate are the machinery and mechanisms of sight. This course looks at what we know about vision from multiple scientific perspectives: perceptual psychology tells us about the process of seeing, and provides important insights into the workings of visual mechanisms; neuropsychology shows us what happens to perception when these mechanisms malfunction; neuroscience tells us about processes at the level of cells and neural systems. At the same time, we discuss modes and techniques of scientific inquiry from these different perspectives. How do vision scientists learn? What kinds of experiments do they conduct? How has the development of new neuroimaging techniques (fMRI, for example) shaped the field?

title: In Search of Lost Time
description: We will read Proust (in translation) as he should be read: hedonistically—with respect and admiration but also with delectation. A prodigious novel of more than 4,000 pages, In Search of Lost Time is one of modern literature’s most challenging and deeply pleasurable reads. The richest of the themes it explores is desire—its remembrance, transformation, perversion, defeat, and final resurgence in the form of art. Often said to be the first modern fiction, In Search of Lost Time is still unparalleled in how it combines finesse and wit with raw emotion, self-examination with social history, profound psychological acuity with a dazzling portrait of the French beau monde at the outset of modernity, how it merges an audacious explosion of literary form with explorations of memory, attachment, deception, lust, jealousy, ambition, and disappointment. Although Marcel Proust (1871–1922) is often cited as France’s greatest novelist (and the novelist’s novelist), his prose is so layered and brilliant that, unfortunately, many readers begin at the beginning and never move past the first fifty pages, reading the same gorgeous sentences again and again. But while In Search of Lost Time’s prose style may have been its most radical contribution to the art of fiction, its vast, thrilling architecture cannot be understood until it has been read once in its entirety. In this intensive class, we will move at a brisk pace through the work, merely glancing at its riches on our way, until we arrive at the uniquely euphoric experience of reading the final volume, when we begin to understand the extraordinarily intimate relationship Proust creates with his reader. In-class creative writing exercises are designed to help with the reading and to expand an expressive, personal response. Reading assignments average 350 pages per week.

Although Proust (1871–1922) is often cited as France’s greatest novelist, many readers never move past the first fifty pages of his work, reading the same gorgeous sentences again and again. When we read the final volume, we begin to understand the extraordinarily intimate and imaginative relationship Proust sustains with his reader, and, most importantly, how the vast structure of In Search of Lost Time reveals the intertwining of life and art to create literature. In-class creative writing exercises and wide-ranging class discussion are designed to assist with the reading and to articulate an expressive, personal response."

title: Homer Versus Vergil
description: The epics of Homer (Iliad and Odyssey) and Vergil (Aeneid) are key foundational texts of the West. But they also represent competing narratives of what it means to be human, particularly with regard to the individual’s role in society. Moreover, not only do these texts offer starkly different paradigms, but they are also acutely aware of their differences and subtly engage with one another. Thus, the Odyssey questions the heroic assumptions underlying the Iliad, and the Aeneid imitates Homer while, at the same time, drastically reworking the Greek myth to explore contemporary Roman concerns. This course will read these texts with particular attention to changing concepts of the individual (a/k/a “hero”)—e.g., the Greek warrior Achilles, who is alienated from his society not only by pride in his military prowess, but also because he makes moral demands out of step with the prevailing values of his society; his comrade Odysseus, more cunning than brave, whose difficult homecoming represents the recovery of a self defined by the domestic joys of family and friends; and, finally, the Trojan Aeneas who also wanders after the war, but as a refugee, for his home has been destroyed, and whose piety (rather than bravery or cunning) compels him to lead his people to a new promised land which, like Moses, he will not live to see. The catastrophic losses suffered by both sides in war, the mass migration and displacement of peoples, the tension between political expediency and ethical choice, and the achievement of public good at great personal cost—these themes are as relevant today as they were in Greece of the 8th century BCE or the Rome of the emperor Augustus. No prior knowledge of these texts or of the ancient world will be assumed. Students who have never read these “great books” will delight in encountering them in the company of other smart readers; and those who are familiar with the works will deepen their understanding of their richness and enduring relevance.

title: Gestures, Movement, and Literature
description: Working in the space of articulation between dance, literature, and politics, this seminar examines movement(s) and dance as a key element with which to read transformative moments of history, culture, politics, and philosophy. How do philosophers use the body dancing as a metaphor for thought? How do we read the body dancing before Columbus’ arrival as the first archive of knowledge and resistance? How does the dancing body enter the stage of race relations in 19th century Cuba? What impact does US modern dance have in the political history of the nation and how is it that a Mexican, José Limón, stands as one of the leading figures in US modern dance? Why is it that political movements use the term “movement” to speak of a politics, and what impact does that have on the political histories of bodies? The course will include texts by Cirilo Villaverde, García Lorca, Luis Palés Matos, Alejo Carpentier, Jorge Luis Borges, Julio Cortázar, Andrés Caicedo, Claudia Salazar and Mario Bellatin; the films of Almodóvar; and flamenco dance and the dances of José Limón, Martha Graham and Pina Bausch, Oscar Araiz and Alicia Díaz. The theoretical and philosophical bases will be provided by Nietzsche, Agamben, Ranciére, Marie Bardet, Lepecki, and Badiou, all of whom talk specifically about the art of movement, about movement and politics, or about movement and dance as metaphor for thought. The course understands as a premise that we can use the history of dance and movement as a way of understanding history and politics in Latin America.

title: Happiness in Film
description: This seminar investigates the representations of happiness in film, drawing on a variety of sources and disciplines including cinema studies, history, philosophy, positive psychology, ethology, and cultural studies. We will discuss the notion of “happiness” through the lens of different historical and cultural contexts, and consider how film techniques are used in those contexts to convey positive emotions. Topics include: the transformation and rebirth of heroes in myths and fairy tales in film; the building of the self away from social determinisms; “happy-endings” in classical Hollywood cinema, including comedies and musicals; the politics of happiness, race, class, and gender in world cinema; happiness and the practice of frugality; the building of common ground across communities, nations, and species.

title: DNA: From the Double Helix to Nanotechnology
description: DNA from the basics to some of today's sophisticated applications. We begin with the experiments that first identified DNA as the molecule of heredity and read The Double Helix by James Watson, which gives a lively (and biased) first-person account of the discovery of this crucial building block of life. The seminar then moves on to technical issues and considerations: how does DNA store genetic information, and how does a cell process this information using the genetic code? At the end of the seminar, we build on these foundations and learn about DNA nanotechnology and its many potential applications in science and healthcare.

title: Kote Nou Ye?: Exploring Black Haitian Diasporic Identity
description: The Haitian-American experience is often riddled with feelings of shame, nostalgia, and confusion. The past several decades have been witness to the rise of several Haitian-American diasporic voices: authors creating works of fiction that cast a light on the unique experience of existing in a liminal space. This course will focus on the work of Black Haitian-American authors such as Edwidge Danticat, Ibi Zoboi, and Katia Ulysse, using them as intimate case studies exploring the following questions: Has the Haitian-American experience shifted in any way in the past several decades? Who can identify as a "Dyaspora"? How is Haitian identity and culture being passed on through these stories? Where is the Haitian Diaspora now? Ultimately, the goal is to deepen our knowledge of Haiti and its people abroad and create a call to action.

title: Quantum Physics, Information and Communications: Why it can change the world and what's next
description: This course will present quantum mechanics (QM), quantum computing and communication in a non-technical manner, focusing on basic concepts. It will cover the foundations of QM, Einstein's philosophical objections to the interpretation of quantum measurement, quantum entanglement, up to present day potentially revolutionary applications of QM in information technology.

title: Love and War. Epic and Romance from Classical Antiquity to Early Modernity
description: This seminar offers the opportunity to study two of the greatest works of Italian literature, Lodovico Ariosto's Orlando furioso (1532) and Torquato Tasso's Gerusalemme liberata (1581) in their historical context, and in relation to the rich literary traditions of romance and epic that converge in them. Thematic focuses include the construction of gender and the representation of religious and racial "otherness."

title: Indigenous Hip Hop Generation: Edutainment and Sonic Sovereignty
description: This seminar explores the growing generation of young musician-activists reshaping global hip-hop to express their Indigenous roots and advocate for their community's rights. It focuses on Indigenous hip-hop as an emerging transnational cultural phenomenon linking communities and diasporas, spanning from New York to some of the world's most geographically remote nations. Because of its oral tradition, communal spirit, resistance culture, and decolonial pedagogical praxis, hip-hop is a natural vehicle for reviving Indigenous languages and cultures, including ways of knowing, thinking, and sustainable living. Indigenous hip-hop draws inspiration from various cultures and traditions, both ancient and modern, global and local. It serves as a soundtrack for Indigenous youths rejecting essentialist and static notions of Indigeneity, instead reclaiming their language and cultural practices, promoting gender inclusivity, Indigenous memory, and the healing of centuries-old trauma and violence. This seminar will examine mainstream and underground hip-hop to understand how Indigenous musicians borrow and reshape globally-circulating elements of hip-hop by integrating Indigenous languages, music traditions, and resistance politics. To foster critical thinking and creativity, in-class discussions include analyses of academic works, hip-hop cultural productions, as well as intellectual reflections with guest speakers, including hip-hop scholars and rappers.

sections.notes: This is a departmental course, and open to all students. Indigenous Hip Hop Generation: Edutainment and Sonic Sovereignty This seminar explores the emerging field of Indigenous hip hop studies by examining how Indigeneity is articulated within hip hop cultures across Abya Yala and Turtle Island—the Americas. The course focuses on a growing generation of Indigenous youth who engage hip hop as transformative edutainment—a convergence of critical education and creative expression that both teaches and mobilizes audiences toward sonic sovereignty, understood as an embodied practice of self-definition, collective determination, and land rematriation emerging through relational forms of community and cultural expression. Rather than simply adopting a globalized cultural form, Indigenous artists use hip hop as a powerful medium to challenge ongoing structures of settler colonialism, state-nation violence, systemic racism, and heteropatriarchy. The seminar examines Indigenous hip hop as protest music, decolonizing praxis, and sonic activism that disrupt dominant colonial and heteropatriarchal logics within mainstream cultural industries—spaces where cultural, gender, and sexual identities intersect with historical Indigenous memory and political resistance. Through analysis of lyrics, performances, and community-based initiatives, students will explore how Indigenous youth employ hip hop to assert sovereignty, revitalize Indigenous languages and knowledge-making practices, and imagine alternative futures. The course includes interdisciplinary readings, guest lectures, artist performances, hip hop workshops, and engagement with the International Indigenous Hip Hop Gathering in the South Bronx (October 8–12, 2026). Taught in English.

sections.topic: Versailles: The Making of a World Heritage
sections.notes: This course is open to first-year students in CAS only. Considered a “place of excellence and French know-how,” recognized as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, the estate that Louis XIV built for his personal glory and that Louis-Philippe transformed into a “monument to all the glories of France” remains one of the most emblematic European sites. Using Versailles as a reference point, this course will be an opportunity to explore the notion of cultural heritage more broadly, as well as the symbolic values that this physical site has had in France and abroad over the course of its history. Through readings of historical and literary works, the study of architecture, decorations and gardens, the analysis of films and other audio-visual documents, participants in this seminar will observe how Versailles embodied certain aesthetic, political, cultural, and economic ideals. A group visit to the Metropolitan Museum will complement classroom activities.

This seminar is open to first-year students in CAS only. This first-year seminar will explore gender and sexuality as generative forces for thought and vision, focusing especially on modes of desire and gendered being that fall outside of available categories. Authors and artists will range from Proust to RuPaul; topics of discussion will include the politics of good versus bad feeling, the uses of shame, friendship, queer ecologies, and the aesthetics of camp and drag. We’ll be especially interested throughout the semester in stories of transformation and metamorphosis. We might assume that queer or trans narratives hinge on the act of “coming out.” Yet in some of the works we’ll discuss this semester, characters live their queerness without any definitive declaration, and without necessarily laying claim to an LGBTQ+ “identity.” Dissident sexuality or gender in these works is not necessarily the inner truth of a subject, let alone the core of a personality. Instead, it’s an aesthetic phenomenon, a way of beholding the world, a tender attention to textures, surfaces, and nuances of affection.

This course is open to first-year students in CAS only. This seminar will be an introduction to both grammatical micro-diversity, via the syntax of dialects, especially English ones, and to grammatical macro-diversity, via the syntax of languages very different from English, from various parts of the world, considering in detail what they may have in common with English, despite initial appearances, and with each other and how best to characterize the ways in which they differ from English and from each other.

This course is open to first-year students in CAS only. The discussions of city, space, place, and globalization are at the center of debates in multiple fields of study. This course explores how cities became dominant features of landscapes; what is the urban-rural dynamic about, how we can compare past and present perspectives on urbanism and globalization, what is the relationship between the histories of the city and globalization, and how cities could have different functions through time and space. This course provides students with the understanding and necessary skills for addressing environmental, political, and socioeconomic issues in urban spaces and develops skills in research, writing, analytical thinking, and spatial understanding. Discussions will be drawn from different disciplines, including anthropology, environmental sciences, urban geography, history, and political economy. We will focus on cities in contemporary times as well as different historical periods from across the world. This flexibility in discipline, temporal, and spatial aspects is an opportunity for students to apply learnings to their fields of study and work.

This course is open to first-year students in CAS only. The word horror brings to mind a genre often rife with supernatural elements, as well as dramatic historical events and, perhaps, even some personal experiences of our past. This class interrogates works of fiction, memoirs, movies, manga, and philosophical texts to study what horror means and why it may fascinate us. In analyzing representations of horror within and beyond the horror genre, we will consider whether it belongs to our modern lives. Honing the participants' close-reading and critical analysis skills, this course will also provide an opportunity to reflect on what horror reveals about our society and ourselves.

sections.topic: Reading for Dear Life: Contemporary Literature Lab
sections.notes: This seminar is open to first-year students in CAS only. This course bases itself on the premise that thinking and talking thoughtfully with others about literary works is a very good thing to do — not just in later life, but also when you are an undergraduate, whatever your planned major or usual interests might be. Asking why the book group has become such a popular social activity and what helps these gatherings run in their most effective manner, the course will also hone your book-group participant skills by making you interact with a variety of short literary works in a range of genres. Two major modes of theoretical engagement will be in play throughout the course. In the first place you will receive a training in the basics of narrative theory, enabling you to apply key narratological concepts to each of our literary texts and thereby bring focus and precision to your analyses. In the second place, with the help of critics such as Fredric Jameson and Franco Moretti, you will learn how to situate both the form and content of our texts in their appropriate historical contexts; additionally, you will be encouraged at all junctures to historicize your own responses to the assigned fiction.

sections.topic: Free Speech in Life, Literature and Law
sections.notes: This seminar is open to first-year students in CAS only. Free Speech in Life, Literature, and Law introduces students to the promises and challenges of free expression in contemporary life. Framing free speech as both a personal right and a shared responsibility, the course examines the idea of "free speech" in different cultural, historical and national contexts. The seminar draws on court cases, essays, stories, poems, and digital media to explore how speech shapes identity, community, and conflict. Students practice close reading, discussion, and analytical writing to come up with real-life solutions to challenging situations. We will consider debates about identity and its link to language, censorship, protest, and the difference between philosophical and legal approaches to free speech to develop skills for speaking—and listening—across difference in the college classroom and beyond.

This seminar is open to first-year students in CAS only. In this course we will cover the varieties of Italian food in their past and present forms. First, we will explore the history of food from past civilizations, leading up to World War I, just after the great immigration to the New World. Time periods examined will be ancient Rome, Medieval, Renaissance, Risorgimento, leading to the modern era. This course includes topics ranging from Pellegrino Artusi’s famous cookbook in the contest of Italian unification to the relationship between Italian Futurism and food. The second part of the course will introduce students to the regional diversity of Italian food using mediums such as TV, art, and film. We will examine the ways in which food shapes contemporary Italian society, from the more intimate family kitchen to the most elegant Italian restaurant in New York City.

This seminar is open to first-year students in CAS only. This course is an introduction to aspects of the Andean world related to the language, culture, civilization, and resistance of the Quechua people. We will focus on the analysis and interpretation of several Andean categories whose cosmogony is not expressed - as it is in the Western world - in statements, axioms, propositions, and conclusions; that is, the rhetoric of concepts. Rather, in the Andean world knowledge and philosophy are expressed in the spoken language itself, through concrete grammatical marks such as suffixes and performative verbs (with a tendency towards action). The notion of death as a transition (regressive suffix -pu), the predominance of the group over the individual (two pronouns for ‘we’: exclusive and inclusive), the struggle between orality and writing, the binary magnitude of time/space (pacha), and the suffixes which distinguish human reasoning from animal instinct (the suffixes -pu and -ku) are some of the topics to be discussed. The course will be taught in English; there are no prerequisites.

sections.topic: Eros and Sexuality in Modern Jewish Literature
sections.notes: This is a departmental course and open to all students. What’s love got to do with it? This is a question that has been debated by Jewish writers since the inception of modern Jewish literature. For decades, Jewish authors, artists, and intellectuals have negotiated the status of romantic and sexual love within Judaism, often as a troubling, at times alien, subject matter in the context of Jewishness and the Jewish tradition. With the rise of modern Yiddish and Hebrew literatures in particular, writers articulated new modes of conceiving desire, love, sex, and gender, especially as they related to Jewish society and politics, and these issues continue to be debated within the different avenues of Jewish culture today. This course is devoted to exploring the transforming status of eros and sexuality in Jewish culture by focusing on a diverse selection of literary works, alongside drama, film, and academic essays. Building on feminist and queer theory, our discussion will revolve around issues such as sexual politics and nationalism, love and religion, border-crossing, constructions of femininity and masculinity, and queer love. All materials are available in English translation.

sections.topic: Contemporary Asian culture in the Americas
sections.notes: This is a departmental course, and open to all students. "Transpacific Memories: Race, Place, Belonging in Contemporary Asian Diasporic Cultural Production in the Americas" The presence of Asians in the Americas dates back to the 16th century, when the Manila Galleon Trade first connected Asia to Latin America through an imperial network of trade and commerce. This course takes a long durée approach to Asian diasporas in the Hemispheric Americas, concentrating on the longstanding presence of Asians in Mexico, the Caribbean, and the U.S./Mexico borderlands. Beginning with the colonial period, and through case studies of key waves of Asian migration engendered by colonialism, racial capitalism, and neoliberal globalization in the late 19th to 21st centuries, we will look at the emergence of Asian Latin American, Asian Caribbean and Asian Latinx racialized subjects vis-à-vis nation-building projects. Moreso, we will engage representations of Asians and cultural production by Asian diasporic writers and artists to question how Asian diasporic populations have engaged in memory-making practices and negotiated place and belonging in response to State violence and racial discrimination. We will pay special attention to how the diasporic experience intersects with race, gender and sexuality, engaging with materials through a feminist and queer lens. Students will learn about the construction of Asian diasporic histories in hemispheric perspective, and develop skills to critically engage with and analyze a diverse array of cultural forms in Spanish and English, including literature, visual and audiovisual art, and performance in addition to primary source materials such as maps, photography, and archival documents. Throughout the course, we will welcome guest speakers including artists, scholars, curators and activists who work at the intersections of the Asian diasporic imagination, community-building, and racial justice.

This is a departmental course and open to all students. This course explores representations of same-sex desire and gender ambiguity in literary traditions from classical antiquity to the early modern period. Far from being a modern invention, homoerotic love—and the anxieties, aspirations, and pleasures surrounding it—has long shaped Western literature, even as its presence has been alternately celebrated, contested, denied, or overwritten across centuries. We will trace these shifting attitudes by reading authors who either explicitly evoke same-sex desire or encode it through indirection, metaphor, and gender play. Beginning with antiquity, we examine Sappho’s lyric fragments, Plato’s Symposium, Ovid’s narratives of transformation, and Martial’s epigrams, alongside moments of gender ambiguity in myth and epic. In the medieval and early modern periods, we turn to Shakespeare’s sonnets, Ariosto’s elusive treatments of homoerotic desire, and the exploration of gender in the Roman de Silence. We also consider lesser-known works, including Giulia Bigolina’s Urania, an unpublished prose narrative that stages complex bonds among women; Immanuel of Rome, a Jewish-Italian poet often compared to Dante; and the poetic Latin letters exchanged between medieval women (the so-called Tegernsee letters, interpreted by Peter Dronke). Throughout the semester, we will investigate how authors encode desire, disguise it, or articulate it openly; how same-sex affection intersects with friendship, politics, and spirituality; and how gender variance and emotional intimacy challenge the boundaries of literary representation. The course welcomes students from all backgrounds and requires no prior knowledge of classical or early modern literature.

This is a departmental course, and open to all students. The letter is one of the oldest genres of writing, and one that despite shifts in technologies, is still with us today in the form of the email. The email is the most common genre you will write in as a student at NYU. Indeed, you will write emails to professors, peers, administrators, and other assorted interlocutors throughout your time here. Oddly, for such a foundational genre, we almost never talk about it. We simply expect you to come prepared to read, write, and track countless numbers of emails every week for the duration of your undergraduate studies. This course seeks to address this gap by centering correspondence practices both digital and analogue, asking you to read classic epistolary (letter) texts as you consider your own epistolary style. Beyond their primary purpose to make introductions, narrate circumstances, and/or make requests of the recipient, writers have harnessed the genre to explore complex themes of loss, absence, desire, etc.. In this course, we will foreground the letter genre, exploring the way that it has been (re)imagined and (re)deployed for a variety of ends from antiquity to the present. We will seek to understand its mediational logics, rooted in the formal conceit of a speaking document that is a proxy for an absent speaker, and the ways that this conceit lends itself to manifold artistic ends. To better understand these artistic ends, we will engage in critical-creative writing assignments that ask you to adopt the persona and epistolary conventions of a given author and reflect on this process in formal writing. You will also have the opportunity to engage in your own (actual) correspondence and reflect on that process as well. Ultimately, the goal of this course is to explore the practical and artistic features of the epistolary genre from antiquity to the present.

sections.topic: The Aesthetics of Health in Lusophone Lit and Art
sections.notes: This is a departmental seminar, and open to all students. This course explores the connections between health practices and artistic expression in Brazil, Portugal, and Lusophone Africa. Through poetry, film, archival materials, and aesthetic practices, students explore how aesthetic representation interacts with medical and scientific discourses shaped by colonial histories, eugenic policies, and institutional violence. Two figures and their medical approaches serve as focal points: Portuguese neurologist Egas Moniz and Brazilian psychiatrist Nise da Silveira. Moniz developed the lobotomy, a procedure that earned him the 1949 Nobel Prize but raised questions about medical authority and bodily autonomy. In contrast, Silveira transformed mental health care by rejecting invasive procedures and introducing art therapy to help restore patients’ agency. Using works by Lima Barreto, Clarice Lispector, Stella do Patrocínio, Arthur Bispo do Rosário, Lygia Clark, Davi Kopenawa, Fernando Pessoa, and African Lusophone authors including Paulina Chiziane, Mia Couto, Luís Bernardo Honwana, and Pepetela, students analyze aesthetic depictions of mental health, pathology, and the body across Luso-African-Brazilian societies. They also explore how these works challenge medicalized ideas of normalcy and deviance, offering alternative ways of understanding and healing. This course will be taught in English.

sections.topic: Power, Memory, and Healing in Latin America
sections.notes: NOTE: This course is taught in English. This is a departmental seminar, and open to all students. This course draws on sensory studies and health humanities to explore how Latin American writers, artists, filmmakers, and thinkers mobilize the body and senses as sources of knowledge, political resistance, and cultural transformation. Students examine the ways sensory experiences shape lived realities and challenge colonial legacies that prioritize abstract rationality over embodied understanding, starting with a historical investigation into the dismantling of colonial myths through physical evidence. A key case study is the 1511 story of the Taíno people in Borikén (Puerto Rico), who, seeking to test the divine claims of their oppressors, submerged the Spaniard Diego Salcedo in a river and observed his body for days to confirm decomposition—an empirical, embodied act that sparked a revolution. Through close analysis of literature, visual arts, performance, and film, students explore the relationship of the body to power, society, violence, healing, and the environment. The course covers a variety of topics, including the baroque body and state violence, shamanism and embodied spirituality, extractivism and more-than-human experiences, feminist perspectives on debt and bodily autonomy, the sensory dimensions of migration and displacement, and the politics of care and vulnerability in contemporary Latin America. Taught in Spanish, this course aims to develop students' critical thinking and analytical skills while deepening their understanding of Latin American cultures through interdisciplinary approaches that treat the body as both subject and method of inquiry.

sections.topic: From Texts to Podcasts: Italian America at School
sections.notes: This is a departmental course, and open to all students. Should Americans only speak English? Is bilingualism an asset or a threat to national identity? This course tackles these urgent questions through the lens of Italian American history, tracing how language became a flashpoint for debates over citizenship, belonging, and identity in U.S. schools. From Dante’s Italy to the immigrant classroom, students explore how Italian migrants and their children navigated — and resisted — educational policies that shaped who counted as truly “American.” Drawing on a rich archive of scholarly essays, memoirs, oral histories, photographs, and audio recordings, the course pays special attention to the role of regional dialects in everyday schooling and community life. The semester culminates in a collaborative podcast project in which students craft original narratives about language, memory, and identity in Italian American communities — no technical experience required.

title: Special Topics for Graduate Interdisciplinary Academics
description: The purpose of this course is to allow for special topics that span multiple disciplines across Tandon Graduate Academics. Any graduate student at Tandon will be able to register for the course, with the permission of their departmental advisor, and Graduate Academics staff.

sections.topic: Writing Your Way into Your Next Academic Position
sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Course Repeatable for Credit. Are you planning on finishing your PhD in the next year or two? If you are considering applying for Postdoctoral fellowships or faculty positions, this class will help you prepare a portfolio of the necessary documents. These might include research statements, tailored cover letters, research proposals, and dissertation abstracts. In our class, you will learn to analyze and deconstruct the written elements of a successful application in order to effectively write your own. The class will also provide a processual structure that demystifies high-stakes documents, accountability partners to help you over writing blocks, and a collaborative environment that provides feedback and support. The class is flexible and tailored to the needs of its participants: the goal is to create a portfolio of documents that make sense for your individual job search within academia. Beyond building a portfolio of successful statements, you will learn transferable writing, revision and communications skills essential to succeeding in competitive STEM labs and careers.

title: Writing and Communication for Engineers and Scientists
description: This course aims to train graduate students in engineering and science to become more effective writers and communicators, using both theoretical instruction and practical examples/exercises. Topics include: principles of good writing, the format of a scientific manuscript, publication and peer review issues, preparation of a scientific talk, and communication with the press and the general public. A mini-course on “improvisation for scientists,” held by a professional teacher/actor, will be a fun part of the class, with the goal of teaching students to talk in public in a more spontaneous and interactive way. Throughout the class, students will be asked to work on both their writing samples and their presentations. Grading will be based on writing and communication quality and on the degree of improvement between initial and final products. | Prerequisite: Standing PhD Candidate, RE-GY 9990 and department permission required

title: Thesis I
description: Thesis 1 is the first of two related courses, Thesis 1 and Thesis 2, in which Game Center MFA students create their thesis projects. The thesis classes are focused on supporting the students’ work towards creating a finished project during their second year. A thesis project can take many forms, including a digital game, a game that exists off the computer, such as a card game or a sport, aa game that combines digital and non-digital components, such as a game that is played in real spaces incorporating the use of smartphones, a series of smaller games that represent the exploration of a set of related ideas, a game-related website, curated exhibition, or other criticism-oriented project, and a traditional research paper. Students will be encouraged to work in groups to create their thesis projects, but the possibility also exists for students to work by themselves. Because of the wide range of forms that a thesis can take, the thesis courses do not present a specific curriculum. Instead, they provide a context and structure to support and guide the students’ research. The thesis process begins during the second semester of the MFA students’ first year, as they generate thesis concepts and form into teams. These project concepts and teams must be approved during the spring semester of the students’ first year by a Game Center faculty. Students will begin the Thesis 1 course with approved project concepts and teams.

title: Games 101
description: Games 101 is the foundational course for the NYU Game Center. The focus of Games 101 is game literacy – a shared understanding of games as complex cultural and aesthetic objects. The class will incorporate lectures, discussion, readings, and writing assignments, but the primary activity of the class is critical play – playing games in order to better understand and appreciate them. The class will cover games on and off the computer, including classic and contemporary board and card games, sports, and games on the PC, internet, and consoles.

title: American Computer Games
description: This survey course covers a selection of the computer games that were produced and played in the United States in the 1980s. While developers often started out in their bedrooms mailing out individual disks in ziplock bags, development and publishing companies sprung up from their early success; when the console game industry of the early 80s crashed in 1983, the relatively high­end computer game market continued to innovate and sometimes even greatly prosper, albeit with a more narrowly targeted idea of its customers. The most popular games of the era retailed for an average of $30 ­ $40 (around $70 ­ $90 in today’s money), often with stylish, lush presentation (thick manuals, cloth maps, scene­setting “feelies”) that often doubled as a physical form of copy protection. Cultivating an aura of expense and quality allowed American game designers to project pop personas, explore new ways of creating meaning via play, and add genuine depth to game worlds. The political, cultural, and technological context of the United States in the 1980s provides a lens to analyze a corpus of games that, while often forgotten in contemporary American games culture, has imposed a powerful influence over our practices, and remains a rich ore of quirky ideas and never­explored byways to mine. The course encourages students to play games critically, to understand different game design strategies as well as the technological constraints that often led to them, and to develop an understanding of the ways in which European, Japanese and American games diverged through the 1980s. While the primary focus of the course is computer—as opposed to console or arcade—games, the latter will also be discussed to a extent; partly because they provide an effective counterpoint to what was going on in home computers, but also because there are more than enough interesting obscurities and touchstones for any game designer to at least be passingly aware of. This course is directed to students of game design and game studies, as well as those with an interest in the study of video games as a cultural form and/or digital media history and development.

sections.notes: Majors only, no exceptions

title: Game Studio I
description: Game studio 1 is the Game Design M.F.A. program’s introductory game development course. Students will gain experience with two game engines with complementary strengths and capabilities, working in teams on a series of four game development project cycles.

sections.notes: Prerequisite: Academic Plan equal to GTGAMMMFA Majors only, no exceptions

title: Prototype Studio
description: Professional game development frequently involves a ‘rapid prototyping’ phase, wherein developers work feverishly to implement a large number of small ideas to test their potential before embarking on the more rigid and costly processes involved in full production. Many or most of the most famous games in history began with a minimalistic prototype created in less than a week. Prototype Studio is an intensive course which aims to build up a student’s repertoire of fast-prototyping skills and provide the student with invaluable experience in starting and finishing games. The course consists almost entirely in the creation of thirteen playable prototype games, one per week. Each prototype will be confined within a certain genre, conceptual theme, or within unique technical constraints

sections.notes: Prerequisite: Academic Plan equal to GTGAMMMFA Game Design MFA students only. Non-majors may request permission a month after registration from the instructor. Please note exceptions are not guaranteed and will be dependent on student's familiarity with the course material.

title: Narrative Game Studio
description: The creation of novel storytelling strategies for digital games is one of the key issues in current game development. Narrative games build bridges between dramatic writing for theatre and film and game design, and opens new avenues for new types of writing for digital media. The Narrative Game Studio is a hands-on course that focuses on games that include a strong storytelling component, providing the opportunity to do interdisciplinary work. This course introduces students to the design of narrative games, including conceptualization, foundational narrative design strategies, and writing. Students will learn how to use three different tools/engines to develop narrative games; they will work individually at first and then in teams. The course uses the adventure game genre as a gateway to the general strategies used to incorporate narrative in games.

sections.notes: Prerequisite: Academic Plan equal to GTGAMMMFA Open to Game Design MFA and BFA students. Undergraduate students may request permission by entering their information at https://forms.gle/jJhCh689h3FEztU37. Non-majors will be placed in classes according to availability. Please note exceptions are not guaranteed and will be dependent on student's familiarity with the course material. Prerequisite for Undergraduate students ONLY: GAMES-UT 161 Introduction to Narrative Design

title: Physics Game Studio
description: Physics Games Studio is an advanced digital development elective combining building literacy of a genre of games and teaching the craft necessary to make an entry in that genre. It combines necessary technical skills students will have learned in their prerequisites with a literacy component like that of an arts history course, and through the technical prerequisites students will be able to analyze and critique this cross section of games, and then immediately turn the development of a critical eye toward the creation of their own work. Literacy is particularly lacking in the games industry since technology becomes obsolete at such a quick clip, a course like Physics Games Studio aims to tie directly this connection of literacy with the artistic practice of students as they finish up their degrees. This 7-week, 2-credit course which meets twice a week (once for class, once for lab) also signals a shift in the curriculum planning of the Game Center as we aim to offer a rotating selection of courses that focus on very specific literacies and skills, following the success of XR Studio: Designing Games for Headsets last semester."

sections.notes: Majors only, no exceptions.

title: Project Studio
description: In Project Studio, students will work alone or in teams to complete a single game over the course of the semester. Those wishing to take Project Studio must propose a concept or prototype to the instructor for approval. Priority will be given to students who propose a clear game concept or provide an interactive prototype. Teams, where applicable, should be formed before the start of the semester. The philosophy of the course is learning through doing, and the majority of student work time will be spent in actual design and production, which will be structured and guided by the instructor. This production time will be supplemented by in-class exercises, student presentations, critiques, playtesting, discussion, and visits from professional game developers.

title: UI/UX for Games
description: This course explores the intersection of UI UX thinking and game experience/interface design. Students will be introduced to UI UX concepts and methods, and then supported in adapting them for game specific contexts. Game design - in fact all interactive design - is a conversational undertaking. Students will become better conversationalists both by adding to their store of experience design knowledge and by learning to focus on, empathize with, and draw out their conversation partners – the players.

sections.notes: Prerequisite: GAMES-GT 200 and Academic Plan equal to GTGAMMMFA Majors only, no exceptions Prerequisite(s): GAMES-GT 200 Visual Lab 0

title: Game Design I
description: Game Design 1 explores the fundamentals of game design. The focus of the class is the actual creation of several non-digital (off the computer) games. Just as art students might take “fundamentals” classes in figure drawing or color theory as part of their education to become visual artists, this class remains rooted squarely in the basics. It focuses on the elements common to all games that are fundamental for a game designer working in any format, from sports to board games to computer and video games. Although the focus of the course is on the creation of non-digital games, digital games will also be discussed and one of the assignments is the creation of a digital game concept pitch.

sections.notes: Prerequisite: Academic Plan equal to GTGAMMMFA Majors only, no exceptions

title: Competition Reality Games Systems and Design
description: This class focuses on the complex systems and designs commonly found in televised competition reality television. Students will be asked to look beyond the overproduced, heavy-handed theatrics often found in modern reality game television and will be asked to study and develop systems that combine long term social games, with short term games that can alter the larger structure without compromising what makes that larger system function.

title: Visual Lab 0
description: "Visual Lab 0 is a fundamentals course that introduces incoming MFA Game Design students to the basics of visual design and communication. Following in the tradition of Code Lab 0, which plays a similar role with game programming, Visual Lab 0 helps students gain basic understanding and skills required for the visual aspects of game creation. The course is meant to be taken alongside Game Design 1, and Game Studio 1, and in a sense serves as a visual design tutorial for these classes. However, there will also be lessons and exercises that exist independently and focus on students learning concepts that might not immediately apply to their concurrent work in other classes."

sections.notes: Prerequisite: Academic Plan equal to GTGAMMMFA Majors only, no exceptions

title: Intro to 2D Animation for Games
description: 2D Art and Animation for Games is a 1-semester, 4-credit class that builds fundamental skills around the design and production of art assets for games. Through a series of individual design assignments, critiques, and exercises, students will explore concepts like art direction, color theory, animation principles, and UI design while building a working knowledge of prominent industry tools.

Non-majors make request permission from the instructor a month after registration. Please note exceptions are not guaranteed and will be dependent on student's familiarity with the course material. Pre-requisite(s): GAMES-GT 200 Visual Lab 0

title: 3D Modeling for Games
description: This course is an introduction to 3D graphics for video games, starting with the foundations of 3D modeling and texturing in industry-standard tools. It focuses on building fluency with basic tools and techniques, as well as developing experience with aesthetic issues of look, style, and critical judgement in visual art.
