sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS V27.0130. GREECE: A GLOBAL HISTORY Is Greece a Western or Eastern country? What is the relationship between ancient and modern Greece? What is the rapport of Greece to its “Others” –Europe, Africa, the Balkans, and the Middle East? And why does the study of Greece matter to contemporary debates on nationalism, democracy, and human rights? This course explores the history of Greece during the transition from multi-ethnic empires to nation-states, to ask broader questions about historical time, geographies of thought, and borders in and across the Mediterranean. The main focus is on refugees, migration, and the entangled histories of Muslims, Jews, and Christians in Greece and Asia Minor. In this multimedia course, blending scholarly literature with primary sources, autobiographical accounts, maps, photography, film, documentary film, and other ephemera, we will ask what it means to read a text, an image, an artifact of material culture, or a landscape, historically.

title: Greek History from The Bronze Age to Alexander
description: Until a few decades ago, Greek history began with Homer and dealt narrowly with the Greek world. Thanks to archaeology, the social sciences, and other historical tools, the chronological and geographical horizons have been pushed back. The history of the Greeks now starts in the third millennium B.C.E. and is connected to the civilization that lay to the east, rooted in Egypt and Mesopotamia. We trace Greek history from the Greeks' earliest appearance to the advent of Alexander.

sections.notes: Understanding Migration: Europe in Global Context (Cross-listed with EURO-UA 292) Migration has transformed societies across the globe, reshaping economies, labor markets, and political systems. This course provides a critical and interdisciplinary introduction to global migration, with a particular focus on Europe as both a destination and a key site of migration governance. Drawing on perspectives from human geography, anthropology, and sociology, the course examines migration as a complex social process embedded in global inequalities and historical transformations. Moving beyond abstract models, the course grounds theoretical debates in detailed case studies. It explores how contemporary migration regimes in Europe are shaped through colonial histories, processes of racialization, and the production of “illegality,” as well as the everyday practices through which borders are enforced and contested. These dynamics are examined through empirical elements including asylum systems, border zones, and migrant labor regimes across Europe, and situates them within broader global migration patterns. Attention is given to models of migration governance, including assimilationist and integration frameworks, which are examined comparatively and critically. The course raises questions regarding how such models structure inclusion and exclusion, shape policy responses and reproduce inequalities across race, class, gender, and legal status. Combining ethnographic case studies with visual anthropology and visual analysis, the course engages documentaries and visual materials to examine how migration is represented, mediated, and contested. Students develop critical tools useful in analyzing both personal experiences and their visual framing of contemporary Europe and beyond.

sections.topic: Immigration in the the Modern World
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. This course explores the governance and lived experience of migration in the 19th and 20th centuries—a period marked by tremendous human dislocations and the rise of nation-states, nationalisms and borders. Though the course moves through multiple geographic sites and fields—Northern Africa, Western Europe, Eastern Europe, the Caribbean, and Asia—it returns most often to the US and the Americas. Key themes broached in the class include the root causes of migration; the centrality of race, gender and class to immigration policy; the building of borders; border policing and the borderlands; the role of sending states and the impact of migration on them; migrant strategies of resistance, adaptation and survival; and more. While the course is primarily historical in its methodology, it draws as well from related fields, including sociology, anthropology and journalism.

title: Materials, Matter, and Materiality in the Middle Ages
description: The theme of the colloquium, materiality, is concerned with the tangible stuff of medieval lives, with those materials -animal parts, vegetable fibers, metal, stones, clay, wood, that were used and processed into finished objects -comestibles, clothing, homes and monuments, artifacts and ornaments, images and the media of written and visual communication. As they emerged from raw materials, things affected social relations and cultural perception, enabling action and provoking reaction. We will consider, for example, the effects of pageantry, with its elaborate display of culinary, heraldic, and sartorial splendor, in asserting and maintaining chivalric claims to dominance. We will examine recent archeological findings to understand the ways accessories to clothing enabled peasants to resist and re-fashion the identities imposed upon them by medieval elites.

sections.notes: The theme of the seminar, materiality, is concerned with the tangible stuff of medieval lives, with those materials -animal parts, vegetable fibers, metal, stones, clay, wood, that were used and processed into finished objects -comestibles, clothing, homes and monuments, artifacts and ornaments, images and the media of written and visual communication. As they emerged from raw materials, things affected social relations and cultural perception, enabling action and provoking reaction. We will consider, for example, the effects of pageantry, with its elaborate display of culinary, heraldic, and sartorial splendor, in asserting and maintaining chivalric claims to dominance. We will examine recent archeological findings to understand the ways accessories to clothing enabled peasants to resist and re-fashion the identities imposed upon them by medieval elites. Objects, thus, shaped history, yet historians tend to write history based upon texts. Avoiding such an exclusive dependency requires methodological reflection. Stimulated by the work of social scientists such as Jane Bennett, Alfred Gell, Tim Ingold, Carl Knappett, Bruno Latour, Dan Miller, and Bjrnar Olsen, lively debates are currently taking place about the theory, goals, and relevance of material culture studies, and we will develop our own perspectives on the issues at stake. Assessing the participation, meaning, and agency of things in pre-modern lives forces one to question boundaries so as to gain a newer historical perspective on such relationships as those between humans and animals (and nature), humans and technology, body and soul, images and memory, the animate and the inanimate. Our exploration of the connections between human and non-human environments will consider the appropriation of animal skins in the production of writing; the extension of human personhood via the use of animal power, tools, weapons, images, and memory aids; human involvement with a living landscape of holy trees, sacred groves and springs, and powerful stars; attitudes toward idols and automata; the perception of art as vibrant matter. Though modern theory inspires present-day archeologists, anthropologists, historians, and art historians to seek agency in a network of social and material relationships, medieval intellectuals were dubious about belief in the power of matter. In fact, for many, the materiality of the human body was suspicious, as was the knowledge that depended upon the mediation of the senses. Such ‘carnal’ knowledge was ascribed to minorities (Jews) and alleged dissenters (magi, witches). Materiality in the Middle Ages was a philosophical topic fraught with ambivalence, imbued with a potential for violence.

title: What is Europe?
description: Considers both the political and intellectual history of Europe?s division between Eastern Europe and Western Europe, from the 18th century to the present. Course material includes travel Considers both the political and intellectual history of Europe?s division between Eastern Europe and Western Europe, from the 18th century to the present. Course material includes travel writing, mental mapping, the Iron Curtain, and the history of the European Union.

sections.notes: This course will explore the changing meaning of Europe, European unity, and European identity over the previous two centuries, with an emphasis on the formation of the European Union during the last 65 years and current European Union issues today. After a brief introduction that explores the deeper history behind the geographical and cultural concept of Europe, this course will trace the rise of a European identity in contrast to national identities, as well as the emergence of a desire to integrate Europe from the middle of the nineteenth century to the present. Class readings and discussion will focus on four main questions. What has Europe meant to intellectuals, politicians, and citizens in the past 150 years, as a concept, as a locus of identity, and as an alternative or counterpart to the nation state? What has been the geography of Europe, and how has this changed over time? How and why have European leaders and citizens fashioned an integrated continent, and how have the obstacles to integration evolved over time? Finally, how have Europe’s recent crises—from refugees to the problems of the Euro—led people to reevaluate European integration, national identities and institutions, and globalization more generally? Course readings will historical studies, contemporary journalism and literature, political science, and sociology.

description: Explores the transformation of France from the Old Regime monarchy of the late eighteenth century to the early Third Republic of the 1870s. We will focus first on the French Revolution, its origins, dynamics and consequences. We will then study the political, social, and cultural conflicts that help explain why the French went through three more revolutions--in 1830, 1848, and 1871--before establishing a stable form of republican government. We will also devote time to social and cultural history, and especially to recent literature on working-class formation, gender relations, and the peasantry.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. This graduate reading course introduces students to classic and cutting-edge works of historical scholarship on labor unions and working-class communities. In the 1970s, labor historians challenged a postwar consensus that emphasized the rarity of class conflict and the success of American political institutions in mediating that conflict. Through detailed, often hyper-local studies of culture and consciousness, they showed how workers had long agitated and organized on the shop floor as well as in their communities. Since then, scholars have broadened this first generation’s focus on mainly white, male industrial workers, expanding their view from the factory to the plantation, the household, and other often-hidden sites of labor, and highlighting the central role of women, workers of color, and migrants in working-class history. Others “brought the state back in,” showing how workers have shaped, and been shaped by, political institutions. And in the wake of the 2008 financial crisis, they have examined how workers interacted with capitalism and markets. Labor history has often been declared “dead,” only to reappear in newly revivified form. Where is this exciting—if often disparately organized—field going today?

title: Creating Digital History
description: A hands-on introduction to “doing history” in the digital age, this course focuses on the evolving methodologies and tools used by public historians to collect, preserve, and present digital sources. Students will become familiar with a range of web-based tools, such as Omeka, and learn best practices for digitizing, adding metadata, tagging, and clearing permissions. By evaluating existing digital history projects and discussing perspectives from leading practitioners, students will also consider the role of the general public as both audiences for, and co-creators of, digital history. The core requirement is a collaborative digital history archive and exhibit that will be developed throughout the semester on a selected historical theme.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Histories of Capitalism Capitalism is once more a keyword of scholarly and popular contention. The course introduces students to dominant approaches to capitalism across distinct conjunctures of the twentieth century. Course readings and class discussion explore the major frameworks (Marxist, Gramscian, World-systemic, economic anthropological, Feminist, and Eco-socialist), that have animated efforts to comprehend capitalism as a dynamic historical phenomenon. This broad-gaged survey aims to elucidate the shifting methods and concepts (from “creative destruction” and “imperialism” to “uneven development” and “racial capitalism”) that have gained prominence at different junctures. The course concludes with a focus on the renewal of feminist theories of capitalism and the emergence of political ecological critiques of contemporary capitalism. Each week, class discussions will ‘unpack’ the arguments of individual works and frameworks first on their own terms before considering their relation to the historical conjuncture of their formulation. Precisely because scholarly and popular debates on the nature, logics, and effects of historical capitalism are so contentious, the course aims to foster research informed by transdisciplinary approaches to capitalism.

sections.topic: Psychoanalysis, Psychology and Psychiatry after Fr
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. This course has two components. The first is a study (2-4:45pm), along with undergraduate students, of key texts and problems of post-1920 psychology and psychoanalysis. In the second part, an in-depth study (5-6:30pm) among the graduate students only, of key concepts and problems in psychology, psychoanalysis, and psychiatry "after" Freud. The course focuses on the major debates in psychology and psychoanalysis after World War II, as these concerned the problem of violence and the theory of the self. We will look at behaviorism, trauma, cybernetics, the rise of cognitive science, ideas of guilt and shame, normativity and perversion, object-relations theory (Melanie Klein and her school), Cold-War links of psychoanalytic and psychological ideas, changing perceptions of psychiatry as a modern institution, structuralism (Lacan and his school), feminism, and transcultural and anti-colonial psychiatry.

title: The Agrarian Question in History
description: This course explores the emergence of what is called the “Agrarian Question” as that question was related to the emergence of modernity (as a tendentially global economic, cultural, social, and political formation). The course begins with formative analyses of the problem of value (where and how is value produced?) and continues into the question of land, peasants, domestic and global revolution, modernization and development, race & labor, gender & reproduction, migration and ecological disaster/pandemics. The aim is to familiarize students with some basic theoretical/philosophical approaches and selected historical texts, as these articulate the agrarian question in modern terms. The course is intended to assist students in analyzing the agrarian question through a broad theoretical/historical/global perspective.

sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
This course explores the emergence of what was called the “Agrarian Question” in the eighteenth, nineteenth, twentieth, and twenty-first centuries, as that question has been related to the modern emergence of urbanism, industrialization, and capitalism. This modern question was tied to shifting analysis of the problem of value (where and how is value produced?), problems posed by the subjects/agents of domestic and global revolution, of production and reproduction, and of modernization and development. We will trace how the question mutates from its physiocratic core, through its articulation in Smith, Ricardo, Marx, Sun Yatsen, Chayanov, and a host of others, and into the later twentieth century as part of the 'peasant problem' in China and the ‘subaltern’ in India, as those relate to the transition to and crisis in socialist economics and Marxist analysis. The aim of the class is to familiarize students with some basic philosophical and historical texts surrounding what came to be called the agrarian question; this is intended to assist students in analyzing contemporary and historical problems through a longer and broader perspective. The course is neither comprehensive nor focused on one geography. Dense theoretical reading, class participation, and a research paper are required. Brief reading memos are to be submitted each week to our class online forum; final paper to be submitted before Christmas, and proposed paper topic discussed with me by mid-October.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS RUSSN GA1322. This seminar explores how (semi)nomadic and tribal communities shaped (and were shaped by) the many institutions of the early modern Middle East and beyond between 1400 and 1900. Rather than viewing tribes and states as opposites, we’ll look at the rich and complicated relationships that connected mobile societies with empires, military households, religious networks, and local authorities. We’ll start by examining how historians have written about tribes and nomadism, questioning the concepts and categories we often take for granted. From there, we’ll dive into new approaches drawn from historical anthropology, mobility studies, environmental history, and more, alongside case studies from different regions. Our goal is to acquire a flexible set of tools for researching both mobile and settled communities and for understanding how they interacted across time and space. The course centers on discussion and close reading, and many weeks will include virtual conversations with authors of our assigned works.

sections.notes: This course serves as an orientation to the discipline of history for doctoral students. It introduces students to key disciplinary and professional aspects of history, as well as to the fields and faculty of NYU’s history department. Rather than emphasizing select debates within the profession, the course presents students with readings that represent selected faculty members’ choice of some of the most notable and interesting recent first books in their own fields. As such, the course aims to investigate the process by which historians combine historiography and primary research to write dissertations and, then, first monographs. The course also explores a range of topics (under the label “professionalization”) involved in doctoral and post-doctoral career making.

Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS EURO-GA 2660 & HEL-UA 902. This course will explore the relationship between law and conceptions of the human in the modern Middle East. We will start with texts by thinkers such as Karl Marx, Hannah Arendt, Carole Pateman, Giorgio Agamben, Mahmood Mamdani, and Uday Mehta. We will then turn to the history of citizenship, nationality, constitutionalism, statelessness, and legal belonging in the Middle East from the 19th century on. Constitutionalist thought played a critical role throughout the region around the turn of the 20th century, expressed in anticolonial and insurrectionist movements making claims about governance, community, and the human that were not always in conformance with liberal political theory or modern state forms of reasoning. During and after World War I, the collapse of the multi-ethnic and multi-lingual Ottoman Empire led to vast efforts—including at the level of international law and institutions—to fix some populations in place, transfer others in the interest of the “unmixing of peoples,” and find homes, often in the form of camps, for the millions of displaced. The political entities established after the war, often under the governance of colonial powers, instituted constitutions and citizenship laws binding humans to the state in new ways, including through logics of sexual, racial, and sectarian difference, while revolutionary movements in the “age of decolonization” after World War II introduced new ruling bargains that altered the form of those binds. In the last decades of the 20th century and into the 21st, experiences of citizenship and belonging were again transformed with the spread of neoliberalism; the expansion of humanitarian interventions disrupting existing systems of sovereignty; and the US-led war on terror. Across this latter time period, the “temporal impasse” (Nasser Abourahme) of Israel’s settler-colonial project produced hundreds of thousands of Palestinian non-citizens suspended in a state of seemingly permanent statelessness, with enormous and ongoing effects on global history.

title: What is History
description: This course provides an introduction to a range of theoretical frameworks and methodologies that have influenced the academic study of history, including microhistory, global history, histories of gender and race, and subaltern/post-colonial historical studies. We will interrogate the key categories of historical temporality and geography by questioning how historians impose temporal and spatial boundaries around their research, as well as ways to expand or dissolve those boundaries. We will also examine how historians construct historiographical debates around particular research themes, such as the changing meaning of national histories. The aim is to acquire knowledge of a variety of historical approaches at work when reading both historical scholarship and historical source materials. Prerequisites: None. Fulfillment: Humanities Foundations/Introductory Courses (18-19 Critical Concepts Core Course).

title: Arab-Islamic Influence on the West
description: This course utilizes multidisciplinary sources of evidence to address Arab-Islamic knowledge and culture, the influences that they had on medieval and early modern Europe, and that they continue to have today, while questioning why many Western scholars have minimized Arab-Islamic contributions in favor of “Western Exceptionalism” narratives. By exploring cross-cultural transmissions of knowledge, students are encouraged to think critically about how ideas and technologies evolve as they are adopted by individuals and groups in order to suit their personal and cultural needs. Prerequisite: None. Fulfillment: Humanities Major Other Introductory Courses; Social Science International Relations Track 200 level focus course.

meetings.room: 567 West Yangsi Rd, Shanghai Room NB105

title: A Global History of Mathematics
description: This unique interdisciplinary course, which fulfills both the Math and STS Core Curriculum requirements, interrogates the persistent notion that mathematics is fundamentally Western, by exploring the invention and evolution of foundational mathematical concepts within their historical and cultural contexts throughout the world. Using hands-on activities to explore historical mathematical challenges, students develop their problem-solving skills, and apply them to practical and theoretical questions. For example, how did earlier societies use sticks, stones, or strings with knots to record numerical data and make advanced calculations long before modern calculators and computers? An underlying theme is that numbers, mathematics, and computational methods do not simply exist, but are highly related to the cultures in which they were produced, and the accompanying historical circumstances. We conclude the course by considering the global future of mathematics, and whether it is capable of becoming increasingly diverse. Prerequisite: None. Fulfillment: CORE STS or Math requirement; Humanities Introductory course.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. In this course, we will seek to analyze the history and function of Jewish humor from the 19th century to the present. We will examine the origins and development of modern Jewish humor in Eastern Europe, and its migration to America, and compare the uses of Jewish humor in a global sense from Europe, America, Israel, the Middle East, North Africa, and indeed around the globe. We will also look at how the Jews have used laughter as both a coping mechanism and an instrument of self-defense against pogroms, forced migrations, and even the Holocaust. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced Non-west OR European

Course Repeatable for Credit. Engaging Early Christian Theology: What does it mean to say that Jesus Christ was both human and divine? How can the Christian divinity be one yet three? How are the sacraments such as baptism effective? Do we have freewill? These were some of the pressing questions the Church Fathers addressed in the early centuries of Christian history and their answers contributed to the Christian theological tradition for centuries to come. In this course we will examine some of the classic works of early Christian theology. Despite the often highly rhetorical and polemical character of their writings the Church Fathers developed an intellectually rigorous field of knowledge, one that has had a significant intellectual historical as well as socio-political impact in the history of the Church and beyond. This is not a theological course but rather an introduction to some of the key texts in a historically significant mode of theological inquiry. History Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced Pre-1800s

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS FREN-UA 965. Médias et crise politique en France au XX–XXIᵉ siècles:The prerequisite for this course is FREN-UA 30 (French Grammar and Composition). Au croisement de l’histoire des médias et de l’histoire politique française, ce cours vous propose d’examiner le rôle joué par les médias français dans certaines des crises politiques majeures qu’a connu la France au cours du XXème siècle (affaire Dreyfus ; 6 février 1934 ; mai 1968). Il interroge plus généralement la participation décisive des médias à la formation de l’opinion publique et les usages stratégiques faits des médias par les hommes politiques confrontés à une situation de crise. Ce cours se veut aussi être une réflexion sur les évolutions de la démocratie française au cours du XX ème siècle et sur ce que la situation politique actuelle doit aux héritages du passé. Il offre enfin une solide initiation à l’analyse critique des sources médiatiques (archives audiovisuelles et collections de presse écrite). This course is taught in French. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced European

title: Early Modern Britain
description: This course examines Britain and the British Isles from the end of the Wars of the Roses (1487) through the Glorious Revolution (1688). Although modern Britain is often characterized as an unusually stable society and polity, the early modern period was dominated by civil wars, schism, and revolution. Topics include Henry VIII and the Reformation; Elizabeth I and European politics; imperialism in the Americas and South Asia; gender and family; popular culture and everyday life; England, Scotland, and Ireland; the Civil War and Commonwealth; Restoration art and drama; and the “Glorious Revolution” and ascendance of Parliament.

sections.notes: History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced European

title: History of Germany in the 20th
description: Germany’s twentieth century has been described as a shattered past. Twice in the first half of the century Germany brought war to Europe. Between 1933 and 1945 the virulently racist Nazi regime murdered millions of Jews, Poles, Roma, homosexuals, and other groups. After 1945 Germany was a main site in the Cold War, the German nation separated by a wall and divided into two rival states. Yet since 1945 West Germany developed, in many ways, into a model of stability, democracy, and prosperity. Today reunited Germany is a functioning democracy, a central player in the European Union, a proponent of multilateralism and human rights in international affairs, and a pioneer in environmental policy. How can we make sense of Germany’s complex and contradictory experience in the 20th century? This course will be a mixture between a lecture and a discussion seminar. Over the course of the semester we will explore German history from World War I to the present by focusing on four interconnected themes. First, we will examine Germany’s rocky road from an authoritarian political culture to one that is liberal and democratic. Second, we will investigate the origins of the Holocaust, as well as the traumatic legacy this disaster had on Germans after 1945. Third, we will explore Germany’s recurring penchant for modernity, in economic as well as cultural matters. Finally, we will look at how Germany’s relationship with Europe and the world has evolved from an aggressive imperialism to more subtle techniques of achieving foreign policy goals through transnational cooperation and economic pressure. By engaging with a variety of sources—memoirs, government files, film, and literature—students will learn how Germans have understood themselves, the challenges facing their society, and their place in the world.

title: Hist of Modern Ireland I: 1580-1800
description: Examines the English conquest of Ireland from the reign of Elizabeth I to the last meeting of the Irish Parliament. Key themes include the plantation of Ireland with settlers from England, Scotland, and Wales, the decline of the Gaelic political order and culture, the religious reformation and Counter Reformation, Ireland as a site of English and European wars, the imposition of a penal code, and the vain attempt to rebel against British rule in the late 18th century resulting in the Act of Union, which disestablished the Irish Parliament in Dublin. title: The Irish in America
description: This course explores the impact of Irish immigrants on American popular culture. Focusing on ports of entry and urban centers of entertainment and migration over the past two centuries, the course looks at the ways in which the Irish and Irish-Americans have shaped American entertainment in the realms of music, dance, drama, film, recording, literature, festivals and sport. In addition, the course delves into issues of race surrounding the American reception of the early Irish immigrants through imagery and media depictions.

title: Greek History from The Bronze Age to Alexander
description: Until a few decades ago, Greek history began with Homer and dealt narrowly with the Greek world. Thanks to archaeology, the social sciences, and other historical tools, the chronological and geographical horizons have been pushed back. The history of the Greeks now starts in the third millennium B.C. and is connected to the civilization that lay to the east, rooted in Egypt and Mesopotamia. Traces Greek history from the Greeks? earliest appearance to the advent of Alexander.

title: Two Diasporas: Irish and Italian
description: Just as the United States received more immigrants than any other country, Ireland and Italy are among the classic nations of emigrants. Why did so many people leave Ireland and Italy? What were the economic, political, religious, and personal motivations? How were people able to leave in such large numbers, given their poverty? Where did they go? How did they travel? And what effect did they have on the societies where they settled, especially the United States, which attracted more than five million Irish immigrants and more than five million Italian immigrants?

title: The History of Western Medicine: Enlightenment to the Present
description: This course covers the history of western medicine and medical thought, from the enlightenment to the present. The course will familiarize students with basic questions and concepts in the history of medicine, models for understanding the historical development of medical thought; the varied historical relationships between medicine and other healing practices such as religion and homeopathy; the influence of culture and politics on the development of medical thought; and the role that the emergence of a medical profession characterized by formal training and informed by a scientific viewpoint played in the development of western societies.

sections.notes: This course is an examination of disease and medicine in the West, with an emphasis on the modern era. Under the conditions of industrialization, population growth, political modernization, and rapid cultural and technological change, the effects of epidemic and endemic diseases led to new definitions of the “public health,” novel theories about disease causation, and innovative and often controversial strategies for containing illness. In addition to studying the development of specific medical ideas and practices, we will also look at medicine as a complex social, cultural, and ideological phenomenon. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced European

title: Renaissance and Early Modern Europe
description: This course provides an introduction to the culture, society, and politics of Renaissance and early modern Europe (ca. 1450-1800). We will explore major topics and themes, including the Italian and Northern Renaissance, the Protestant Reformation and the ensuing religious wars, Europe’s “discovery” of other societies and cultures, the origins and development of nation states, the Scientific Revolution, the European Enlightenment, and the origins of the French Revolution. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Pre-1800s and European

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Vikings and Celts: Northern Europe produced a number of long-form literary pieces during the Middle Ages, such as the Old English Beowulf, the early Irish Táin Bó Cúailnge and its associated tales, the Middle Welsh Mabinogion and the Old Norse sagas. This course will explore these tales and others and question the definition of this genre (or genres) of literature, examining connections between the different types of tales and what we can know about their composition. Students will investigate the connections between these tales and earlier examples of epic literature, such as Virgil’s The Aeneid, and examine what we know regarding the transmission of earlier forms of heroic tales from Late Antiquity and the ancient world to medieval Western Europe. Major themes such as violence, heroism and the role of women in these stories will be discussed throughout the course and students will be expected to engage with both questions presented by the individual examples of these forms of literature as well as to compare across cultural and literary boundaries. The reception of these tales in both the medieval and modern worlds will be discussed in the conclusion to the course. This class will give students a grounding in critical thinking and an appreciation of different approaches to literary texts and the environments in which they were created. By engaging with some of the foremost medieval literary productions of the European Middle Ages, this course will chart a journey through some of the greatest written achievements of the cultures of the Celts, Vikings and early English and question students’ understanding of literature as well as the cultural construction and portrayal of the heroic past. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced European and Pre-1800s

sections.topic: Capitalism and Religion in the Western World
sections.notes:
Requires Department Consent
Capitalism and Religion in the Western World: This seminar investigates the historical relationship between the development of capitalism and Christianity in Western Europe and the United States from the nineteenth to the twentieth century. It seeks to elucidate the reciprocal influences between economic transformation and religious institutions, beliefs, and practices. Particular attention will be given to the ways in which Christian thought and organization both facilitated and resisted the emergence and consolidation of capitalist society as well as how capitalism itself has been interpreted and represented in religious terms. The course will further examine how the expansion of capitalism altered or on the contrary consolidated the social position, moral authority, and political engagement of Christian churches and movements. Through the analysis of key theological debates, ecclesiastical responses, and religious or lay initiatives, students will explore the diverse forms of Christian involvement in capitalist societies—whether critical, as in Christian socialism and social Christianity, or positive, as in the Prosperity Gospel, Christian employers’ associations, and various strands of Christian democracy. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: European OR U.S. Please email history.undergrad@nyu.edu to inquire about enrollment.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. This course explores the juridical, political, and cultural histories between Asia, the Americas (especially the United States), and the myriad diasporas across the Pacific. Beginning in the wake of the Haitian Revolution and the systematization of new forms of (un)free migration into the Caribbean, we will trace the history of “Asian America” as it moves through: the abolition of chattel slavery and the importation of "coolie" labor; the rise of free-market imperialism and American capitalism; the twinned histories of Ellis and Angel Islands; the rise of the nation-state and the 20th-century international order; the world wars through the Cold War; and the neoliberal and post-neoliberal eras. Students will place the development of Asian immigration in a global perspective, through the histories of race, empire, and capitalism. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced U.S. OR Non-west.

sections.topic: The Revolutionary Tradition in the Philippines
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. "This course examines the revolutionary tradition in the Philippines after the birth of modern capitalism and free-market imperialism in the late 18th century. As a systematically impoverished country long considered as an imperial hinterland, the Philippine archipelago boasts a veritable revolutionary tradition that have shaken empires (Spanish, British, American, Japanese), overthrown dictators, and shaped a global security regime. And today, as a nation defined by its multiple diasporas (especially the migrant workers that sustain North American and global economies), Philippine revolutionary movements can be found around the world, just as the world itself shapes insurrections in the mother country. Beginning with the upheavals during the Seven Years’ War (1756-1763) and the British Occupation of Manila (1762-1764), we will chart the development of a racial capitalist regime in the Philippines, as the islands became integrated into the world market through multiple means: steamship routes, the opening of the Suez Canal, and forced agricultural production. Then, we will discuss the origins and the aftermath of the Philippine Revolution (1896-1898) from both elite and nonelite perspectives, and trace the emergence of a transpacific security state during and after the American occupation (1898-1946). Finally, we will evaluate the legacies of Cold War anticommunism, the dictatorship of Ferdinand Marcos (1965-1986), and the People Power Revolution (1986) in today’s political culture." History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced Non-west

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. The Soviet Century, 1914-1999: By its own definition, the Soviet Union was neither nation-state nor empire, neither capitalist nor communist, neither east nor west. What was the Soviet Union? What was Soviet socialism? Who made it? What was the role of the Communist Party in creating and maintaining Soviet rule? What is a personal dictatorship, and how did the Soviet Union become one? How did the Soviet party-state maintain its rule over one-sixth the world’s landmass? Did it enjoy legitimacy among the population, and if so, why? What was the role of violence in the maintenance of Soviet power? Did people “believe” in the Soviet project, and if so, in what exactly? How did the Soviet party-state use or relate to institutional structures, social class, information networks, consumer desire, ethnic minorities, expert knowledge, cultural production, the outside world? In the wake of recent challenges to liberal institutions across the Western world, the history of the Soviet Union offers its students critical insight into the characteristics and functioning of illiberal politics and an unfree society. This course will examine the project of building socialism in the Soviet Union and its satellites from inception to collapse. Though focused on the investigation of Soviet institutions, practices, and ideologies, the course aims to situate the Soviet project in an explicitly global frame. As a class, we will assess the claim that Soviet socialism (though not necessarily the Soviet Union) was a project with a shelf life, conditioned by global politics and its own capacities for self-reproduction. Through extensive use of memoir, we will examine individual processes of “illusionment” and disillusionment with the Soviet project. We analyze the life cycles of peasants, workers, bureaucrats, artists, writers, reformers and other members of the Soviet establishment over time. We carry the Soviet engagement with the outside world, and the search for development or modernity that inspired it, from the First World War, through the creation of a socialist society, the geographical expansion of the socialist project and its subsequent implosion, into the new programs of liberalization, marketization, and modernization that succeeded it in the 1990s and 2000s. We trace Soviet dominion, real and attempted, from Berlin to Baku, Vladimir to Vladivostok. Readings for the course will include both primary and secondary sources, with an emphasis on works of memoir and literature. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced Non-west OR European

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Through the lens of vaccination, this interdisciplinary course explores how epidemics have shaped the modern world. By tracing ideas of disease and immunity across science, politics, culture, and media, students will examine how health crises have influenced belief systems, social institutions, and public policy. sections.notes: SAME AS HEL-UA 130; GREECE: A GLOBAL HISTORY Is Greece a Western or Eastern country? What is the relationship between ancient and modern Greece? What is the rapport of Greece to its “Others” –Europe, Africa, the Balkans, and the Middle East? And why does the study of Greece matter to contemporary debates on nationalism, democracy, and human rights? This course explores the history of Greece during the transition from multi-ethnic empires to nation-states, to ask broader questions about historical time, geographies of thought, and borders in and across the Mediterranean. The main focus is on refugees, migration, and the entangled histories of Muslims, Jews, and Christians in Greece and Asia Minor. In this multimedia course, blending scholarly literature with primary sources, autobiographical accounts, maps, photography, film, documentary film, and other ephemera, we will ask what it means to read a text, an image, an artifact of material culture, or a landscape, historically.

title: Empires in Early Modern Global Asia
description: This course aims to survey the geographically extensive; ethnically, culturally and religiously diverse; and politically dynamic empires of early modern Asia from a global perspective. We will look at this period through the eyes of Asian peoples, rather than from the isolated and Eurocentric point of view that created artificial boundaries and dominated the historical narratives for centuries. The course connects the Middle East, Southeast Asia, the intruding maritime empires of the Indian Ocean, and China. While there will be some emphasis on chronological developments and major historical, socio-political, and cultural events, the course is primarily organized on a thematic basis. Topics include: state and identity formation; military expansion and navigation technologies; environment and natural resources; urban and rural populations and their daily life routines; religious and ethnic minorities; and developments in science, art, and architecture.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Prerequisite: Any HIST-UA 9## except for HIST-UA 980 or HIST-UA 997 or HIST-UA 998 This course has two purposes. The first is to have you learn the fundamentals of historical research and a produce a research paper. In this class you will come to understand how historians engage in their craft, how they construct historical narratives, and how they ensure their accuracy. This course is designed to have you engage in your own historical research and analysis. During the semester you will complete assignments that provide you the building blocks that will teach you how to conduct archival research and engage in historical analysis. By the end of this course, you will produce a 25-page research paper. The second purpose of this course is to learn a good deal about U.S. Labor History, which includes not only the study of the workplace, but also how families interacted and reacted to the labor conditions as they made their homes. We will also look at how human labor impacts the environment. Finally, we will also place particular emphasis on the labor history of New York City, as we will use the Tamiment library to conduct much of your primary research. Through your weekly readings as well as your research assignments, you will come to understand how American labor has been organized and challenged over the course of U.S. history. Each week we will spend part of our time analyzing primary documents, secondary sources, and learning how to glean and analyze information. I have chosen these readings because they represent some of the best historical writing in the field, and I hope that you will learn much from reading these scholars. title: Histories of Neoliberalism
description: The class introduces students to the growing historical and historically-minded literature on neoliberalism, querying the origins of the phenomenon, its regional variants, and the methodological challenges of studying an ongoing phenomenon as a complex historical process. The readings and discussion assess the virtues of the three major approaches to the phenomenon. First, a group of scholars have sought to provide a multi-causal historical explanation of neoliberalism, linking its emergence to transformations in the order of global capitalism, particularly the rise of finance capital and the expansion of extractive economies. Second, other scholars have emphasized the key role played by ideational shifts, especially the movement of once marginal economic theories forged in the 1930s into new prominence in the 1970s. A third group of scholars approach neoliberalism as a new political rationality, manifest in techniques of governance. We will assess these different interpretative approaches both on their own terms and in relation to specific regions of the world economy.

Prerequisite: Any HIST-UA 9## except for HIST-UA 980 or HIST-UA 997 or HIST-UA 998 Remaking Greenwich Village: On the eve of World War II, Greenwich Village was already famous as a bohemian neighborhood. Rooms rented for as little as $15 per month. In the 1950s and 1960s, folk musicians and artists, most famously Bob Dylan, sought out the Village’s inexpensive housing, the architectural critic Jane Jacobs used the neighborhood to show the benefits of community, and the modern gay rights movement took shape in its bars and streets. In the early 1970s, its real estate was so inexpensive that NYU, on the verge of bankruptcy, relocated its undergraduate college to the neighborhood from University Heights in the Bronx. Today, Greenwich Village is among the most expensive neighborhoods in the world, with average rental prices over $6,000 for a one-bedroom apartment and a median home price of $1.4 million as of August 2024. title: The Global Age of Revolutions, 1757–1868
description: Analyzes revolutions from the 1750s to the 1860s, encompassing the East India Company’s takeover of Bengal followed by the American, French, and Haitian revolutions and independence struggles in Latin America. The course situates the European industrial revolution in this context and considers its destabilizing effects in the nineteenth century: in Europe, North America, and East Asia via the Opium Wars and Japan’s Meiji Restoration of 1868. The course considers whether a political crisis of global capitalism could have been what linked these revolutions together. Students will write a research paper on any aspect of this Age of Revolutions.

title: Japan’s Empire in Asia
description: This seminar examines the rise and demise of the Japanese empire in the making of modern Asia. As the world’s territory was divided between the colonizers and colonized during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, Japan’s case was unusual. The country started out as a victim of imperialism in the nineteenth century, but became an aggressor in the twentieth, ruling over other Asian people. We will situate the Japanese empire vis-à-vis the rest of Asia and pay particular attention to the circulation of goods, ideas, people and practices across imperial boundaries, which shaped both the empire and the countries that surrounded it. Topics will include: the formation of the modern imperialist global system; colonialism, “colonial modernity,” colonial identities, and colony-metropole relations; collaboration and the anti-colonial movements; regional migration; empire and total war; and decolonization.

sections.topic: Media and Communication in the Middle Ages
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Medieval circumstances presented multiple challenges to media, mobility, and communication. Cultivators were bound to the land and monks to their monasteries; pilgrims traveled to holy places, crusaders and warriors invaded and then settled foreign lands, and rulers and nobles were frequently itinerant. Literacy was largely limited to reading and writing Latin, and writing was mostly done by specialists --monastic scribes, notaries, and clerics. The transmission of ideas therefore occurred mainly through the spoken vernacular word, and by means of gestures, images, and the manipulation of symbolic objects (thus, for instance, the relics of saints were carried to distant lands to collect alms, to recover possessions appropriated by nobles, or to aid in battle). While seas, rivers, ports, ferries, bridges, and networks of roads provided with rest houses were generally available, routes and means of transportation differed markedly according to the traveler’s status and the journey’s purpose. Christianity stimulated pilgrimages, missions to convert the heathen, and crusades. Marriage took brides to foreign courts where they became cultural ambassadors. Medieval kings and great nobles were continually on the road, changing their abode every two or three days. Ambassadors, lesser officials, and messengers traveled on government business. Knights sought out tournaments and distant wars to advance their fortunes and reputations. Merchants transported goods to regional fairs, and engaged in international trade. Minstrels, jongleurs, and troubadours traveled to gain patronage and to extend their repertoire, spreading news and influencing the reputations of warriors, heroes, and kings. Students too journeyed extensively from place to place to sit at the feet of famous masters; some wandering scholars came to be known as Goliards. Artists were invited to various loci to decorate manuscripts and architects to construct buildings. The pursuit of favorable opinion was an essential feature in the process of state-building during the Middle Ages. Challengers of traditional norms also came to rely on the efficacy of communication systems to expand their ranks with adherents. In disseminating propaganda, medieval society experimented with such forms and methods of communication as heraldry, emblems, stereotypes, and slogans, thereby elaborating modes of interaction which, though modified, are still in use today. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced European and Pre-1800s

title: History of Modern Japan
description: Emphasizes historical problems in Japan?s economic development, their challenge to political and social institutions, and their role in shaping foreign policy. Focuses on Japan?s transition from an agrarian economy to commercial capitalism, from hierarchical social organization to constitutional authority, and from isolation from the rest of the world to involvement with Western culture and diplomatic relations. Traces Japan?s development into an industrial giant fully engaged in world affairs.

description: A historical and comparative approach to the first half millennium of Islamic history. title: Mao and The Chinese Revolution
description: The revolution made Mao as much as Mao made the revolution. We investigate Mao’s thought and theories, as well as his revolutionary practice, not as biographical artifacts but as products of and contributors to the revolutionary situation in China and the world in the 20th century. We end with Mao’s afterlives. This is a reading- and writing-intensive course.

title: Africa Before Colonialism
description: Africa, the ‘Dark Continent’ of the euro-American imagination, was long portrayed as a land without history. In this course we debunk the myths, exploring African civilization and culture in the centuries before European colonialism. We will examine how ecology, slavery and the slave trades, and Africa’s place in Atlantic and Indian Ocean networks shaped medieval Mali, the Swahilli Coast, the South African cape colony—and the world. There are no prerequisites for this course. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Pre-1800s and Non-west

title: Topics in Middle Eastern History
description: Focuses on a particular aspect of Islamic, Ottoman, or modern Middle Eastern history, with an emphasis on historiographical and comparative issues. Intended primarily for advanced undergraduates in Middle Eastern studies and in history, but other students may register with permission of the instructor.

sections.topic: Borders and Borderlands in the Middle East
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS MEIS-UA.0688. PLEASE EMAIL Sara D Pursley, spursley@nyu.edu, for permission to enroll. Problems in the Middle East are frequently explained by reference to nation-state borders in the region, which are often said to have been created “artificially” by the European colonial powers after World War I. Using this narrative as our starting point, the course will explore some of the complex ways in which borders have shaped and been shaped by European imperialism, anticolonial and other forms of resistance, state formation, migration, labor, neoliberalism, citizenship, ethnic cleansing, and refugee crises in the modern Middle East. People living in borderland regions—often but not always desert or mountainous terrain—have used their location to resist central state powers, play multiple states off one another, and insert themselves into new economic networks, legal and illegal, even as their lives have been transformed by the hardening of borders and the expansion of capitalist relations in this period. During and after World War I, vast efforts were made to fix some populations in place, transfer others in the interest of the “unmixing of peoples,” and find homes, permanent or temporary, for the millions of displaced. In the last decades of the twentieth century and into the twenty-first, the Middle East again became central to changing spatial experiences of bordering, with the emergence of a global neoliberal economy based partly on the circulation of petrodollars and new forms of labor migration; the expansion of humanitarian interventions disrupting existing systems of sovereignty; and the US-led "war on terror,” including the proliferation of CIA “black sites” around the world. History Major Requirements Fulfilled: Advanced Non-west and Pre-1800s

Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS MEIS-UA.0688. SAME AS: MEIS-UA 518 Topics in Middle Eastern History: Gender, Empire and Nation in Modern Middle East: Beginning in the 17th century and continuing to this day, Western and colonial descriptions of the Orient have shown a consistent fascination with ‘Oriental’ and Muslim gender roles in general, and the status of women within the Middle East and South Asia in particular. Perhaps in response, these same themes have played a central role in the national rhetoric of various states within these regions. This course examines the diverse gender and sexual regimes, regulations and experiences across these regions from a historical and comparative perspective. Students will study how major cultural, economic, political and social processes, from the 18th century to the present day, have impacted gender roles, and in particular women’s experiences in these societies, and how various subjective and collective strategies have in turn responded to and been constitutive of such processes. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced, Pre-1800s and Non-west

title: Seminar in Intellectual History
description: Covers a topic in intellectual history. Topics vary by semester. Does not satisfy the capstone seminar (HIST-UA 4xx) requirement for majors.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. History, Theory, and Politics of Psychoanalysis: This course focuses on the major debates in psychology and psychoanalysis, especially after World War II, as these concerned the problem of violence and the theory of the self. We will look at behaviorism, various trauma theories, the rise of cognitive science in the 1960s, ideas of guilt and shame, object-relations theory (Melanie Klein and her school), changing perceptions and critiques of psychoanalysis, structuralism (Lacan and his school), transcultural and anti-colonial psychiatry, and the treatment of disability. We will be reading theory, psychiatric and psychological texts, and history in more or less equal measure. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced European

title: Autobiography and History
description: This course is concerned with historians as autobiographers, and autobiographers as historians. Critically and thoughtfully reading a range of works that combine history with personal experience, we will explore the ways in which scholars and writers invoke autobiography in the writing of history, and the ways in which autobiographers serve as historians. Around the seminar table, we will pay attention to research, sources, evidence, method, argument, interpretation, intention, audience, memory, style, and voice. Students will also make their own forays into history and autobiography, sharing their work and reflecting on one another’s efforts. Although our readings focus mainly on United States history, students’ own writings can focus on history anywhere in the world.

sections.notes: History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced U.S.

title: Capitalism and Geopolitics
description: This course introduces students to significant events and trends in world politics over the past five centuries, and considers their relationship to the history of capitalism. Capitalism and geopolitics, the course will show, have long been intertwined. The evolution in Europe, and eventual global spread, of a system of independent states cannot be understood separate from the emergence of capitalism. Neither can the construction of vast overseas empires by European states, their subsequent collapse, and the rise of a postcolonial, globalized international order. Conversely, we cannot adequately understand the history of capitalism without appreciating how geopolitics has shaped its emergence, spread, and transformation.

sections.topic: American Wars and the 20th Century World,1898-2000
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. This course explores the history of American wars from the Spanish-American War to the end of the 1990s, employing war and the military as a vehicle to explore a nexus of social, cultural, racial, human rights, citizenship, and state-building aspects of American history in the 20th century. This course seeks to illustrate how analyzing the breadth of US military and war history illuminates enduring trends, challenges, and truths about the nature of warfare, the United States, American society, the US in the World, soldiering, and society. By seeking to understand how war and peace shaped the history of the United States in the vital twentieth century, it also investigates the world in which it inhabited and the role of not only policymakers but grassroots actors in defining the nature of war. This course will focus on the broad sweep of issues that stem from American wars, covering topics such as occupations, race and the desegregation of the Armed Forces, the rise and impact of human and individual rights in American imaginations of war, the privatization of military functions, and the impacts of military victories and defeats on American society. We will be concerned with questions such as the relationship of the military to state-building in the United States and abroad, war as a mechanism for hardening or softening categories of state power or race, and the importance of diverse perspectives in challenging our conceptions of wars and American military power in the 20th century. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced U.S.

title: Topics in African History
description: Topics in African History course. African history topics will vary.

sections.topic: A History of Race and Slavery in Africa
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. A History of Race and Slavery in Africa: In this course, students will explore the history of slavery across Africa, with a focus on the Trans-Saharan slave trade and the societies by which it was shaped. Beginning with the networks connecting West, Central, and North Africa, students will examine how systems of enslavement functioned within African political, economic, and social life—from royal courts and military systems to households. Through African frameworks, students will analyze different forms of servitude and the roles African actors played within them. The course also invites students to think critically about how “African” identity has been defined and contested in Africa, and how the legacies of slavery continue to shape the experiences of sub-Saharan Africans today, especially in North Africa. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced Non-west and Pre-1800s

title: African Ways of Knowing
description: This seminar explores the production of scientific, technical, and embodied knowledge about Africa. The course will focus on three broad themes covered across four units. First, we will read debates over the nature and definition of science, technology, and tradition. Is there such a thing as African science? What does it mean to decolonize African thought or culture? Second, we will examine the nature of rationality. Is reason singular or plural? Culturally-bound or universal? To what extent are witchcraft, African healing practices, and ancestor veneration “rational” practices? Third, we will explore the relationship between scientific representations, social practices, and local culture. What relationship exists between social practices and culturally shared categories of knowledge? Lastly, we will examine how diverse forms of knowledge become materialized in artistic practice and architecture on the African continent. Previous coursework on Africa is not required. History Major requirements fulfilled by this course: Advanced Non-west

title: American Jews and the Law
description: Identical to HBRJD-UA 164. How have American Jews encountered the law, and how has American law encountered Jews? This course introduces students to theories about the relationship between law and society as it traces the history of Jews' treatment under criminal, constitutional, property, immigration, and humanitarian laws. It examines how Jews used legal ideals to broaden their rights while also highlighting divisions among Jews and between Jews and others about topics ranging from the freedom of speech to reproductive rights to church-state matters. As students explore legal battles, they will learn to ask new questions about how the law works and when it fails.

title: Intro to US Education Historical and Contemporary
description: Sponsored by Steinhardt. Central themes, issues, and controversies in American education. What is the purpose of “school”? How did schools begin in the United States, and how have they evolved across time? How do children learn? How are they different from each other, and why and when should that matter? How should we teach them? And how should we structure schools and classrooms to promote learning?

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. The Caribbean and the World: For many, the Caribbean evokes images of an exotic place with beautiful beaches, friendly, happy “natives” and unbridled hedonism. Yet, much more than a distant vacation destination for “first world” consumption, the Caribbean has long been closely intertwined with major events in World History. The lectures and readings, which will sometimes be supplemented by films, will engage important themes such as: the Haitian Revolution and its global significance, US imperialism in the Caribbean, the impact of Caribbean migration on British culture, race, gender and Caribbean identities. The course will also examine prevailing assumptions/stereotypes about Caribbean peoples and realities as depicted in media representations. It provides historical context for varying responses to contemporary issues such as the earthquake in Haiti, immigration from the Caribbean to the United States, and sex tourism. Through the assignments and class discussions, students will hone their talents for historical interpretation and critical thinking. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced Non-west
Course Repeatable for Credit.

title: African-American History to 1865
description: Survey of the experience of African Americans to 1865, emphasizing living conditions, treatment, images, attitudes, important figures and events, and culture using a chronological and topical approach. Topics include African way of life, initial contact between Africans and Europeans, slave trade, early slavery, freedom and control in slave society, abolitionism, slave resistance, free blacks, and gender.

title: Global Culture Wars
description: This course will examine the origins, development, and meanings of so-called cultural conflict in the United States. Topics will include abortion, gay rights, bilingualism, and the teaching of evolution in public schools. Liberal Arts Core/CORE Equivalent - satisfies the requirement for Cultures & Contexts but NOT for CAS students

title: Race and Reproduction
description: Examines the connections between gender, racial ideology and history of medicine to consider the range of ways that reproduction—medically, culturally, and experientially—produces and troubles racial ideology. In this course we will explore issues in the history of race and reproduction, focusing primarily (though not exclusively) on North American contexts. Cross-cultural breadth will help us to consider the relationship between biological experiences (which are often portrayed as universal) and socio-cultural context. While questions about biology will be central to this history, we will also locate biology within a wider set of issues around social reproduction and the practices of motherhood. Through our readings we will consider how different disciplinary orientations (social history, medical anthropology, feminist theory, art history, etc.) help us to illuminate and problematize the connections between technologies and politics of biology and difference.

sections.notes: History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced U.S. OR Non-west and Pre-1800s

title: History in the Headlines
description: The key events you read about in your morning twitter feed or on your favorite news sites are usually not unique in world affairs. They have a background, a context, that makes them more understandable and often more interesting. History is about everything that happened before you started reading this course description. And thinking historically means trying to make sense of the new in the context of what human beings have done before. In this lecture series, NYU's historians take you on a behind the scenes tour of current events you thought you knew, with the goal of making you a better observer and analyst of news about the world around you. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: *2 credits* of U.S., Non-west, OR European

title: The Cold War in Asia: 1945-2001
description: This course will focus on US foreign policy in Asia since 1945. The ways US global interests and concerns sought to shape Asian realities (and were shaped in turn by them) will be the touchstone for examining the Cold War in Asia. We will examine the following topics: the occupation of Japan and early US global economic visions; the US and the Chinese revolution before the Korean War; the Korean War and the isolation of China; the Vietnam War and the Kennedy/Johnson years; Nixon’s global geopolitical vision and his policies towards Vietnam, China, and Japan; Carter and the meaning of human rights diplomacy in Asia; Reagan and the Asian issues involved in an intensified Cold War against Russia; George H. W. Bush and Asia’s place in “a New World Order”; and finally, the Clinton and George W. Bush years. Throughout the course, we shall examine key declassified National Security documents, interpreting their meaning and language, while carefully assessing the arguments used to justify American policy.

title: Contemporary Latin America
description: A comparative survey of Latin American social, economic, cultural, and political history from 1800 to the present.

title: Introduction to Native American and Indigenous Studies
description: This course is a general introduction to the field of Native American and Indigenous Studies (NAIS). The course will introduce students to the central questions and debates of NAIS, including but not limited to Indigenous hidden histories and oral histories; comparative indigeneities; questions of ‘discovery’ and colonialism; the politics and representations of lands, massacres, and museums; and questions of law, gender, and sexuality. It begins by asking students to consider the history of the field and weaves throughout questions about the complicated and contested terrain of the term Indigeneity. It ends with discussions about decolonizing research and Indigenous survivance and futures, thus preparing students to consider theories and methodologies they will encounter in more advanced courses for the NAIS minor. By the end of the semester, students will have gained both historical and ethnographic perspectives on how NAIS and other forms of representation help us to know and reproduce ourselves and ‘Others’; the different questions of historical trauma and survival that affect Indigenous communities today and how institutions continue to hold a significant role in constructing, controlling and circulating Indigenous cultural heritage and representations of the past. The course begins by recognizing and locating the history and continued presence of Native American Lenape people here in Mannahatta. It then uses this as a point of departure reaching beyond Native North America to the histories, politics, and experiences of Indigenous populations in an international and hemispheric context.

sections.notes: History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced U.S. OR Non-west and Pre-1800s

title: Topics:
description: Topics and prerequisites vary by semester. The last decade has seen a resurgence of issues related to Constitutional law where political parties, social movements, and interest groups routinely invoke the U.S. Constitution in debates that touch on the most urgent and divisive current affairs. Such topics include birthright citizenship for non-citizens’ children; women’s right to cross state lines seeking reproductive rights under state law; states’ assertion of powers to refuse to assist federal deportation of immigrants; and presidential assertion of powers to override Congress’ statutes by firing civil servants and re-programming federal funds. All of these contentious fights have roots deep in American Constitutional History. This Topics course will provide an overview of those historical roots through fourteen lectures, followed by discussion. These presentations will cover topics that explore the origins and development of key constitutional concepts such as birthright citizenship, federalism, and presidential powers. The course will use critical historical moments such as: the battles over interstate mobility of enslaved and free Black persons in the 1850s; Lincoln’s assertion of presidential powers during the Civil War; the fight over contraception and the Comstock Acts from the 1880s through the 1960s; and the fight over equal protection, due process and scope of Presidential powers in Japanese Internment. History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: *2 credits* of U.S.

description: Eustace, Hodes, W. Johnson. Offered every year. 4 points. Main currents of American historical development from the precolonial epoch to the Civil War. title: Modern Europe
description: A survey of Europe from 1789 to the present. Investigates the political, social, economic, and cultural developments that shaped and continue to shape the modern age. Topics include Europe and the French Revolution; the rise of the nation-state, 1848-1914; the impact of totalitarian ideologies on 20th-century Europe, and Europe today.

title: Workshop: Cultural History and Everyday Technology in Early Modern China
description: This research seminar explores daily life and technology in early modern China (1500-1900), a period of major change marked by commercial growth, urban expansion, and new consumer culture. As a research workshop, students develop historical research skills by analyzing primary sources and creating original projects that contribute to understanding this pivotal period in global history.

sections.topic: Democracy, Authoritarianism in Germany and France
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Democracy and Authoritarianism in Germany and France, 1848-1940: "The European revolutions of 1848 produced elements of democracy in both Germany and France. In both countries, however, democracy quickly gave way to forms of authoritarianism, first under Napoleon III in France and then under Otto von Bismarck in Germany. France established a new democratic republic in the 1870s, while Germany developed liberal institutions under the auspices of an authoritarian state. In the late 19th century, France's democratic republic undermined many of its core values by conquering an extensive overseas empire, and German colonialism was at least as repressive as its French counterpart. After its defeat in World War I, Germany developed a democratic republic, but its democratic institutions enabled the anti-democratic Nazi party to win power and abolish democracy. In France, fascist-style movements attempted to undermine its democratic regime, which ultimately collapsed during the German invasion of 1940. In this course we will examine how ordinary citizens and leaders fostered the survival or failure of democracy. And while highlighting the specific characteristics of each country, we will also emphasize their mutual influences, such as the circulation of democratic ideas during the revolution of 1848 or, conversely, the development of a French “fascism” influenced by German Nazism. Through our readings and discussions, we will encourage critical comparison of Germany and France and reflection on the fragility and resilience of democratic institutions." History Major Requirements Fulfilled by this course: Advanced Workshop and European

title: Mediev Church: Religious Hist of Crisis & Creativ
description: Wielding nearly unlimited authority over the lives - and the after-life – of millions of Europeans, the Catholic Church was by far the most important political, as well as cultural, power of the Middle Ages. The only global institution of this era, the Church was at the same time able to nourish strong local roots: its cardinals and popes came from all over the continent and dealt with international politics at the highest level, while priests and friars brought home to the people a faith tied to the neighborhood church and confraternity, and personified by a saint’s shrine and relics.Through a combination of lectures, students’ presentations, films and site visits, this course will explore selected aspects of the Medieval Church’s history: its often rocky relations with the other supreme power of the time, the Holy Roman Empire; the rise of monasticism and its different versions; the spread of heretical movements and their repression by the Inquisition; sainthood, and how “heavenly” women and men could serve to articulate very earthly ideologies on state, society, gender roles.

description: This course presents an overview of the political, social, and cultural history of Italy from roughly 1300 to 1600. title: A History of London
description: This course examines the growth and importance of London from the Roman invasion of 43 AD to the present day. Students will learn about London’s changing economic and political role, and will understand how London grew to dominate the commerce, industry and culture of England. They will find out how London became the biggest city the world had ever known, and how it coped (or failed to cope) with the social and environmental problems created by its enormous size. The classroom sessions will be divided between a lecture and a class discussion. From week two onwards the class will begin with a discussion of the topic or period covered in the previous week‚s lecture, in which students will be expected to use knowledge and ideas gathered from lectures and from their weekly reading. There will also be four walking tours of parts of London which relate to the period we are studying at a particular time.
