title: Adler Conservatory Transfer Track
description: Overall mission/training philosophy of the studio: The Stella Adler Studio of Acting does not endeavor to create a wax-museum of the teachings of Stella Adler, but rather to create curricula dedicated to the spirit of Stella Adler, based on the insight that growth as an actor and growth as a human being are synonymous. From this emerges our mission to create an environment that nurtures theater artists and audiences so that they value humanity, their own and others, as their first priority, while bringing art and education to the community. What is crucial to this mission is the fact that it favors the collective impacts of theater and education over mere careerism. We do not oppose our students pursuing and attaining successful careers in or out of the theater. Whatever their path, we hope our students will carry with them the consciousness of humanity that is so central to the spirit of Stella Adler. How this specific semester of training fits into the larger arc of the studio's training curriculum: As we look at the excellent acting techniques that the 20th century brought to us to help us grapple with the actors' dilemma, to become another human being, the techniques of Stella Adler are both unique and powerful. Awareness Without Judgement gives Tisch undergraduate acting students, who weren't placed at the Stella Adler Studio of Acting, for the first time ever the opportunity, within their undergraduate training, to immerse themselves in these techniques. The course includes Adler's Foundation Technique, which roots the actor in place, action, given circumstances, expansive use of the imagination. Character class, which offers an approach to character through the portal of archetypes, costumes, study of paintings and periods. Stella's famous Script Interpretation class which takes a deep dive into texts focusing on the playwright, the playwright's big ideas, the big ideas that animate the play, the social situation the play emerges from and that the play addresses. Scene Study will be the class where all of this work will come together. What makes these pillars of the techniques of Stella Adler so unique and powerful is Stella Adler's unabashed cry for depth of heart and mind and size of soul. Stella Adler sought to nurture the empowered actor. She wanted actors to see themselves as co-creative members of creative act of play, film or television production. "Your talent is in your choice." For Stella Adler the goal of training was never merely the actors ability to get work but rather the actors ability to become an ever evolving human being for the sake of making themselves a worthy vessel for the big ideas great plays contain. "Growth as an actor and growth as a human being are synonymous." Actors who take this 14 week journey will be strengthened thereby not only as actors but also as artists and as human beings. --

title: Classical Studio I
description: By Audition. Access Code Required. Advanced Training. The Classical Studio is a production-oriented ensemble concentrating on Shakespeare. Each semester a complete play is presented, focusing on the interaction of actor and text. This requires six weeks of evening and weekend rehearsals, followed by a week of performances. This is in addition to a full class schedule which includes Acting, Voice & Speech, Alexander Technique, Movement, and Stage Combat. Additionally, in the spring semester, we remount the fall play in repertory with the spring play, followed by our annual Word Orgy, a celebration of word and song that brings the year to a close. Acting classes focus on the intensive development and presentation of monologues, soliloquies, and scenes. The goal of the studio is to create THOUGHT IN ACTION: the presentation of classical texts in an immediate and forceful present. The Studio embraces traditional, experimental, and emerging techniques, while building upon a basic emotional reality.

title: Stonestreet Film/TV I
description: 1st Semester Stonestreet. Advanced Studio open to all Drama Majors. Call (212) 229-0020 for orientation. The Stonestreet Screen Acting Workshop offers a professional environment in which to continue and broaden training, adapt theater skills and embrace the art of film acting and directing, and experience the film and television mediums, from the audition phase through to the production and post-production phases, completing their first or early professional work before they graduate. Students experience the unique challenges of acting on sets for all size screens, from three camera set-ups and the big screen arena to the iPod, by continuing to build on and surmount their previous training by playing challenging and varied roles in original films, sit-coms, dramatic series, and PSAs. Students learn to embrace both naturalism and character work that is both believable and interesting on camera and work on a variety of material from original unproduced film & tv material to film classics as well as adaptations of modern classic and classical material. Stonestreet's multi-tiered audition class allows students to become practiced, professional auditioners while making industry contacts with agents and casting directors on a weekly basis for the entire semester. All student work is recorded, editors help students compile actor reels after Stonestreet I or during Stonestreet II and final projects are showcased on Stonestreet's movie website www.stonestreetmovies.com.

title: Stonestreet Film/TV II
description: 2nd Semester Stonestreet. Advanced Studio. (Prerequisite: Stonestreet I) Stonestreet II includes a special collaboration with the NYU TSOA Goldberg Dept. of Dramatic Writing in our Annual Film Festival that creates feature & short screenplays, tv pilots and series, specifically for our advanced returning Stonestreet Students along with advanced coursework. Many of our shorts and features continue to be presented in film festivals & win awards, opening new doors for actors to the industry, directors, producers and writers. Students shoot professionally lit, directed and edited films of original material which can include classical adaptations as well. Participating in Stonestreet's new webseries (www.the47thfloor.com) allows students to work on detailed characters that are specifically designed for them, participate in full-blown production from the start of the semester, and have an accessible, professional way to showcase their work. Student involvement is from preproduction to production as well as from the editing process where a good deal more about acting is learned. The Stonestreet-Golberg Film Festival gives students additional performance, character and film opportunities to work on professional level projects that shot & edited are showcased in international film festivals and to the professional world via www.stonestreetmovies.com. Stonestreet Movies also serves as a cost free Actor's Reel where students can literally email a link of their work anywhere in the world in lieu of an audition or as a way of introducing themselves to potential work sources. DIRECTING, PRODUCING, WRITING: PILOT PROJECTS. Specialized programs for directing, producing, and writing are set up on an individual basis with students each semester. An interview with the program director and/or managing director is necessary.

title: Stonestreet Intro Screen Acting
description: This course is an introduction to the craft of screen acting and to the protocols of a film and television set. A highly focussed intensive developed in collaboration with faculty from Tisch Undergraduate Film and Television and the Stonestreet Screen Acting Workshop, the course provides essential working knowledge of acting and auditioning for the camera. It will embrace and build upon the theatrical training received in primary studio training while opening an actor's eyes to the differences that exist between film and theatre acting. Students will have an opportunity to experience where camera, material and technology meet actor and director so as not to be intimidated but instead be empowered to work in the medium.

This independent study examines artists whose work defies traditional categories, using transdisciplinary practice as a lens for exploring authorship, experimentation, appropriation, and artistic innovation. Through the study of influential artists working across forms and cultural contexts, students will analyze how artists challenge established conventions and expand the possibilities of their disciplines. Coursework will combine short analytical writing with creative responses, moving from individual artistic forms to transdisciplinary approaches.

title: Intro to Theatre Studies
description: Drama majors only. This course is designed to foster students? intellectual engagement with drama and theatre by introducing them to the basic terminology and methodology used in understanding plays and performances. A range of critical perspectives are applied to a variety of plays from different periods and places; additionally, a number of contexts for theatre study are introduced, including theatre history and performance studies. Through free discussion, serious analysis, and friendly debate, students actively enter into the creative life of the Department and of the rich theatre culture that surrounds us in New York City. Regular critical reading and writing assignments will be made.

This course offers students an introduction to the study of theatre and performance, both on and off stage. We will begin by identifying the different elements that make up performance across cultural contexts, including theater’s vital relation to play and ritual. Starting with three different festivals, the Mysteries of Osiris in ancient Egypt, the City Dionysia in Classical Greece, and the pilgrimage to Quyllurit'i in contemporary Peru, we will consider how roleplay, storytelling, dance, and music emerge out of festive structures that reflect specific worldviews, territories, and historical contexts. We will then explore how early theatrical treaties, including Bharata’s Natyasastra and Aristotle’s Poetics, set up ideas and programs for theatrical practice that live up to the present day. Through the work of Stuart Hall, William Shakespeare, and Aimé Césaire, we will consider how the centuries-long process of European modernity/colonialism shaped cultural imaginaries and how performance artists continue to reckon with this history. The course will then trace how the dominant form of theater in the West, characterized by “individual entertaining effects of the staging, the textual elements of plot, character (or at least dramatis personae) and a moving story predominantly told in dialogue” (Hans-Thies Lehmann) is a particular model of European bourgeois theater that emerged and institutionalized itself during the 18th century. We will consider how this historical process led to theater’s overdependence on written scripts, its categorization as a “fine art,” and its role as part of the cultural project of “modernity.” From a contemporary vantage point, we will also examine twentieth and twenty-first century films, critical texts, and performances that expand the limits of bourgeoise drama by experimenting with theater, not just as an art form, but as a social practice that continuously mediates and transforms our place in the world. Drama Majors Only

title: African American Drama
description: The study of African American dramatic traditions from early minstrelsy to turn of the century musical extravaganzas; from the Harlem Renaissance folk plays to realistic drama of the 1950s; from the militant protest drama of the 1960s to the historical and experimental works of the present. Issues of race, gender, class; of oppression and empowerment; of marginality and assimilation are explored in the works of such playwrights as Langston Hughes, Alice Childress, Lorraine Hansberry, Amiri Baraka, Adrienne Kennedy, George C. Wolfe, Ntozake Shange, August Wilson, Suzan-Lori Parks, and Anna Deavere Smith. The socio-historical context of each author is also briefly explored. (Theatre Studies B)

sections.notes: SAME AS V30.0255. Category: TOPICS or GEOGRAPHIES This course examines African American plays and musical librettos from the nineteenth century to the present, emphasizing playwrights’ artistic innovations and political strategies. Beginning with nineteenth-century melodrama and resistance to enslavement, we then enter the twentieth century to radically contrast comedies and anti-lynching plays during the early Jim Crow Era and Harlem Renaissance. We will read censored and popular plays from the Federal Theatre Project and Black Arts Movement, as well as realistic and formally innovative work produced on and off-Broadway from the 1970s-90s. Reading twenty-first century plays and librettos allows us to interrogate what aspects of African American drama are currently celebrated as literary and theatrical achievements. Additional reading will include manifestos, reviews, and scholarly essays. Students will review live performance, draft short scripts, and conduct and present original archival research. Drama Majors Only
SAME AS V30.0255. Course Title: Suzan-Lori Parks: Transgressions of Race, Gender, and History

title: Major Playwrights:
description: This course (different each time) focuses on one or two related major playwrights. Recent course offerings include Wilson, Kennedy and Parks, Williams, Beckett, Fornes, Ludlam and Theatre of the Ridiculous, and Contemporary playwrights. (Theatre Studies B)

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS V41.0652 AND V30.0254 V30.0245. Drama Majors Only - The Tony Awards honor Broadway’s best. This course surveys the award’s history from its 1947 inception to the present day. Reading, analyzing and contextualizing top honor plays and musicals is the class focus. Works covered include Tony Award Best Play winners from Arthur Miller’s The Crucible (1953) to Stephen Karam’s The Humans (2015) and Best Musical winners from Cole Porter, Bella and Samuel Spewack’s Kiss Me Kate (1949) to Michael R. Jackson’s A Strange Loop (2022). Field trips and lecture visits are also part of the course plan. Students will create final projects.

title: Feminism & Theatre
description: A study of plays by female playwrights and feminist theatre from the perspective of contemporary feminist theory. Considerations include strategies for asserting new images of women on stage, the dramatic devices employed by female playwrights, lesbian aesthetics, race, class, and the rejection of realism. Possible plays and performance texts treated include those of Maria Irene Fornes, Caryl Churchill, Ntozake Shange, Adrienne Kennedy, Susan Glaspell, Aphra Behn, Holly Hughes, Karen Finley and Suzan-Lori Parks. (THEATRE STUDIES B)

sections.notes: SAME AS V97.0623 Category: TOPICS This class will ask how feminism is relevant for theatre studies, demonstrate how feminist theory has shaped theatre production, and investigate possible points of connection in past and present moments. Within these endeavors, we will interrogate the shift between theatre and performance, between textuality and embodiment, and between theory and practice. We will focus on key issues such as the definitions of various types of feminisms—including intersectional feminism—and the current resurgence of feminist and anti-feminist sentiment. The class will dialectically engage the perils of performance for women, as well as the potential for empowerment through feminist theatre. Drama Majors Only

title: Community-Based Theatre in the US
description: A study of the contemporary interdisciplinary movement inserting theatre into educational, therapeutic, and activist contexts, as evidenced in practices such as TIE (theatre-in-education), psychodrama, and "theatre of the oppressed." Examination of the collaboration of artists and people untrained in art to create work meaningful to their cultural loci; the problematic concept of community itself, to both include and exclude, and to oversimplify identity; the recentering of the theatrical event from playwright, director, or actor to the interaction between performer and spectator.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. This course will meet in 721 Broadway, 2nd Floor, Studio #5. Category: PRAXIS Drama Majors Only Counts toward the Applied Theatre Minor This course looks at the development of site-specific performance/immersive theatre in the US and beyond with a special emphasis on projects that include activist agendas and engage communities. "Site-specific" is a term frequently associated with the visual arts but since the Happenings of the 60's and 70's, a body of work termed "site-specific performance" has evolved as highly structured works of art/performance that are designed around, for, and in response to sites. In the streets, in fields, deserts, forests, garbage dumps, abandoned buildings, on the border, aboard boats, in virtual space and outer space, this genre has unleashed the power of performance to indelibly mark our sense of locational identity and investigate the increasingly complex notions of how theatre as a form is changing in response to contemporary life. As site artists confront the matrix of social forces and overlapping communities that relate to a given site, their aesthetics, creative processes, forms and goals have shifted. How are they blurring the lines between art and activism, art and urban renewal, art and spirituality, art and real life? This course will include reading about and viewing of documentation of site work by seminal artists in this field. We will also be creating short site-specific performance studies, individually and in groups, to apply theory to practice and explore how site-based aesthetic strategies might inform and expand our artistic development. We will be exploring core inquiries into the intent of site work, the hidden histories and systems of power embedded in place/space, the nature of audience/performer relationships, the ethics involved in artist/community interactions and the ways in which site works can function as forms of activism and civic engagement. Readings include texts by Allan Kaprow, Bertie Ferdman, Maaike Bleeke, Karen Savage and Jan Cohen-Cruz, among others.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Category: PRAXIS. Drama Majors only. In this course, students will learn about the field and history of Theatre for Young Audiences (TYA) via readings, viewings, writing assignments, and hands-on practice. Students will have the opportunity to develop TYA short plays, workshop a new project with NYC Children's Theatre and Laurie Berkner, and tour their work to community sites for young audiences, applying theory to practice and exploring how TYA strategies inform and expand our artistic craft. Play is at the heart of what we do. By tapping into the boundlessly imaginative world of TYA, we learn to better access the raw vulnerability it takes to be a performer. As we study TYA play structures, we both simplify our understanding of dramatic composition while also pushing the boundaries of form. Students emerge from this course not only connected to professional TYA artists, theatres and venues, but also more in touch with the invincible joy necessary to carry us through the lifespan of a career in the arts.

title: Theatrical Genres:
description: This course (different each time) explores one or more distinctive theatrical genres such as tragedy or comedy; melodrama, satire or farce; or plays of distinctive theatrical types, such as experimental ensembles, theatre of the absurd, solo performance, documentary theatre or same-sex plays. Since theatrical genres and theatrical types come into being because playwrights respond to historical necessity by visualizing specific world views, the course presents a study of the role and function of the theatre within societies as a response to historical, psychological and spiritual forces. (Theatre Studies B)

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. This course will meet in 721 Broadway, 2nd Floor, Studio #2 Category: PRAXIS This class will take a detailed look at Augusto Boal and the impact of his body of work, known collectively as the Theatre of the Oppressed. Boal, one of the most well known theatre artists from Latin America, has influenced a wide number of areas in applied and political theatre. The class will begin by locating Boal autobiographically and through his idea of the facilitator or Joker. We will then investigate Boal in light of some of his central influences including Aristotle, Brecht, Freire and others. We will continue with hands on and theoretical investigations of the many stages of the Theatre of the Oppressed such as Image Theatre, Forum Theatre, Invisible Theatre, Rainbow of Desire, and Legislative Theatre. In the later parts of the class, we will investigate a number of case studies where Boal’s techniques have been applied in other contexts, some more successfully than others. Throughout, Boal’s idea of the spect/actor, an animated audience member who co-creates the material, will guide us philosophically and pedagogically. This means that students are fully expected to co-create the class alongside the teacher. Drama Majors Only

Course Repeatable for Credit. Category: Topics - Location: 181 Mercer, Rm. 521 Studio E - The shift into Post-Industrialism for wealthy Industrial nations - like the United States - began gradually in the late 20th century, but has escalated significantly in the last 25 years. It's an economy that moves away from manufacturing and agriculture as it becomes driven by service, information, and technology industries. So - what does it mean for something to be a “Post-Industrial” performance? Can we look at performance materials from this era and see the impact Post-Industrialism has had on our cultures, our choices, our ways of thinking, our relationships, and how we understand ourselves? We will discuss five plays written and/or set between 2000-2018, as well as other texts and media, exploring the nature of our Post-Industrial world, how it came to be, where it might be going, and the role it plays in shaping our lives in the 21st century. Drama Majors Only

sections.topic: Sorcery, Seduction, and Murder: Bad Women
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Category: TOPICS or HISTORIES Sorcery, Seduction, and Murder: Bad Women on the Pre-Modern Stage This course explores so-called “bad women” in drama before the nineteenth century. We will explore how gender constructs, law, and class shaped how past audiences saw characters like Medea, Eve, Lady Macbeth, the Witch of Endor, and others. Readings will include analysis of plays, but also social history. We will pay particular attention to primary sources, ranging from medical texts, court records, and accounts of witch trials.

meetings.room: 79 Wash Sq E (Goddard Hall) Room C14

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Catagory: TOPICS Drama Majors Only - Category: TOPICS This class focuses on the work of new American playwrights over the last 25 years. The century dawned with the cold war over and a new free-market globalism ascendent, only to be taken over rapidly by the War on Terror, multiple economic booms and busts, and the climate emergency. During this time, political movements rooted in identity politics arose within the United States, and would have a great impact on our culture and politics. Meanwhile, American playwrights were doing what they have always done: expressing the character of the age through their characters on the page. By looking at the work of many playwrights who broke out during this period, including Annie Baker, Kristoffer Diaz, Branden Jacobs Jenkins, Young Jean Lee, and Jackie Sibblies Drury, we'll ask what has the 21st century meant so far, and how has this time that we have all lived through both influenced and been transformed into dramatic art.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Course Title: Contemporary German Theater & Performance - Deconstructing, Decolonizing, and De-Choreographing the Canon For US audiences, German theater often has the reputation of being bizarre, loud, confusing, other-worldly, excessive, excessively long, filled with screaming, naked bodies covered in fluids - and in German. German theater also has been nominated as a world heritage site by UNESCO, as one of the most formally, politically, and culturally diverse art panoramas on planet Earth. And one of the most generously funded to boot: the city of Berlin alone has an annual cultural budget more than four times larger than the entire US National Endowment for the Arts. In this course, we will examine key artists, ensembles, institutions, and theoretical frameworks for making sense of, learning to love, and also critically questioning the German theater. Artists and groups under consideration include Thomas Ostermeier, Milo Rau, Yael Ronen, Marie Schleef, Vinge & Muller, Rimini Protokoll, Gob Squad, She She Pop, andcompany&Co, and others. Alongside new playwriting, performance art, and dance, we will explore pressing topics that include postmigrant theater, feminist theater, documentary theater, ""directors' theater,"" and postdramatic theater. Students will respond to the course material through their own creative interventions and explorations. For those of us steeped in Anglo-American naturalism, this course will offer a radically different perspective on what is possible at the theater. (No knowledge of the German language is required.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Category: PRAXIS What is comedy? WHY do we laugh at all? WHAT makes us laugh? How is comedy today different from yesterday; how is it the same? Combining theory with practice, this class endeavors to explore comedy both critically and in performance, embodying the comic even as we theorize about it. We will look at comedy historically, and as it manifests in various genres, as well as break it down structurally – all the while keeping an eye to the cultural influences that inform all comedy. The primary mode of exploration for this class will be stand-up. Arguably the most prevalent form of comedy of our age, stand-up offers us a window into how all comedy works, including: the importance of surprise; comedic timing; comedic structure; and comic situations and characters. In terms of content, we will address status as a location for humor; the importance of the body in comedy; and cultural taboos. In addition to working on our stand up routines, each class will have a critical component, and class discussions will serve to deepen our evolving routines. Of particular interest is the examination of (and distinction between) comedy that affirms cultural norms versus comedy that subverts these norms. Drama Majors Only

sections.topic: Race and Rebellion on the Victorian Stage
sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. CATEGORY: TOPICS or HISTORIES. Drama Majors Only. Nineteenth-century British theater wrestled with issues around race, colonialism, and slavery in ways distinct from other parts of British literature, culture, and politics. Whereas the abolition movement promoted the image of enslaved people suffering oppression with saintly patience, drama explored the ethics of militant resistance to slavery and colonial rule, embodying Black rebellion again and again. This course looks at the long history of racial representation in British theater through the lens of the repertoire of the great African-American actor Ira Aldridge, who in the 1820s moved from New York City to England, where he became one of the major theatrical stars of the century. Aldridge performed in array of genres – from tragedies like Othello (ca. 1603) and Edward Young’s The Revenge (1721) to melodramas like Obi, or the Three-Fingered Jack (1830) and The Black Doctor (1847) to musical comedies and minstrel fare. Alongside Aldridge, we will read work by the first African-American playwright Victor Séjour, the memoir of the Jamaican nurse and entrepreneur Mary Seacole, and narratives by formerly enslaved people, including Mary Prince and William Wells Brown. Finally, we will look at two examples of contemporary plays that think about the legacy of Victorian theater, Lolita Chakrabarti’s Red Velvet and Brandon Jacobs Jenkin’s An Octoroon.

title: Topics in Performance Studies:
description: This course (different each time) uses key theoretical concepts of the field of performance studies to examine a diverse range of performance practices. Topics include ritual, interculturalism, tourist performances, electronic and computer performance, sports performance, erotics, burlesque, masquerade and animality. (THEATRE STUDIES B)

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Category: PRAXIS and TOPICS. Location: 181 Mercer St. Room 521 Studio E - This course examines the mechanics of choice-making in games as a strategy for storytelling, world-building, and making meaning through action-based art. We will study artists and companies whose works center gaming and interactivity, and explore the breadth of how this kind of dramaturgical strategy can manifest in performance. We will also play and analyze a selection of games in different media and experiment with adapting their dramaturgies into interactive performance scores. The class is structured as a combination of a performance studies class, a dramaturgy class, a gaming group, a rehearsal studio, and an embodied research laboratory. You will not be required to purchase games or gaming equipment in order to participate. Drama Majors Only

Course Repeatable for Credit. Category: PRAXIS or TOPICS. “Art is not a mirror that reflects reality, but a hammer with which to shape it.” — Bertolt Brecht. In this course, we will examine the history of performance, dance, poetry, music, visual art, and film to uncover groundbreaking acts of artistic rebellion and discover how they shattered norms, influenced their contemporaries, and changed the way we understand art today. Students will explore theories and practices from a wide range of global traditions and respond through short essays as well as artistic projects in the form of performance, photography, music, and video. Course materials include works by Maya Deren, Kazuo Ohno, Nina Simone, and Alejandro Jodorowsky, among others. Drawing from new technologies as modes of philosophical expression, students will propose their own manifestos to challenge contemporary customs, redefine what it means to be an artist, and shape new realities within their communities.

title: Theatre in New York: Practicum
description: The course introduces students to the great variety of theatrical activity going on in the City, in order to recognize the vast number of theoretical issues and practical questions it raises, and to develop serious intellectual and critical vocabulary for responding to it. We attend performances having prepared by reading the play or related theoretical material. We follow each show with an in-depth class discussion of the major issues raised by the performance.

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Category: PRAXIS This course, taught by theatremaker and producer James Clements, introduces students to the diverse range of theatrical programming in New York City, aiming to unpack and demystify the industry's ecosystem and situate the current season within it. We will attend weekly productions throughout the semester On, Off and Off-Off Broadway, supported by readings, rigorous in-class discussion and interviews with guest speakers, to place each piece we see within the artistic and producorial infrastructure of the field. Over the course of the semester, students will strengthen their analytical, intellectual and critical toolkits for viewing and discussing theatre. PLEASE NOTE: Students are REQUIRED to attend weekly professional theatrical performances on WEDNESDAY evenings beginning at 7:00pm. There is a $425 ticket fee attached to this course for attending live performances. Drama Majors Only.

title: Perf Art Practicum:
description: An exploration of the methodology for making the personal presentational. Using storytelling, automatic writing, and the facts and fictions of one's own life each student creates material for a solo performance piece. (Theatre Studies B)

sections.notes: Category: PRAXIS (Offered On-Line Only) All students must hold Reading Day for class meetings and events. What are the differences between telling one’s story as a memoir and trying to tell it through an “adaptation” or reworking of an earlier source? Does fiction allow us to escape revealing our most private histories or ultimately produce a more intimate self-portrait than the recitation of the facts of one’s life? A 1544 image of a horse and a bewitched stable groom by Hans Baldung has been called one of Baldung’s most profoundly autobiographical works, a self-portrait. Yet in addition to the fact that its subject matter bears no relation to the historical details of Baldung’s actual life, the picture is an “adaptation” of a series of images by his teacher Albrecht Dürer. In what sense can it be autobiographical? In this class we will experiment with different methods of writing about our own lives and approach the production of “autobiography” in at least two opposite ways. Writers will be asked to write both in explicitly autobiographical ways, beginning with moments of their own lives, and they will be asked to experiment with “adapting” sources which might produce narratives which speak to these autobiographical moments. For this purpose, the class will draw on a variety of different kinds of “sources” drawn from paintings, classical myth and the bible among others. The goal is to give each writer a series of different lenses through which to dramatize moments of personal importance. A dancer or ex-dancer might imagine their life through the paintings of Degas’ exhausted ballerinas. Alternatively, a writer seeking distance from a difficult personal moment might write a pseudo-autobiography or an autobiography of someone else like The Autobiography of Alice B. Toklas written not by Alice B. Toklas but by Gertrude Stein. This is a writing-intensive course which counts for PRAXIS credit. Although most of the writing will be the kind described above, there will be one long or two short papers. Students needing TOPICS credit (or other kinds of credit) may petition for it, and their requests will be reviewed on a case-by-case basis. A successful petition for credit outside the praxis rubric will be based on a proposal for an essay project appropriate to a different rubric. Students interested in art-history, for instance, might produce substantial essay work on a given artist. Students interested in autobiography as a genre might propose essays on the conventions of autobiography itself. This class requires a Zoom interview for permission of the instructor. Interviews will begin the weekend of October 24th and continue until the class is filled. Interested students should email Professor Levine at LL17@nyu.edu providing their graduation date, advisor’s name, and studio as well as any questions they have. All students must hold open the day and evening of Friday Dec 15 Reading day. All classes will be held on Zoom. Drama Majors Only

title: Theories of Acting and Directing
description: Most systems of actor training have been developed by a director with a specific vision of theatre and a particular idea about its place in the world. For example, the director, actor, and acting teacher Konstantin Stanislavsky believed that theatre is "the art of reflecting life," so he developed a method of physical actions to bridge the gap between fiction and reality. Director Anne Bogart feels she lives in a mediated world: for her theatre is a way of making unmediated connections between people, and she has developed a practice of actor training that teaches actors to make immediate and unmediated connections with each other and with the audience. Kavalam Narayana Panikkar, working after India's Independence, used theatre as a means to decolonize his culture. Augusto Boal used theatre as a rehearsal for social change. These directors have developed specific systems of actor training which express particular philosophies about theatre and its relationship to the world – and reflect the political and social world they live in. Thus, methods of actor training are tied to the practical, philosophical, and political goals of the people who created them. In this course we will examine some of the most influential twentieth-century methods of actor training created by directors, and ask ourselves how these methods of theatrical creation reflect and shape the work and the world. By the end of this course you will be familiar with the work of many of the most influential twentieth century directors and their rehearsal practices, with most of the major theories of actor training, and with a number of important conceptual frameworks for making theatre. The goal of this course is to put your own training into historical, political, social, and cultural context.This is a theory course: most of the time we will be reading about, looking at, and analyzing the work of these directors. However, in most cases I will give you practical exercises and assignments so you gain an in-body understanding of the theories and practices under discussion.

title: Theatre and Therapy
description: This course explores the healing and therapeutic aspects of theatre and drama using drama therapy. Beginning with a study of play in child development, we will explore the three types of play - practice play, symbolic play, and games with rules - and examine their purposes in child development. We will then examine the four major techniques in drama therapy and their relationships to play and performance. We will study the Five Phase Model (Emunah), Developmental Transformations (Johnson), Rose Method (Landy), and Psychodrama (Moreno). The course will be theoretical, experiential, and technical. Students will have the opportunity to participate in each method of drama therapy, as well as lead drama therapy training sessions. (THEATRE STUDIES B)

sections.notes: Category: PRAXIS Drama therapy is defined as the intentional use of dramatic processes in order to facilitate change, healing, and growth. In this course, we will learn what drama therapy is, from a theoretical and experiential point of view. Drama therapy is an active form of psychotherapy, experiential in essence, and therefore in order to understand drama therapy and how it can help others, we must experience it. In addition, each class will consist of a theoretical presentation on the drama therapy method that we experience. This course will meet at 721 Broadway, 2nd Floor, Studio #5. Drama Majors Only.

title: Directing Practicum
description: This class introduces students to fundamental directing tools: principles of stage composition and visual story telling, action based script analysis, basic directing theory, applied Viewpoints and theatrical conceptualization. Through weekly composition and scene exercises students learn to create communicative stage imagery, physicalize dramatic action and articulate sub-textual behavior. Class work includes written analysis and production concept papers. Readings include writings of Brecht, Erving Goffman, Stanislavski, Grotowski, Bogart and Francis Hodges. (THEATRE STUDIES B)

sections.notes: Catagory: PRAXIS Students are introduced to skills and concepts that are fundamental to the art of stage directing, as well as other performance platforms. These include script analysis and production research (from given circumstances, dramatic action, character and “ideas” through to interpretation and production concept), theatrical composition (staging and visual storytelling), crafting (how to go from analysis to concrete, active and specific stage reality), and communicating with actors. These skills and concepts are applicable to a wide range of production aesthetics and performance forms. They will be applied to creating and directing devised work and scenes from major playwrights, which students will select. Students will create and/or show work in almost every class. Much, but not all, of the class work will be created inside a basic Stanislavskian framework of learning to clearly and dynamically physicalize the dramatic action. Readings from Grotowski, Richards and Hodges on “action” will be studied and applied to scene work. Students will be introduced to fundamental aspects of Stanislavski’s Active Analysis. A very close reading of Chekhov’s Three Sisters will be used to model a way of reading a play as a director, focusing on the relationship between given circumstances and the characters actions, intentions and emotional points of view and how those may suggest themes and overall ideas in the play. Social theories of Erving Goffman will be studied and applied to the creation of original theater pieces in order to expand the student's understanding of the potential communicative power of sub-textual behavior. In conjunction with learning how to use secondary research and critical essays to prepare production concepts, students will read theoretical writings of Bertolt Brecht and apply them to the creation of original work that introduces them to the use of multiple tracks inside a performance, the use of meta-theatrical “frames”, ways to create critical distance, ways to illuminate the influence of socio/political context on characters behavior, ways to use dramaturgical research to support interpretations of the text and ways to creatively reveal unconscious bias embedded in dramatic material. An analysis of a production of Drums on the Dam by Helene Cixous will be used to provide examples of how dramaturgical research in conjunction with practical skills from post dramatic theater can support a director’s directorial concept and influence choices in design, character’s actions, emotional points of view and intentions. There will be two major writing assignments. These focus on play analysis, production concept and research. The students will select the plays they choose to analyze There will also be several one-page basic analysis assignments. Each class will begin with a physical warm up and improvisational movement exercises to help students anchor composition concepts in their bodies. These exercises are from many sources including aspects of Viewpoint theory primarily: Space, Shape, Time and Kinetics. Students should wear comfortable clothing. This course will meet in 721 Broadway, 2nd Floor, Studio #2. Drama Majors Only

title: Producing: Artistic Entrepreneurship
description: This course outlines a framework through which to make artistic creation a reality. It focuses on the necessary steps to successfully found a company, enter work in a festival and produce self-created performance in a professional context. Issues explored include articulating a mission, the options for different producing models, choosing collaborators, developing a strategic plan, basic fund raising, marketing and managing the legal, financial and regulatory issues essential for start up enterprises in a theatrical environment. (Theatre Studies B)

title: Immersive, Participatory, Site-Based and Multi-Sensory Theater
description: Immersive, interactive, site-based, and multi-sensory productions have become very popular genres of theatre. Why? What do these genres do? What makes them interesting and powerful? This praxis seminar invites students to investigate immersive, interactive, and site-based performance by experiencing it live, by examining the theoretical ideas and historical contexts at play, and by learning the techniques and tools of immersive and interactive theatre so they can create their own work for their own purposes, which include entertainment, theatre for social change, drama therapy, and numerous other possible applications.

sections.notes: Prerequisite: THEA-UT 500 Category: PRAXIS Immersive, interactive, site-based, and multi-sensory productions have become very popular genres of theatre. Why? What do these genres do? What makes them interesting and powerful? This praxis seminar invites students to investigate immersive, interactive, and site-based performance by experiencing it live, by examining the theoretical ideas and historical contexts at play, and by learning the techniques and tools of immersive and interactive theatre so they can create their own work for their own purposes, which include entertainment, theatre for social change, drama therapy, and numerous other possible applications. Most proscenium theatre uses only two of the senses, sight and sound, to communicate. Not only is this difficult for those with visual or auditory issues, it is a waste of the other senses, which are vital modes of communication (babies put everything in their mouths because they apprehend the world through taste). Multi-sensory experiential productions challenge the performer/spectator relationships and aesthetic goals of proscenium theatre. They also follow Maria Montessori‘s teachings and the discoveries of anthropologist Stuart Brown in that they engage participants in various forms of multi-sensory play for more robust learning and emotional development. These works offer us new ways of engaging with the world and each other, and many of them consciously try to create theatre that is more accessible to participants who are -- in the case of Teatro Ciego, whose work we experience during the course -- blind (their productions all take place in the dark, focusing the audience’s attention on what can be smelled and felt on the skin as well as heard), or in the case of several other examples, not neurotypical. While multi-sensory theatre is not “more” accessible – Teatro Ciego’s productions are ideal for the blind but not for the hearing impaired -- they are differently accessible, and they focus attention on accessibility as a negotiable topic. Multi-sensorial experiential theatre invites previously marginalized people to the theatre, allowing us all to learn new modes of being and interacting. In fact, multi-sensory experiential theatre does not just accommodate marginalized people, it caters to them. In this course we will read excerpts of articles and books by the leading practitioners and theorists in the field, including: Experiential Performance (eds Bartley and Lewis), Immersive Theatres: Intimacy and Immediacy in Contemporary Performance (Machon), Immersive Theatre: Engaging The Audience (Machamer), Reframing Immersive Theatre: The Politics and Pragmatics of Participatory Performance (Frieze), Creating Worlds, How To Make Immersive Theatre (Warren), Beyond Immersive Theatre: Aesethetics, Politics, and Productive Participation (Alston), Theatre in the Dark (Alston), Interactive Acting (Wirth), Staging Spectators (Kolesch), Off-Site (Ferdman), Audience Participation (White), and articles in TDR, Performance Research, and HowlRound. Drama Majors Only

title: Theatre Management:
description: Leading and Managing Theatre in a Global Context. This course explores central themes and challenges in the leadership and management of theatre organizations in the 20th and 21st century from a global perspective. The course places a special emphasis on understanding the shifts and changes that are currently transforming the field. Students will address issues of leadership and service in producing and managing theatre and identify the skills and attributes required to facilitate the ongoing vitality of theatre making. The course will feature prominent guest lecturers who helm consequential and path-finding companies here in New York city. Projects will include primary research and presentations based on the examination of global practice models.

title: Studies in Shakespeare:
description: Focussed each time by genre (comedies, tragedies, romances, histories), or by theme or topic (theatricality, gender, race, politics, religion, etc.), this course explores the works of Shakespeare as text and performance - on stage or on film. Various critical methodologies, including biographical and cultural analysis, are used to reveal the continuing vitality of these plays and their relevance to the theatre of our time. (THEATRE STUDIES C)

sections.notes: Course Title: Law & Shakespeare; How can key works by William Shakespeare help introduce us both to the history of law in the Anglo-American and Roman civil-law traditions and to current theories about law and political power? Beginning with legal history and comic drama, our seminar will compare common law and equity in England as rival systems that place competing versions of the public good (inheritance as common wealth, and commonwealth as state power) above particular interests. Then, through a range of tragedies and late tragicomedies, we will consider different versions of ""political theology"" in the Renaissance, that is, the application of religious categories of thought to the juridico-political sphere of law and government. The historical placement of the sovereign both inside and outside human law was already a theoretical issue in Shakespeare's drama. We will read a selection of Shakespeare's works along with a critical article or two each week. The plays include The Comedy of Errors, The Merchant of Venice, Measure for Measure, King Lear, Hamlet, and Coriolanus. Theorists and critics include Giorgio Agamben, Lorna Hutson, Braden Cormack, and Julia Reinhard Lupton. A presentation, term papers, and in-class essays will make up the grade along with informed and lively class participation.

title: Realism & Naturalism
description: This course will examine the primarily 19th century European movement toward Realism and Naturalism that remains a major influence in today's theater, shaping both dramatic practice and audience expectation. The question of how to define these sometimes synonymous and often divergent terms will be tackled head-on, leading to a recognition that neither can be separated from each other or from the larger historical and theoretical context from which they arose. We will look at the relationship of Realism and Naturalism to the philosophical climate of the 1800s (Hegel, Darwin, Marx, Freud), to other theatrical movements (Romanticism, Symbolism, Expressionism and Aestheticism), to contemporaneous dramatic and literary forms (melodrama, the well-made play, the novel, photography), and to concrete historical trends (the rise of nation states, changing sex roles and family structures). The course focuses on the plays of the major European dramatists who defined the movement (Zola, Ibsen, Strindberg, Chekhov, Shaw), and tentatively traces its transformation in early to middle 20th century American drama. The inevitable question as to whether "the real" and "the natural" can ever be truly represented will be faced, but not at the expense of failing to ask what may or may not be gained from the attempt. (Theatre Studies C)

sections.notes: SAME AS V30.0113 H99.2817. Category: HISTORIES or GEOGRAPHIES The paired terms Realism and Naturalism, sometimes synonymous but often divergent, represent a mainly 19th-century European movement that still shapes dramatic practice and audience expectation. We will look at the movement's relationship to the philosophical climate of the time, to other theatrical movements (such as Romanticism and Symbolism), to contemporaneous genres and forms (melodrama, the well-made play, the novel) and to historical trends (the nation state, sex and gender roles, family structures). The course focuses on the chief European dramatists who defined the movement (Zola, Ibsen, Strindberg, Chekhov) as well as the contributions of writers such as Laura Kieler, Victoria Benedictsson, Lou Salomé, and Elizabeth Robins. The influence of the movement on 20th-century U.S. playwrights, including O'Neill, Hellman, and Hansberry, is examined, along with critical challenges to its core assumptions. Drama majors only.

title: Thea in Ancient Greece
description: This course will investigate ancient Greek theatre in its historical and theatrical context. We will cover a broad range of classical drama, paying special attention to current scholarship and debates in the field. Students will develop a comprehensive knowledge of Athenian drama, with an in-depth focus on ancient culture and stagecraft. Through a wide variety of readings, we will address topics such as textual interpretation, postcoloniality, gender, and cultural theory in fifth-century BCE Athens. Since ancient drama has been consistently appropriated by performers in subsequent periods, we will also look at the methodologies and contexts of versions from antiquity to the current season. (Theatre Studies C)

title: History of Acting
description: The history of acting introduces the student to the major actors and acting styles of both the comic and tragic stages from the late 16th to early 20th centuries. Debates over the actor?s craft have breached the controversies of their day, exploring the meaning of the sublime, the human capacity for sentiment, the functioning of the human body, the make up of the nation, even the nature of race. This class charts the evolution of these debates in Europe and the U.S. and asks why actors and acting have inspired invectives, paeans, and riots.

title: History of Directing
description: Working semi-chronologically through the late 19th and 20th centuries, we will examine how the director emerged as the seminal force to be reckoned with in the theatre. We will read historical texts and examine visual research as well as dramatic texts and the critical response to the work. In each case we will consider the relationship of the director to the "text," to actor training, to the ensemble and collaboration, and to the design and technology. How did the director address the community he/she sought to engage? Students will also deliver oral presentations and formally lead discussions examining a contemporary director's theory and practice. In addition, we will conduct in-class experiential exercises exploring various directorial approaches. (THEATRE STUDIES C)

sections.notes: Category: HISTORIES We will work semi-chronologically from the late 19th to the early 21st century, examining how the “director” emerged as a seminal force in the experimental theater. We will read historic manifestos, critical responses, and examine visual research. At the same time we may read contemporary case studies to explore how current directors work collaboratively to overturn theatrical conventions. We will consider the relationship of the director to the “text,” (written, physical, visual, aural), to actor training, to the ensemble and collaboration, and to design and technology. How do directors address the community they seek to engage? Students will deliver oral presentations and lead discussions examining a theater/performance artist’s theory and practice. In addition, we will conduct in-class experiential exercises invoked in various directorial approaches. Drama Majors only.

title: Theatrical Genres:
description: This course (different each time) explores one or more distinctive theatrical genres such as tragedy or comedy; melodrama, satire or farce; or plays of distinctive theatrical types, such as experimental ensembles, theatre of the absurd. Since theatrical genres and theatrical types come into being because playwrights respond to historical necessity by visualizing specific world views, the course presents a study of the role and function of the theatre within societies as a response to historical, psychological and spiritual forces. (Theatre Studies C)

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. CATEGORY: TOPICS or HISTORIES. Drama Majors Only. This junior seminar will focus on the theory and practice of tragedy through three case studies: Sophocles, Shakespeare, and Arthur Miller. Theoretical readings will include Aristotle, Poetics; A. C. Bradley, Shakespearean Tragedy; Hegel, Lectures on Aesthetics; Nietzsche, The Birth of Tragedy; and Raymond Williams, Modern Tragedy. Students will conduct research into contemporary scholarship about tragedy with the goal of producing a journal-article-length research essay at the end of the term. The goal of the Junior Seminar is to prepare students for the independent work required by the Senior Seminar.

Course Repeatable for Credit. Category: TOPICS or HISTORIES. This course will explore the history and theories of comedy and humor from antiquity to the present day. What makes us laugh and why? What are some cultural differences in humor perception? Is comedy a conservative or politically progressive theatrical genre? Which material is appropriate for comedy, and which is not? We will trace the development of a range of comic theories, paying attention to comedy’s connections to philosophy, politics, economics, and other arts. Primary texts might include plays by Aristophanes, Annie Baker, Samuel Beckett, Aphra Behn, Anton Chekhov, Branden Jacobs-Jenkins, Young Jean Lee, Martin McDonaugh, Molière, William Shakespeare, Phoebe Waller-Bridge, and Oscar Wilde. We will also read critical texts by Aristotle, Bakhtin, Bergson, Cavell, Freud, Hutcheon, Plato, and many others. Drama Majors Only.

title: Interartistic Genres:
description: This course (different each time) explores the history and semiotics of one of several hybrid genres, such as dance drama, film adaptations of plays, or multimedia works. Recent topics include: Art History for Theatre-Makers, and Opera.. (Theatre Studies C)

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. Category: HISTORIES or GEOGRAPHIES. Many of Shakespeare’s plays focus on the plight of an alien or cultural “other:” the Jew, the witch, the woman. These plays often seem to articulate a skepticism about a culture’s scapegoating practices which brings them to the brink of critique before they draw back to ratify the very practices they’ve just anatomized. “Hath not a Jew eyes?” asks Shylock. But he is made not only to convert at the end of the play but to say “I am content” about the conversion. Similarly, Kate says “I see a woman may be made a fool/If she had not a spirit to resist” when Petruchio shows up in rags like a rude groom to their wedding. But by the end of the play Kate has advised women to put their hands beneath their husband’s feet. What is the precise logic of “othering” which animates these texts? Do these plays offer alternatives to the misogyny and prejudice they often seem to embody? Looking at Shakespeare against a background of historical texts about witchcraft this course will seek to grapple with such questions. Probable texts will combine some of the following: Shakespeare’s The Taming of the Shrew, Troilus and Cressida, The Merchant of Venice, The Winter’s Tale the anonymous Newes from Scotland and The Notorious Doctor Lambe (pamphlets which describe witch trials) as well as analogues and responses to Shakespeare’s plays (The Taming of A Shrew, The Tamer Tamed) This is a writing-intensive course. It presupposes no knowledge of Shakespeare or special expertise but it presumes a willingness to set aside time to work in detail on Shakespeare’s plays. Recommended for students interested in concentrating in Shakespeare, students in or hoping to join The Classical Studio and students considering RADA. Admission to this course is by zoom interview. Intersted students should contact Professor Levine at lauraellenlevine@outlook.com providing their graduation date, studio and advisor as well as any questions they have. All classes on ON-LINE via ZOOM Drama Majors Only

title: Theatre in Asia:
description: This course (different each time) examines different traditions, innovations, representations, and locations of Asian Theatre. The influence of major aesthetic texts such as the Natyashastra and the Kadensho are studied in relationship to specific forms of theatre such as Kagura, Bugaku, Noh, Bunraku, Kabuki, Shingeki, Jingxi, Geju, Zaju, Kathakali, Kathak, Odissi, Chau, Manipuri, Krishnattam, Kutiyattam, Raslila, and P'ansori. The dramatization of religious beliefs, myths, and legends is examined in a contemporary context. Different focuses include Japanese theatre, traditional Asian performances on contemporary stages, religion and drama in Southeast Asia, and traditions of India. (Theatre Studies C)

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS V30.0294. Category: GEOGRAPHIES or HISTORIES This course is an in depth look at the performing arts of Japan. Over the course of the semester, students will trace the evolution of Japanese performance from ritual, to early forms like bugaku, gigaku, and saragaku, to the emergence of the Classical Theaters of noh, kabuki, and bunraku. Students will consider how these forms continue to endure and adapt today, as well as explore new theatrical styles that emerged throughout the 20th century, like shingeki, shinpa, and shōgekijō. Special attention will be paid to examples of women's performance, for example the Takarazuka Theater. Students will explore readings on Japanese history and culture, as well as acting theory from Zeami to Suzuki. Students will encounter examples of Classical to Contemporary dramatic literature, including plays by contemporary authors like Okada, Sakate, and Ichihara. Students will view performance videos, documentaries, and participate in performance exercises. We will also consider examples of Japanese American performance in the United States. Drama Majors Only

Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS V30.0294. Category: GEOGRAPHIES or TOPICS or HISTORIES In this course we will use the Sanskrit aesthetic theory of rasa to shed light on the extraordinary range of practices, dramaturgical structures, and modes of spectatorship embodied in contemporary South Asian performance. We will focus mainly on performance in India and the questions raised about tradition, modernity/alternative modernities, national identity, gender, sexuality, postcolonialism, interculturalism, and globalization. Units will be devoted to: kutiyattam, theyyattam, mudiyettu, chhau, ramlila, nineteenth century theatre in Bombay and Calcutta (now Mumbai and Kolkata), the Indian People’s Theatre Association (IPTA), the theatre of roots movement (Girish Karnad, Kavalam Narayana Panikkar, and Ratan Thiyam), street theatre (Janam, Sharma, and Mangai), English-language theatre (Dattani, Padmanabhan), Dalit theatre (Datta Bhagat), adaptations of Western classics (Antigone), the work of directors who identify as women (Kapur, Allana, Chaudhuri), and performances of self in everyday life (hijra and “loitering”). Drama Majors Only

Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS V77.0747 & V30.0747 Category: GEOGRAPHIES This class will examine recent trends in contemporary Arab theatre and film, contextualizing them within a broader history of Arab performance. Particular attention will be given to how experimental theatre practitioners have addressed issues of human rights and various forms of state control within their art. It is interesting to note how the major preoccupation in modern Arabic drama with the contemporary social and political Arab scene frequently broadens to reflect a universal appeal. The writers’ prime commitment lies in bringing out the absurdities, the cruelty, the wanton tyranny, the duplicity that assail Arab life but also represent an everlasting problem in human life in general. Strategies addressed will include: - The use of parable to talk truth to power - The incorporation of populist entertainment forms that directly engage the audience. - The use of familiar tales to explore new political realities. Also, the course will examine shared themes such as: Gender oppression, human rights abuses, the tension between heritage and modernity. In our discussions we will focus on how the plays we read relate to our own lives. To what extent do you connect to the characters in the plays and how these plays inspire you both as an actor and individual. How do you relate to the plays as a statement on Arab culture and society and as a statement on your different cultures and societies. Sometimes it becomes easier to look at oneself through the lens of another culture. As such I hope this class becomes a cross-cultural sphere experience. Schedule of plays and films to be discussed in class will include plays and films from Egypt, Syria, Palestine, Lebanon, Tunisia, Algeria, and Morocco. Drama Majors Only

title: Pre-Conquest & Colonial Theatre of Latin America
description: This course provides an overview of the role of ritual, theatre and performance in Latin America from the precolonial to the colonial period. It will look at the changing role of ritual in the region, from the qhapaq hucha of the Incas to the autos-de-fe of colonial Spanish America. With the advent of Spanish imperialism we will explore how theatre was deployed as part of a larger project of evangelization and colonization. The latter part of the course will examine theatre culture in colonial Latin America through dramatic texts by Sor Juana Ines de la Cruz, Juan Ruiz de Alarcon and others. Central to our discussion will be the relationship between ritual and theatre, performance and power, and the emergence of a baroque culture in the Americas.

sections.notes: Category: Geographies / Histories. This course provides a survey of the role of ritual, theatre, and performance in Latin America / Abya Yala starting from the 3rd century preconquest Classic Maya period to the viceroyalties of Peru and New Spain in the late 17th century. We will begin by looking at the central role of performance in Maya, Inca, and Mexica social life before Spanish colonization, from the Inti Raymi of the Tahuantinsuyo to the Mexica’s New Fire Ceremony. We will consider anthropological and historical approaches to the study of performance to understand not just what happened but also how performance history is conceptualized and constructed. With the arrival of Spanish imperialism, we will analyze how theatre and ceremony were deployed as part of a political project of dispossession, evangelization, and colonization. Performances during this phase include viceregal entries, the Inquisition's autos de fé, as well as fiestas that begin to syncretize Spanish and indigenous cultural forms. The latter part of the course will examine baroque theatre, ritual, and ceremony in colonial Mexico and Peru through historical accounts and the work of playwrights such as Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz. The class will also incorporate films by Paula Heredia, Salvador Carrasco, Heidi Brandenburg, and Mathew Orzel, among others, which explore different themes present in the readings. Central to our discussions will be the relationship between power and performance, knowledge and embodiment, continuity and transformation, and the legacy of coloniality in the Americas. Drama Majors Only

title: Honors Seminar:
description: The Honors Seminar in Theatre Studies focusses on a different topic in dramatic literature, theatre history, or performance studies each semester. The seminar offers intense and rigorous academic study with an emphasis on critical thinking and research skills. A substantial amount of critical writing is required, as is an oral presentation. Students apply for consideration, and a limited number are accepted. (THEATRE STUDIES C)

sections.notes: Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS THEA-UT.0700, THEA-UT 0715 & THEA-UT 0732. In this course, we will explore the dramatic representations and performances of love and intimacy in the age of capital. The rise of capitalism engendered many new ideas about romantic love: from the bourgeois custom of marrying for love to the bohemian experiment of free love. Theatre was at the center of these debates and transformations. Beginning with modern drama and continuing onto contemporary performance, we will look at how artists imagine, encourage, and challenge their audiences’ attitudes toward love in the context of shifting socio-economic factors. The coeval development of neoclassical economics and sexology in the late nineteenth century made explicit that economic questions are intertwined with erotic desires. This entanglement persists to this day. Primary texts include Hedda Gabler, Miss Julie, Three Sisters, Spring Awakening, An Ideal Husband, Yerma, Pride and Prejudice, The Awful Truth, Fool for Love, Hadestown, The Tinder Swindler, and Bridgerton. We will also read critical texts by Adorno, Cavell, Freud, Engels, Luhmann, Marx, Simmel, and many others. Find Application Instructions here: https://tisch.nyu.edu/drama/about/theatre-studies-honors.html

Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS THEA-UT.0700, THEA-UT 0715 & THEA-UT 0732. Female murderers are portrayed as unnatural, manlike, willful, passionate, sexually crazed, and plotting among other things. They disrupt legal, social, and political ideas about gender, relationships with children, parents, love, and violence. Plays about women who kill forge connections between a distant or near past and the present. British suffragists, for example, used Medea’s ‘women of Corinth’ speech as a rallying cry for the delimited legal rights of women. But who are women who kill really? What is the relationship between fictional and nonfictional female murders? What are the economic and legal circumstances of women at the time of the murders? Are there recurring reasons for who, how, and why do women kill? Are there common plot structures, characters, and theatrical styles? In this Seminar, we will study the portrayal of women who kill in the contexts of the historical moment of the authorship, the circumstances in which the protagonists find themselves, and the motives that inform their murders. We will read plays and articles by legal scholars, scholars of feminism, and theatre scholars as well as watch films featuring women murders. Medea, Agamemnon, Song of Death, Yerma, Blood Relations, Trifles, Machinal, Kokoro (True Heart), Tea, My Sister in This House, and The Maids. Students in the course must purchase specific physical copies of the plays and bring them to class. No open laptops, Ipads, or phones. Find Application Instructions here: https://tisch.nyu.edu/drama/about/theatre-studies-honors.html

Course Repeatable for Credit. SAME AS THEA-UT.0700, THEA-UT 0715 & THEA-UT 0732. The phrase “American Dream” was first used by author James Truslow Adams in his 1931 book The Epic of America. Adams dreamed that all Americans would be able to achieve “the fullest stature of which they are innately capable,” regardless of the circumstances of their birth. This course includes a multi-ethnic and international roster of playwrights and composers who explore the highs and lows of the American Dream, including mid-20th century writers and composers like Edward Albee, Arthur Miller, and Stephen Sondheim. Also included are contemporary first-and second-generation immigrant perspectives from Nilo Cruz, Ayad Akhtar, Lin-Manuel Miranda, and Mfoniso Udofia; the intimate kitchen-table play cycles of Richard Nelson and Lucy Thurber; feminist perspectives from Suzan-Lori Parks, Dominique Morriseau, Lorraine Hansberry, and Heidi Schreck; and UK and European playwrights tackling questions of American identity like Lucy Prebble (Enron) and Stefano Massini (The Lehman Trilogy). By examining a wide range of plays and musicals about the American Dream from the mid-20th century to the present, students will study how the American Dream has shaped the creative imagination of a broad group of theater artists. Find application guidelines here: https://tisch.nyu.edu/drama/about/theatre-studies-honors.html

title: Honors Thesis
description: The honors thesis is a substantial piece of original research and critical writing. To write a Thesis, a student must have completed two Honors Seminars with grades of B or better in both, and must also have successfully proposed a thesis proposal to her/his perspective faculty mentor.
